\section*{Actual curvature phases, continuous histories and their remaining spectral defects}

This construction uses the original finite physical vacua, Hamiltonians, time parameter and spatial coordinates. The working curvature observable is \(C_{f,j}^{de}=a_j\sum_{p:de}f(x_{p,j})(2-W_p)\), with precisely this coefficient. Its phase is bounded even though its absolute moments have no proved uniform bound. The completed \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/yang-mills-interacting-workbench/blob/213bdaa7d5f2583ef938651ac6d882cc194db0e3/yang-mills/continuations/20261011-central-signs-shrinking-window/ACTUAL_LOW_ENERGY_MAPS.md}{LEM proof} remains unchanged. The new \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/yang-mills-interacting-workbench/blob/213bdaa7d5f2583ef938651ac6d882cc194db0e3/yang-mills/continuations/20261011-central-signs-shrinking-window/LOCAL_CURVATURE_BUDGET.md}{LC1–LC42 proof}, read in full, provides actual local moments, including every crossing face and the actual inside kinetic energy. Those moments suffice for an enlarged cyclic representation and continuous phase histories without a uniform gradient supremum.

The reversible argument is proved below with its full drift and constants. For comparison, Grothaus, Kondratiev, Lytvynov and Röckner, \href{https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0211323}{original author source math/0211323}, Section 6.1, theorem labelled pr777 and equation eq1605, also use a reversed martingale and random bracket moments to prove tightness. Their configuration space, Gibbs assumptions and scaling are not substituted here. The intact downloaded source and exact reading coverage are retained. Existing disk literature indexes were queried first. A routing hit is not treated as source evidence.

\subsection*{1. Original objects and the checked local moment input}

For \(j\ge2\) and fixed \(\kappa_*>0\), retain
\[
\begin{gathered}
L_j=j^4,\quad m_j=2j^4,\quad n_j=2j^4+1,\quad
a_j=(100j)^{-1},\quad g_j^2=\kappa_*/(200j),\quad
b_j=(2g_j^2a_j)^{-1}=10000j^2/\kappa_*,\quad s_j=\kappa_*/j,\\
N_j=3m_jn_j^2,\quad M_j=3m_j^2n_j,\quad
H_j=\kappa_*K_j+b_j\sum_{p\in\mathcal P_j}(2-W_p),\\
K_j=-\sum_{e,\alpha}X_{e,\alpha}^2,\quad
T_\alpha=-i\sigma_\alpha/2,\quad
H_j\psi_j=E_j\psi_j,\quad\psi_j>0,\quad\|\psi_j\|=1,\quad
A_j=H_j-E_j,\quad d\mu_j=\psi_j^2dU_j .
\end{gathered}\tag{CP1}
\]
The original configuration manifold is \(\mathrm{SU}(2)^{E_j}\) with probability Haar and the radius-two edge metric. Every original vertex, including boundary vertices, acts in the physical gauge constraint. Explicitly \(W_{(z;d,e)}=\operatorname{Tr}[U_d(z)U_e(z+e_d)U_d(z+e_e)^{-1}U_e(z)^{-1}]\), and \(D_p=2-W_p\in[0,4]\). The scalar \(2b_jM_j\) and full vacuum energy remain in (CP1). The positive ground state is physical, its eigenspace is one-dimensional, and the exact original ground-state form is
\[
q_j(\psi_jh)=\|A_j^{1/2}\psi_jh\|^2
 =\kappa_*\mu_j\Gamma(h),\qquad
\Gamma(h)=\sum_{e,\alpha}|X_{e,\alpha}h|^2 .
\tag{CP2}
\]
Expand \(K_j(\psi_jh)\), substitute (CP1) and integrate against probability Haar to prove this identity, with the potential and scalar cancelling by the full eigen-equation. A second ground vector has constant ratio to \(\psi_j\), by (CP2) and connectedness. This also proves the equality of full and physical ground energies used in the local comparison.

For \(f\in C_c(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)\), choose a physical cube \(\prod_d[c_d,c_d+R]\) containing its support. Use exactly the LC patch
\[
v_{d,j}=L_j+\lfloor(c_d-o_d)/a_j\rfloor-1,\quad
q_j^{\rm side}=\lceil R/a_j\rceil+3,\quad
Q_j=v_j+\{0,\ldots,q_j^{\rm side}\}^3 .
\tag{CP3}
\]
The superscript distinguishes its side count from the form \(q_j\). For sufficiently large \(j\) it is strictly interior. Its lower corner is between \(c_d-2a_j\) and \(c_d-a_j\), and its upper corner exceeds \(c_d+R+a_j\), so every face whose center meets the support is inside. Put \(q=q_j^{\rm side}\). The original patch counts and full budget are
\[
\begin{gathered}
N_Q=3q(q+1)^2,\quad M_Q=3q^2(q+1),\quad
C_Q=12q(q+1),\quad W_Q=\sum_{p\subset Q}D_p,\\
\Lambda_j=\min\{2M_Q,6g_j^2\sqrt{N_QM_Q}\}+2C_Q,\quad
\rho_j=4g_j^2,\quad
\mu_jH_{\rm in}\le b_j\Lambda_j,\\
\mu_jW_Q^k\le\min\{(4M_Q)^k,U_{k,j}\},\quad
U_{0,j}=1,\ U_{1,j}=\Lambda_j,\quad
U_{k+1,j}=\Lambda_jU_{k,j}+\rho_j^2k^2U_{k-1,j}.
\end{gathered}\tag{CP4}
\]
Here \(H_{\rm in}=\kappa_*K_Q+b_jW_Q\); its kinetic part has not been discarded. To check the LC input, partition all original edges into those with both endpoints in \(Q\) and the complement. Every mixed face has one inside and three outside edges: two inside edges would put all four square vertices in the Cartesian patch. Each of six sides supplies \(2q(q+1)\) mixed faces. The outside positive ground vector is invariant under each restricted original vertex action. Its open three-edge path across a mixed face has expectation zero by the central gauge element \(-I\) at one endpoint. Thus the tensor trial pays exactly \(2b_jC_Q\), with the original outside energy retained on both sides. The inside product trial \(Z_t^{-N_Q/2}\prod_e\exp[t\,\operatorname{Tr}U_e/2]\) has energy at most \(3\kappa_*N_Qt/8+6b_jM_Q/t\). Its optimized value is \(3\sqrt{N_QM_Q}/a_j\); the constant trial has energy \(2b_jM_Q\). The same outside spectral lower bound in the actual vacuum proves the budget in (CP4).

The derivative calculation retains every incidence and gives \(\Gamma(W_Q)\le16W_Q\). The form inequality \(H_j-E_{\rm out}\ge b_jW_Q\), applied to \((W_Q+\epsilon)^{k/2}\psi_j\), consequently gives
\(b_j\mu W_Q^{k+1}\le b_j\Lambda_j\mu W_Q^k+4\kappa_*k^2\mu W_Q^{k-1}\).
The limit \(\epsilon\downarrow0\) uses the bound four for the derivative term at \(k=1\), and boundedness on the finite compact space for \(k\ge2\). Since \(4\kappa_*/b_j=16(g_j^2)^2=\rho_j^2\), induction proves (CP4), including its exact coefficient.

The eventual branch and the constants needed here are
\[
\begin{gathered}
\Lambda_j=18g_j^2[q(q+1)]^{3/2}+24q(q+1),\qquad
a_j^2\Lambda_j\longrightarrow
\mathcal L_R:=9\kappa_*R^3+24R^2,\\
a_j^2\rho_j\longrightarrow0,\qquad
U_{p,j}/\Lambda_j^p\longrightarrow1
\quad(p\ \hbox{fixed}),\qquad
U_{p,j}\le(\Lambda_j+p\rho_j)^p .
\end{gathered}\tag{CP5}
\]
These follow directly from \(a_jq\to R\), \(g_j^2=\kappa_*a_j/2\), and the finite recurrence. For the last inequality, insert the preceding majorants into its two terms and bound
\(\Lambda_j(\Lambda_j+p\rho_j)+p^2\rho_j^2\le(\Lambda_j+p\rho_j)^2\).
The next asserted majorant is larger. The \(24R^2\) contribution is the full crossing surface cost.

\subsection*{2. Curvature phases and all their actual gradient moments}

For one orientation \(de\), keep the original physical face centers and observables
\[
\begin{gathered}
x_{p,j}=o+a_j(z-L_j\mathbf1+(e_d+e_e)/2),\quad
C_{f,j}^{de}=a_j\sum_{p:de}f(x_{p,j})D_p,\quad
B_{\theta,f,j}^{de}=\exp(i\theta C_{f,j}^{de}),\\
c_{f,j}^{de}=\mu_jC_{f,j}^{de},\qquad
\widehat B_{\theta,f,j}^{de}
 =e^{-i\theta c_{f,j}^{de}} B_{\theta,f,j}^{de}.
\end{gathered}\tag{CP6}
\]
The last line is a separate explicit centering factor, not a changed definition of \(C_{f,j}^{de}\). Every \(C\) is a real smooth gauge-invariant function of the link variables even when the fixed spatial test is only continuous: its sampled coefficients are constants in those variables. In the following displays write \(F=\|f\|_\infty\) and suppress \(de\) only in the notation.

For each incident edge, \(\sum_\alpha|X_{e,\alpha}D_p|^2=D_p-D_p^2/4\). The complete derivative sum and its bound are
\[
\begin{aligned}
X_{e,\alpha}C_{f,j}
 &=a_j\sum_{\substack{p:de\\e\in\partial p}}f(x_{p,j})X_{e,\alpha}D_p,\\
\Gamma(C_{f,j})
 &\le a_j^2\sum_e r_e^{de}
       \sum_{\substack{p:de\\e\in\partial p}}
             |f(x_{p,j})|^2(D_p-D_p^2/4)
 \le8a_j^2F^2W_Q .
\end{aligned}\tag{CP7}
\]
Here \(r_e^{de}\le2\) is the actual orientation incidence; each face has four edges. Thus every cross term and boundary incidence occurs before Cauchy–Schwarz. For every integer \(p\ge1\),
\[
\begin{gathered}
\mu_j[\Gamma(C_{f,j})^p]\le
G_{p,f,j}:=(8a_j^2F^2)^p
                   \min\{(4M_Q)^p,U_{p,j}\},\\
\sup_{j\ge j_0}G_{p,f,j}<\infty,\qquad
\limsup_j\mu_j[\Gamma(C_{f,j})^p]\le
\mathcal G_f^p,\quad
\mathcal G_f:=8F^2\mathcal L_R,\\
q_j(B_{\theta,f,j}\psi_j)
=\kappa_*\theta^2\mu_j\Gamma(C_{f,j})
\le\kappa_*\theta^2G_{1,f,j}.
\end{gathered}\tag{CP8}
\]
The form identity is exact, since \(XB=i\theta B\,XC\). The centered phase has the same energy and gradient moments. A finite initial segment before the patch is interior has finite constants at each original volume and does not affect the ultraproduct or asymptotic assertions.

The corresponding absolute curvature bounds remain
\[
|C_{f,j}|\le a_jF W_Q,\qquad
|c_{f,j}|\le a_jF\Lambda_j,\qquad
\mu_j|C_{f,j}|^p\le (a_jF)^p\min\{(4M_Q)^p,U_{p,j}\}.
\tag{CP9}
\]
Their available \(p\)-th roots grow like \(F\mathcal L_R/a_j\). They do not prove a finite limiting mean, variance, or continuous parameter field. The gradient supremum bound from (CP7) is \(32a_j^2F^2M_Q\), which grows like \(a_j^{-1}\). It is not the estimate used for histories below.

The exact phase algebra, with no removed scalar, is
\[
B_{\theta,f,j}B_{\eta,g,j}=e^{i(\theta C_{f,j}+\eta C_{g,j})},
\quad B_{\theta,f,j}^*=B_{-\theta,f,j},\quad
B_{\theta,f,j}B_{\eta,f,j}=B_{\theta+\eta,f,j},\quad
\|B_{\theta,f,j}\|=1 .
\tag{CP10}
\]
Curvatures add exactly within an orientation; products across orientations retain the sum of their full curvatures. For \(D_j=\sum_{\ell=1}^r\theta_\ell C_{f_\ell,j}^{d_\ell e_\ell}\), the gradient is the sum of those full gradients. Minkowski in \(L^{2p}(\mu_j;\mathbb C^{3N_j})\) gives
\[
\big(\mu_j\Gamma(D_j)^p\big)^{1/(2p)}
\le\sum_{\ell=1}^r|\theta_\ell|G_{p,f_\ell,j}^{1/(2p)}.
\tag{CP11}
\]
The exact square contains every diagonal term and
\(2\sum_{\ell<k}\theta_\ell\theta_k\Gamma(C_{f_\ell,j},C_{f_k,j})\);
none is assumed to vanish. The same formulas keep the scalar product of all centering factors.

\subsection*{3. Ground-state Markov words and an enlarged actual cyclic space}

The full ground-state generator, including the vacuum drift, is
\[
\mathscr L_j=\kappa_*\sum_{e,\alpha}X_{e,\alpha}^2
 +2\kappa_*\sum_{e,\alpha}(X_{e,\alpha}\log\psi_j)X_{e,\alpha},
\qquad
S_j(t)h=\psi_j^{-1}e^{-tA_j}(\psi_jh).
\tag{CP12}
\]
Expanding the full Hamiltonian leaves the scalar bracket
\(\kappa_*\psi_j^{-1}\sum X^2\psi_j-b_j\sum_pD_p+E_j\), which is zero by (CP1), rather than being omitted. Integration by parts gives
\(\mu_j(\bar h\mathscr L_jk)=-\kappa_*\mu_j\Gamma(\bar h,k)\).
The smooth diffusion fields \(\sqrt{2\kappa_*}X_{e,\alpha}\) and the displayed smooth drift on a compact manifold give a global continuous diffusion at every \(j\). Its parabolic equation identifies its transition semigroup with \(S_j\). Consequently
\[
S_j(t)1=1,\quad S_j(t)\ge0,\quad
\|S_j(t)h\|_\infty\le\|h\|_\infty,\quad
\mu_jS_j(t)h=\mu_jh,\quad
q_j(e^{-tA_j}v)\le q_j(v).
\tag{CP13}
\]
No bound for the drift uniform in \(j\) is used.

Let \(b,h\) be original bounded smooth multipliers. The complete product form is
\[
\begin{aligned}
q_j(b\psi_jh)=\kappa_*\mu_j\big[
 |b|^2\Gamma(h)+|h|^2\Gamma(b)
 +2\operatorname{Re}(\bar b h\,\nabla b\cdot\overline{\nabla h})\big],\\
\sqrt{q_j(b\psi_jh)}
\le\|b\|_\infty\sqrt{q_j(\psi_jh)}
       +\|h\|_\infty\sqrt{q_j(b\psi_j)}.
\end{aligned}\tag{CP14}
\]
The second line is Minkowski applied to the two differentiated terms in the first, and implies the two-factor bound with coefficient two in each square. Smoothness holds for every finite word; extension to bounded form-domain ratios follows by approximation and the displayed bound.

Take any fixed finite word built from curvature phases, their adjoints, fixed-length original Wilson polynomials, and nonnegative physical semigroup times. Its vector is
\[
w_j=b_{0,j}e^{-t_1A_j}b_{1,j}\cdots e^{-t_kA_j}b_{k,j}\psi_j
 =\psi_jh_j,\qquad t_r\ge0 .
\tag{CP15}
\]
Starting at \(H=1,E=0\), propagate from the right to the left by
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
\hbox{operation}&\hbox{ratio bound }H&\hbox{form-root bound }E\\\hline
e^{-tA_j}&H&E\\
b_j&H\|b_j\|_\infty&
          \|b_j\|_\infty E+H\sqrt{q_j(b_j\psi_j)} .
\end{array}\tag{CP16}
\]
The old value of \(H\) is used in the last entry. Equations (CP8), (CP13) and (CP14) prove by induction that \(\|h_j\|_\infty\le H\) and \(\sqrt{q_j(w_j)}\le E\), uniformly in \(j\) for each word. Original fixed-length Wilson factors have their established uniform form bounds; growing physical loops are not inserted under that designation. For phase-only words \(H=1\) and \(E\le\sum_r\sqrt{q_j(b_{r,j}\psi_j)}\). Finite linear combinations keep the sum of their respective bounds.

Use the same actual ultraproduct, continuous projection \(P\), escape projection \(Q\), semigroup \(T(t)=e^{-tA}P\), and unit vacuum \(\Omega=[\psi_j]\) as ASL. Spectral calculus gives
\[
\|(I-e^{-tA_j})w_j\|^2\le tq_j(w_j)\le tE^2.
\tag{CP17}
\]
Every word class therefore belongs to \(P\mathcal H_{\mathcal U}\). Define \(\mathcal K\) to be the closure of all such word classes for the chosen phase family and chosen original Wilson family. It contains their vacuum cyclic space and is reducing for each bounded multiplier and its adjoint, because multiplication adds a factor to a word. It is also reducing for \(T(t)\): positive-time multiplication by \(T(t)\) adds a time factor, and \(T(t)\) is self-adjoint. Thus
\[
\mathcal K\subset P\mathcal H_{\mathcal U},\quad
T(t)|_{\mathcal K}=e^{-tA_{\mathcal K}},\quad
A_{\mathcal K}\ge0,\quad A_{\mathcal K}\Omega=0,\quad
B_{\theta,f}|_{\mathcal K}\ \hbox{is unitary}.
\tag{CP18}
\]
The products and adjoints are the exact original ones in (CP10). In particular, for this space the ASL product defect vanishes:
\[
PBQCP|_{\mathcal K}=0,\qquad
(PBP)(PCP)|_{\mathcal K}=PBCP|_{\mathcal K}.
\tag{CP19}
\]
Here \(B,C\) denote any two selected bounded multiplier operators. We have not proved that a curvature phase reduces \(P\) on the entire ultraproduct; the global ASL defect remains defined there.

Zero-time collisions in every finite correlation now hold exactly by (CP10), (CP17) and density. Inserting a time interval \(h\) in a word changes its acted-on vector by at most \(\sqrt h E\), times the norms of the preceding factors. Therefore all its original nonnegative-time correlations are continuous, including coincident times, and converge to the displayed represented products along the same ultrafilter. Vacuum norm, stationarity, time reflection and reflection positivity are retained. Explicitly, for a positive-time cylinder \(F\), its conditional expectation at time zero is a Markov word ratio \(g_{F,j}\), and
\[
\mathbb E_j[\overline{F\circ\vartheta}\,G]
=\mu_j(\overline{g_{F,j}}g_{G,j})
=\langle\psi_jg_{F,j},\psi_jg_{G,j}\rangle .
\tag{CP20}
\]
Detailed balance from (CP12) and the Markov property at zero prove the first equality, including all internal time factors. Its Gram matrix is positive at every \(j\), and its limit is the Gram matrix in \(\mathcal K\). The null quotient and completion of positive-time cylinders therefore map isometrically onto the cyclic space just constructed. No Markov property of the observed phase coordinates alone is asserted.

\subsection*{4. Reversible increments with random, moment-controlled brackets}

Run the actual diffusion (CP12) in its stationary law \(\mu_j\), writing \(U_j(t)\). Symmetry of \(S_j\) reverses its finite-dimensional kernel products, so the reversed stationary process has the same generator. Fix a real original curvature combination \(D_j\), a horizon \(T\), and retain both terms of
\[
\ell_j(r)=\kappa_*\sum X^2D_j(U_j(r))
 +2\kappa_*\sum (X\log\psi_j)(U_j(r))XD_j(U_j(r)).
\tag{CP21}
\]
Its forward and reverse martingales are
\[
\begin{gathered}
M_t=D_j(U_j(t))-D_j(U_j(0))-\int_0^t\ell_j(r)\,dr,\\
N_r=D_j(U_j(T-r))-D_j(U_j(T))-\int_0^r\ell_j(T-v)\,dv,\\
\langle M\rangle_t=2\kappa_*\int_0^t\Gamma(D_j)(U_j(r))\,dr,\quad
\langle N\rangle_r=2\kappa_*\int_0^r\Gamma(D_j)(U_j(T-v))\,dv,\\
D_j(U_j(t))-D_j(U_j(0))
 ={M_t\over2}-{N_T-N_{T-t}\over2}.
\end{gathered}\tag{CP22}
\]
The reverse process is adapted to its own reverse filtration. Subtract its defining equations at \(T\) and \(T-t\): the remaining drift is precisely \(-\int_0^t\ell_j(r)dr\), with the same sign as in the forward definition. Subtraction therefore proves the last line. There is no independence assumption and no discarded drift. At the two endpoints of an interval of length \(h\), use that interval's reversal horizon, obtaining \((M_h-N_h)/2\).

Here is the needed moment estimate with its exact constant. For a real continuous martingale \(Z_0=0\) with bracket density \(a_r\), stopping, Itô and Hölder give
\[
\begin{aligned}
F_p(t)&:=\mathbb E|Z_t|^{2p},\\
F_p'(r)&\le p(2p-1)F_p(r)^{(p-1)/p}
                      (\mathbb E a_r^p)^{1/p},\\
F_p(t)&\le\left[(2p-1)\int_0^t
                         (\mathbb E a_r^p)^{1/p}dr\right]^p .
\end{aligned}\tag{CP23}
\]
For the second line, Itô contributes \(p(2p-1)|Z|^{2p-2}a_r\). Hölder has exponents \(p/(p-1)\) and \(p\). Integrate the differential inequality for \((F_p+\epsilon)^{1/p}\), then let \(\epsilon\downarrow0\). Stopping at \(|Z|=R\) proves it first with finite moments; the bracket moment bound still applies to the stopped density, and Fatou removes the stop. The case \(p=1\) is the bracket identity. Thus no deterministic bracket bound is required.

For \(D_j=C_{f,j}\), stationarity and (CP8), followed by convexity in the last line of (CP22), give
\[
\begin{gathered}
\mathbb E_j|C_{f,j}(U_j(t))-C_{f,j}(U_j(s))|^{2p}
\le[2\kappa_*(2p-1)]^pG_{p,f,j}|t-s|^p,\\
\mathbb E_j|B_{\theta,f,j}(U_j(t))-B_{\theta,f,j}(U_j(s))|^{2p}
\le\min\{2^{2p},
|\theta|^{2p}[2\kappa_*(2p-1)]^pG_{p,f,j}|t-s|^p\}.
\end{gathered}\tag{CP24}
\]
The scalar inequality \(|e^{i\theta x}-e^{i\theta y}|\le|\theta||x-y|\) proves the second line without a component factor. The centered phase has the identical increment bound. For any finite curvature combination replace \(G_{p,f,j}\) by the complete right side of (CP11) to the power \(2p\).

In particular the real anchored variables
\[
Y_{f,j}(t)=C_{f,j}(U_j(t))-C_{f,j}(U_j(0)),\qquad Y_{f,j}(0)=0
\tag{CP25}
\]
have uniformly bounded \(2p\)-th moments and time increments on every compact time interval. This is an actual difference of the two unchanged observables. It does not declare their individual time-zero values bounded or replace them by a new initial state.

The full all-order LC input yields a further strengthening for limiting laws. For \(V_j=\Gamma(C_{f,j})\), (CP8) gives
\[
\mu_j[(V_j-\mathcal G_f)_+^p]\longrightarrow0
\quad\hbox{for each fixed integer }p\ge1 .
\tag{CP26}
\]
To prove it, on \(V_j\le\mathcal G_f+\epsilon\) the integrand is at most \(\epsilon^p\). On the complement bound it by \(V_j^{p+k}/(\mathcal G_f+\epsilon)^k\). Its limiting upper mean is at most
\(\mathcal G_f^{p+k}/(\mathcal G_f+\epsilon)^k\) by (CP8). Let \(k\to\infty\), then \(\epsilon\downarrow0\). If \(\mathcal G_f=0\), (CP8) proves it directly.

Write the martingale bracket density as at most
\(2\kappa_*\mathcal G_f+2\kappa_*(V_j-\mathcal G_f)_+\).
Its second term, multiplied by \(|M_r|^{2p-2}\) in Itô's formula, has mean tending to zero uniformly for \(r\) in a fixed compact interval: apply Hölder, (CP23)'s uniform \(2p\) moment bound and (CP26). Induction in the Itô integral now gives the sharper limiting estimates
\[
\begin{gathered}
\limsup_j\mathbb E_j|M_h|^{2p}
\le(2p-1)!!(2\kappa_*\mathcal G_f)^p h^p,\\
\limsup_j\mathbb E_j|Y_{f,j}(t)-Y_{f,j}(s)|^{2p}
\le(2p-1)!!(2\kappa_*\mathcal G_f)^p|t-s|^p .
\end{gathered}\tag{CP27}
\]
For the induction, integrate the preceding moment bound:
\(p(2p-1)\int_0^h(2p-3)!!c^pr^{p-1}dr=(2p-1)!!c^ph^p\), with \(c=2\kappa_*\mathcal G_f\). The uniform moment majorant from (CP23) permits passing limiting upper bounds inside the integral. The two reverse moments obey the same estimate, so convexity proves the second line. This improves the limiting constant; it does not assert a finite-\(j\) deterministic gradient supremum.

\subsection*{5. One specified countable family and its continuous history law}

Choose the countable real vector space \(\mathcal D_{\mathbb Q}\) of finite rational linear combinations of
\[
f_{v,r}(x)=\prod_{d=1}^3(1-|x_d-v_d|/r_d)_+,\qquad
v\in\mathbb Q^3,\quad r\in(\mathbb Q_{>0})^3 .
\tag{CP28}
\]
Each test is continuous and compactly supported. Include all three orientations and all rational \(\theta\), with their original phases (CP6). As an optional simultaneous original Wilson family, take all finite closed walks in the integer cubic graph translated by \(L_j\mathbf1\) into the finite box, their trace products and rational complex linear combinations; each fixed walk fits eventually and keeps its full original edge count. This is a concrete countable family. The previous cyclic argument also works for any enlarged family of these energy-bounded phase observables, without claiming that its uncountable path space is metrizable.

Put \(G=\mathcal D_{\mathbb Q}^{\oplus3}\) as an additive discrete countable group, and let
\[
\mathbb K=\{\chi:G\to\mathbb S^1:
 \chi(0)=1,\ \chi(g+h)=\chi(g)\chi(h)\}
 \subset(\mathbb S^1)^G .
\tag{CP29}
\]
This is a closed compact metrizable group, with the product topology. At finite \(j\) its actual random character is
\(\chi_j(t)(g)=\exp(i\sum_{de}C_{g_{de},j}^{de}(U_j(t)))\).
The use of \(G\) indexes the exact original product relations; it changes no curvature coefficient. Write \(Y_{g,j}\) for the corresponding sum of anchored variables (CP25), and
\(\mathcal Y=\{y:G\to\mathbb R:y(g+h)=y(g)+y(h)\}\), a closed subspace of \(\mathbb R^G\). The exact relation is
\[
\chi_j(t)(g)=\chi_j(0)(g)e^{iY_{g,j}(t)},\qquad
Y_{g+h,j}=Y_{g,j}+Y_{h,j},\qquad Y_{g,j}(0)=0 .
\tag{CP30}
\]

Here is a direct continuity and tightness proof, including its exponents. If a real or complex coordinate \(X_j\) satisfies
\(\mathbb E|X_j(t)-X_j(s)|^{2p}\le K_p|t-s|^p\), then on dyadic mesh \(T2^{-n}\), the probability of any adjacent increment exceeding \(R2^{-n\gamma}\) is at most
\[
K_pT^pR^{-2p}2^{-n[p-1-2p\gamma]} .
\tag{CP31}
\]
There are \(2^n\) adjacent increments; Markov's inequality proves the formula. Choose \(p>1\) and \(0<\gamma<(p-1)/(2p)\). Summing (CP31) bounds the failure probability of all dyadic increments by
\(K_pT^pR^{-2p}/(1-2^{-[p-1-2p\gamma]})\).
For paths satisfying those increments, approximate both times by successive dyadic points. The two geometric tails and at most one coarser increment give a Hölder bound with constant at most
\(2^\gamma[1+2\sum_{r\ge1}2^{-r\gamma}]R/T^\gamma\).
Each finite-\(j\) path is continuous already, so the inequality extends from dyadic to every time.

Apply this argument to every \(Y_{g,j}\) using (CP24)–(CP25), to the phases, and to any selected Wilson coordinates with their known gradient bounds. For each coordinate and each integer horizon choose thresholds with summable total failure probability. Anchored values are zero; phase values lie in the unit circle; the optional Wilson coordinates have their fixed finite range. Arzelà–Ascoli on each coordinate and time interval, followed by a diagonal extraction, proves tightness in
\[
\mathbb K\times C_0(\mathbb R,\mathcal Y),
\quad\hbox{and jointly in the chosen continuous phase/Wilson path coordinates}.
\tag{CP32}
\]
The topology is the product of compact-uniform coordinate topologies; the subscript zero fixes \(Y(0)=0\). It is Polish because \(G\) is countable and all additivity relations are closed. The finite exceptional volumes can be included individually without changing tightness.

One common subsequence realizes the same ultrafilter correlations as \(\mathcal K\). Choose a countable determining family of bounded continuous finite-coordinate functions at rational times for the tight laws in (CP32), and include all chosen rational-time word correlations and deterministic centering characters. For its first \(n\) members choose an increasing index from the common ultrafilter set where their errors from their ultralimits are less than \(1/n\). Tightness supplies weakly convergent subsubsequences. Their rational-time finite-dimensional laws agree, and these determine a continuous-path law: compact-uniform distances are suprema over rational times, so those evaluations generate its Borel sigma algebra. Thus all weak subsequential limits agree, proving convergence of the selected full subsequence.

Denote that actual law by \(\mathbb P\). Closedness of the character and additive relations and continuity of the finite-coordinate maps give, for all real times simultaneously,
\[
\boxed{\quad
\chi(t)(g)=\chi(0)(g)e^{iY_g(t)},\qquad
Y(t)\in\mathcal Y,\quad Y(0)=0 .
\quad}\tag{CP33}
\]
The equality is first simultaneous at rational times and all countably many \(g\), then extends by continuity. Its correlations are exactly the ultraproduct correlations in (CP20); hence its positive-time null quotient is the same chosen cyclic space. Stationarity, reversal, reflection positivity and all time collisions pass from the original bounded cylinder functions. The anchored process has stationary increments in the precise joint sense
\[
(\chi(r),\,Y(r+t)-Y(r))_{t\in\mathbb R}
\ \stackrel{\rm law}{=}\
(\chi(0),\,Y(t))_{t\in\mathbb R}.
\tag{CP34}
\]
This is the exact finite stationary identity passed to the tight joint limit. Independence, Gaussianity and a Markov property of the observed coordinates do not follow from it.

All exponents \(\gamma<1/2\) hold simultaneously for this countable family by taking a countable collection of \(p,\gamma\) in (CP31). There is also an explicit stronger limiting modulus. Truncated moments and (CP27) yield, with \(c_f=2\kappa_*\mathcal G_f\),
\[
\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\cosh(\lambda[Y_f(t)-Y_f(s)])
\le e^{c_f\lambda^2|t-s|/2},\qquad
\mathbb P(|Y_f(t)-Y_f(s)|>r)
\le2e^{-r^2/(2c_f|t-s|)} .
\tag{CP35}
\]
Expand cosh in its nonnegative even series and use
\((2p-1)!!/(2p)!=1/(2^pp!)\) to prove the first inequality. Since \(\cosh(\lambda x)\ge e^{\lambda|x|}/2\), exponential Markov and \(\lambda=r/(c_f|t-s|)\) prove the second. The zero-constant case is deterministic. These are bounds, not an identification of Gaussian finite-dimensional laws.

Define \(H_{\log,T}\) as the supremum of all dyadic adjacent increments divided by \(\sqrt{T(n+1)2^{-n}}\). The union bound in (CP35) gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
\mathbb P(H_{\log,T}>r)
\le {2e^{-r^2/(2c_f)}\over1-2e^{-r^2/(2c_f)}}
\quad(r^2>2c_f\log2),\\
|Y_f(t)-Y_f(s)|
\le\sqrt2\,B\,H_{\log,T}
 \sqrt{|t-s|\,[1+\log_2(T/|t-s|)]},\\
B=1+2\sum_{r\ge1}\sqrt{r+1}\,2^{-r/2}
\le {2\over(1-2^{-1/2})^2}-1,\quad 0<|t-s|\le T .
\end{gathered}\tag{CP36}
\]
For the second line choose the mesh size between \(|t-s|\) and \(2|t-s|\), and sum the two dyadic approximation tails, using \(\sqrt{n+r+1}\le\sqrt{n+1}\sqrt{r+1}\). The first line tends to zero as \(r\to\infty\), so this modulus holds almost surely. It holds simultaneously on all chosen coordinates and integer horizons. Phase relative paths inherit it through their exact exponential in (CP33).

\subsection*{6. Exact parameter-continuity defect and explicit centering}

Fix one nonzero test and orientation, and restrict its phase parameters to the specified \(\mathbb Q\). Write
\(\mathbb K_{\mathbb Q}=\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb Q,\mathbb S^1)\)
with the pointwise topology, and
\[
\iota:\mathbb R\longrightarrow\mathbb K_{\mathbb Q},\qquad
\iota(x)(q)=e^{iqx},\qquad
\mathbb K_{\rm real}=\iota(\mathbb R)
  =\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}\iota([-n,n]).
\tag{CP37}
\]
The map is continuous and injective: equality for all rational \(q\to0\) forces the two real exponents to agree. Each compact interval maps homeomorphically to a compact set in the Hausdorff group, so the image is a Borel set. A character of \(\mathbb Q\) is continuous for its inherited real topology exactly when it is \(\iota(x)\): uniform continuity from the character identity extends it uniquely to \(\mathbb R\); on a small interval choose a continuous argument in \((-\pi,\pi)\), whose additive identity forces a linear argument, and then use the character identity globally.

The commuting unitaries \(B_{q,f}|_{\mathcal K}\) have a joint spectral measure \(\mathsf E_f\) on this compact group. One direct construction is the continuous functional calculus of their unital abelian algebra: evaluation at a character respects precisely \(B_qB_r=B_{q+r}\), and the coordinate characters separate the group. Their polynomials and conjugates are dense in its continuous functions; the spectral theorem supplies the projection measure, supported on the representation's actual spectrum. Define
\[
R_f=\mathsf E_f(\mathbb K_{\rm real}),\qquad
\mathcal K_f^{\rm reg}
=\{v\in\mathcal K:\|(B_{q,f}-I)v\|\longrightarrow0
                         \text{ as }q\in\mathbb Q,\ q\to0\}.
\tag{CP38}
\]
Then \(\mathcal K_f^{\rm reg}=R_f\mathcal K\). Indeed, a spectral measure supported on (CP37) gives strong continuity by dominated convergence. Conversely \(\mathcal K_f^{\rm reg}\) is closed and reducing for the commuting unitary group. Its rational group extends strongly to a continuous real unitary group, whose self-adjoint generator gives \(B_q=e^{iqX_f}\) there. Its real spectral measure pushes forward under \(\iota\); uniqueness on the dense character polynomials makes it exactly \(\mathsf E_f\), hence concentrated on (CP37).

For completeness, the generator assertion in that argument uses only the self-adjoint spectral theorem. For a strongly continuous real unitary group \(V(t)\), the norm-bounded strong integral \(R=\int_0^\infty e^{-t}V(t)\,dt\) has
\(R+R^*=2R^*R\), by multiplying the two integrals and changing their difference variable. It is normal. Also
\((V(h)R-R)/h\to R-I\), so \(R\) and \(R^*\) are injective and their ranges are dense. On \(\operatorname{ran}R\) put \(X=i(R^{-1}-I)\). The displayed identity proves symmetry, and \(X+iI=iR^{-1}\) is onto. Since \(I-2R\) is unitary, \(X-iI=iR^{-1}(I-2R)\) is onto too. These two range conditions prove self-adjointness. Differentiation on this invariant domain gives \(V(t)=e^{itX}\). Thus no continuity of the original phase group was silently assumed in (CP38); the argument applies exactly to the defined regular subspace.

This subspace is also reducing for the actual time semigroup. The needed estimate is on bounded word ratios, not on the whole gradient supremum. Conditional expectation in the original stationary process gives
\[
\begin{gathered}\relax
[b,S_j(t)]h(U_j(0))
=\mathbb E_j[(b(U_j(0))-b(U_j(t)))h(U_j(t))\mid U_j(0)],\\
\|[B_{q,f,j},e^{-tA_j}]\psi_jh_j\|
\le |q|\,\|h_j\|_\infty
            \sqrt{2\kappa_*t\,\mu_j\Gamma(C_{f,j})},\\
\|[B_{q,f},T(t)]w\|
\le |q|H\sqrt{2\kappa_*t\mathcal G_f}
\quad\hbox{for a word ratio bounded by }H .
\end{gathered}\tag{CP39}
\]
Conditional Jensen and the \(p=1\) case of (CP24) prove the second line, and the actual ultralimit proves the third. By density and the bound \(2\|v-w\|\) for the commutator on an approximating difference, it follows that \([B_{q,f},T(t)]v\to0\) as \(q\to0\) for every \(v\in\mathcal K\). Hence \(T(t)\) preserves (CP38), and its self-adjointness makes that subspace reducing. All original multiplication operators commute with every \(B_{q,f}\), so they preserve it and its orthogonal complement as well. Consequently
\[
[R_f,T(t)]=0,\quad [R_f,B_{r,g}]=0,\quad
[R_f,W_\gamma]=0,\quad
A_{\mathcal K}R_f\Omega=0 .
\tag{CP40}
\]
Thus the parameter-continuity defect is a proved reducing space, with both its vacuum norm and dynamics retained.

Its exact vacuum weight and continuity criterion are
\[
\begin{gathered}
d_f^\theta:=\|(I-R_f)\Omega\|^2
=1-\lim_{n\to\infty}
 \langle\Omega,\mathsf E_f(\iota([-n,n]))\Omega\rangle,\\
\|(B_{q,f}-I)\Omega\|^2
=2\left[1-\operatorname{Re}\lim_{\mathcal U}
                         \mu_j e^{iqC_{f,j}}\right],\\
d_f^\theta=0
\ \Longleftrightarrow\
\lim_{q\in\mathbb Q,\ q\to0}\lim_{\mathcal U}
                         \mu_j e^{iqC_{f,j}}=1
\ \Longleftrightarrow\ R_f=I_{\mathcal K}.
\end{gathered}\tag{CP41}
\]
The first equivalence uses (CP38); the last follows from cyclicity and (CP40). The current local curvature bounds do not evaluate these quantities. In particular (CP9) is not a uniform covariance bound. The real-image spectral sets in (CP41) should not be replaced by raw amplitude tails: the real numbers \(2\pi j!\) diverge, while their characters on every fixed rational parameter are eventually one. This exact example shows the additional winding information lost by the selected rational character coordinates; it is not a proposed value of the actual curvature.

The deterministic original centering factors have the common character limit
\[
\sigma_f(q)=\lim_{\mathcal U}e^{-iqc_{f,j}},\qquad
\widehat B_{q,f}=\sigma_f(q)B_{q,f},\qquad
\widehat R_f=\mathsf E_f(\sigma_f^{-1}\mathbb K_{\rm real}).
\tag{CP42}
\]
Their product identity makes \(\sigma_f\) a character without assuming its continuity. The centered spectral measure is its explicit translation of \(\mathsf E_f\); (CP38) proves the last equality. Its commutator estimate differs only by the unit scalar \(\sigma_f(q)\), so \(\widehat R_f\) is reducing for all the same dynamics and observables. If \(\sigma_f=\iota(-c)\) for an actual real \(c\), the regular space is unchanged and its generator becomes \(X_f-cI\). Distinct cosets of \(\mathbb K_{\rm real}\) give mutually orthogonal reducing spectral projections. No convergence of the actual means has been inferred.

In contrast, every relative phase has a proved continuous real-parameter limit:
\[

The first convergence is jointly in compact \((\theta,t)\) sets: the exponential map from a compact-uniform real path to that two-variable function is continuous. \subsection*{7. Positive energy, zero energy and possible loss of first energy}

For \(v_{\theta,f}=B_{\theta,f}\Omega\in\mathcal K\) at a selected parameter, its norm is exactly one. There is no Hilbert mass escape, since (CP17) proves \(Pv_{\theta,f}=v_{\theta,f}\). Write \(Z=\mathbf1_{\{0\}}(A_{\mathcal K})\). The complete fixed-time correlation and zero-energy mass are

The first equality is the original two-time Markov identity, with the initial phase and its conjugate retained before their exact cancellation. The original finite Wilson observations retain a fully calculated shrinking-window weight under the specified auxiliary positive generator: the coefficient decays as j\textasciicircum{}(-63/4) for aC and j\textasciicircum{}(-55/4) for raw C, with a relative norm error of order j\textasciicircum{}(-4). Complete energy matrices and HP37 contrast this auxiliary spectrum with the actual quantum leading receiver, whose original first energy tends to zero. HP38–HP40 prove the exact composition-generator restriction and reflection-form comparisons, keeping the direct Euclidean interpretation distinct from analytic continuation. These comparisons do not assign the actual quantum window weight or establish the interacting no-gap endpoint.

\section*{Spatial distribution histories of the original curvature increments}

The original curvature differences admit a continuous distribution-valued subsequential limit on physical space. The result strengthens the coordinatewise history construction in CP21–CP36: its test values belong to one random spatial distribution, with explicit local negative Sobolev bounds. It keeps the original lattice coefficient, time, state and spatial positions. It does not assert that the distribution is a function, smooth, or nonzero.

The argument below uses the actual local moment theorem LC1–LC42 and the complete reversible calculation CP21–CP27. Grothaus, Kondratiev, Lytvynov and Röckner, *Scaling limit of stochastic dynamics in classical continuous systems*, original author TeX arXiv:math/0211323, Section 6.1, theorem `pr777`, equations `eq1605` and `eq95`, provide a human-source comparison for lifting martingale coordinate bounds to a negative Hilbert space. Their Gibbs hypotheses, configuration space, initial law and scaling are different. The following receiving calculation is proved on the original Yang–Mills objects.

\subsection*{1. Original spatial distributions}

For fixed \(\kappa_*>0\), keep
\[
 L_j=j^4,\quad m_j=2j^4,\quad n_j=2j^4+1,\quad
 a_j=(100j)^{-1},\quad g_j^2=\kappa_*a_j/2,
 \quad b_j=(\kappa_*a_j^2)^{-1},\quad s_j=\kappa_*/j.
 \tag{DH1}
\]
The original directed positive links carry \(U_e\in\mathrm{SU}(2)\), probability Haar and the radius-two metric with \(T_\alpha=-i\sigma_\alpha/2\). Every original vertex gauge action, including boundary vertices, is imposed in the physical space. Write
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 K_j=-\sum_{e,\alpha}X_{e,\alpha}^2,\qquad
 H_j=\kappa_*K_j+b_j\sum_p D_p,\qquad D_p=2-W_p,\\
 W_{(z;d,e)}=\operatorname{Tr}
 [U_d(z)U_e(z+e_d)U_d(z+e_e)^{-1}U_e(z)^{-1}],\\
 H_j\psi_j=E_j\psi_j,\quad \psi_j>0,\quad\|\psi_j\|=1,
 \quad d\mu_j=\psi_j^2dU,\quad A_j=H_j-E_j,\\
 x_{p,j}=o+a_j(z-L_j\mathbf1+(e_d+e_e)/2).
 \end{gathered}\tag{DH2}
\]
Here \(o\in\mathbb R^3\) is the fixed original physical origin. The scalar \(2b_jM_j\), with \(M_j=3m_j^2n_j\), remains in \(H_j\). The actual stationary reversible process \(U_j(t)\), \(t\in\mathbb R\), has generator
\[
 \mathscr L_j=\kappa_*\sum X^2+
               2\kappa_*\sum (X\log\psi_j)X.
 \tag{DH3}
\]
For each of the three orientations \(d<e\), define the finite atomic distributions
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathscr C_j^{de}(t)&=a_j\sum_{p:de}D_p(U_j(t))\delta_{x_{p,j}},\\
 \mathscr Y_j^{de}(t)&=a_j\sum_{p:de}
       [D_p(U_j(t))-D_p(U_j(0))]\delta_{x_{p,j}},\\
 \langle\mathscr C_j^{de}(t),f\rangle&=C_{f,j}^{de}(U_j(t)),
 \quad C_{f,j}^{de}=a_j\sum_{p:de}f(x_{p,j})D_p,\\
 \langle\mathscr Y_j^{de}(t),f\rangle&=Y_{f,j}^{de}(t).
 \end{aligned}\tag{DH4}
\]
No mean or scalar term has been omitted from \(\mathscr C_j\). The difference defining \(\mathscr Y_j\) cancels its two identical \(2a_j\sum f(x_{p,j})\) contributions exactly. It is anchored at zero and uses the same actual stationary law at both times.

\subsection*{2. A uniform local test bound with every factor retained}

Let \(O_n=(-n,n)^3\), \(R_n=2n\), and \(n\ge1\). For all sufficiently large \(j\), the LC patch covering \([-n,n]^3\) is strictly inside the original box. Its lower vertex in direction \(d\) is
\(L_j+\lfloor(-n-o_d)/a_j\rfloor-1\), and its side count is
\(q=\lceil R_n/a_j\rceil+3\). Retain
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 N_Q=3q(q+1)^2,\quad M_Q=3q^2(q+1),\quad C_Q=12q(q+1),\\
 \Lambda_{n,j}=\min\{2M_Q,6g_j^2\sqrt{N_QM_Q}\}+2C_Q,
 \quad\rho_j=4g_j^2=2\kappa_*a_j,\\
 U_{0,n,j}=1,\quad U_{1,n,j}=\Lambda_{n,j},\quad
 U_{p+1,n,j}=\Lambda_{n,j}U_{p,n,j}
                       +\rho_j^2p^2U_{p-1,n,j}.
 \end{gathered}\tag{DH5}
\]
LC proves \(\mu_jW_Q^p\le\min\{(4M_Q)^p,U_{p,n,j}\}\) and
\(U_{p,n,j}\le(\Lambda_{n,j}+p\rho_j)^p\), where \(W_Q=\sum_{p\subset Q}D_p\). It also retains the inside kinetic part in
\(\kappa_*\langle K_Q\rangle+b_j\mu_jW_Q\le b_j\Lambda_{n,j}\).

For one orientation and a real continuous \(f\) supported in \([-n,n]^3\), the exact face incidence calculation and the forward/reverse martingales of CP give
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \Gamma(C_{f,j}^{de})\le8a_j^2\|f\|_\infty^2W_Q,\\
 V_{p,n,j}=8a_j^2\min\{4M_Q,U_{p,n,j}^{1/p}\},\\
 \mathbb E_j|Y_{f,j}^{de}(t)-Y_{f,j}^{de}(s)|^{2p}
 \le[2\kappa_*(2p-1)V_{p,n,j}]^p
          \|f\|_\infty^{2p}|t-s|^p .
 \end{gathered}\tag{DH6}
\]
Indeed the two martingales have bracket density \(2\kappa_*\Gamma(C_f)\); Itô and Hölder give
\(\mathbb E|M_h|^{2p}\le[(2p-1)h]^{p}\mu_j[2\kappa_*\Gamma(C_f)]^p\).
The original drift in (DH3) cancels in their exact half-difference, and convexity gives (DH6), without an independence assumption or a deterministic gradient bound.

The constants are uniformly finite. To exhibit one bound, put \(a_2=1/200\) and
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 B_n=9\kappa_*(R_n+4a_2)^{3/2}(R_n+5a_2)^{3/2}
                      +24(R_n+4a_2)(R_n+5a_2),\\
 \overline V_{p,n}=8(B_n+2\kappa_*p a_2^3),\qquad
 K_{p,n}=[2\kappa_*(2p-1)\overline V_{p,n}]^p,\\
 V_{p,n,j}\le\overline V_{p,n},\qquad
 \limsup_{j\to\infty}V_{p,n,j}\le8\mathsf L_{R_n},\quad
 \mathsf L_R=9\kappa_*R^3+24R^2.
 \end{gathered}\tag{DH7}
\]
To verify the finite bound, \(q\le R_n/a_j+4\), \(q+1\le R_n/a_j+5\), and
\(a_j^2\Lambda_{n,j}\le9\kappa_*[a_jq\,a_j(q+1)]^{3/2}+24a_jq\,a_j(q+1)\).
Use the monotonicity of this displayed expression in \(a_j\), followed by
\(a_j^2p\rho_j=2\kappa_*p a_j^3\). The minimum and original counts in (DH5) are retained before this estimate. Finitely many volumes before the patch fits do not affect subsequential tightness; each has a finite deterministic gradient bound from its finite face sum.

\subsection*{3. Exact local Hilbert spaces and the distribution map}

For \(k\in\mathbb N^3\), with each \(k_d\ge1\), define
\[
 e_{k,n}(x)=n^{-3/2}\prod_{d=1}^3
       \sin\frac{\pi k_d(x_d+n)}{2n},\quad x\in O_n,
 \qquad\lambda_{k,n}=\frac{\pi^2|k|^2}{4n^2}.
 \tag{DH8}
\]
Extend \(e_{k,n}\) by zero outside \(O_n\). These extensions are continuous, their exact supremum is \(n^{-3/2}\), and they are an orthonormal basis of \(L^2(O_n)\). Orthogonality and the factor follow by integrating each sine product over an interval of length \(2n\). Completeness follows by odd reflection in each coordinate to the complete exponential Fourier basis on the corresponding torus; a function orthogonal to every sine product has every Fourier coefficient of its odd extension zero and hence has zero norm.

Define the spaces, rather than identifying them with an unspecified convention for boundary Sobolev norms:
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \mathcal H_n^s=\{f=\sum_k f_ke_{k,n}:
                  \sum_k(1+\lambda_{k,n})^s|f_k|^2<\infty\},\\
 \mathcal H_n^{-s}=\{y=(y_k):
                  \|y\|_{-s,n}^2:=\sum_k(1+\lambda_{k,n})^{-s}|y_k|^2<\infty\},\\
 S_{s,n}:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb N^3}(1+\lambda_{k,n})^{-s}<\infty
                                 \quad(s>3/2).
 \end{gathered}\tag{DH9}
\]
The pairing is \(\sum_k y_k f_k\) on real functions; complexification uses the corresponding conjugate convention. The last series converges because the shell \(\max k_d=r\) has exactly \(r^3-(r-1)^3=3r^2-3r+1\) points and \(|k|^2\ge r^2\). Its tail after \(\max k_d\le M\) obeys
\[
 \sum_{\max k_d>M}(1+\lambda_{k,n})^{-s}
 \le\left(\frac{4n^2}{\pi^2}\right)^s
       \frac{3M^{3-2s}}{2s-3},\qquad M\ge1.
 \tag{DH10}
\]
Use \(3r^2-3r+1\le3r^2\) and the integral bound for the decreasing function \(x^{2-2s}\). For \(f\in\mathcal H_n^s\), Cauchy–Schwarz gives
\(\|f\|_\infty\le n^{-3/2}S_{s,n}^{1/2}\|f\|_{s,n}\); the series converges uniformly to a continuous function vanishing on the boundary. Thus each interior point mass has norm at most \(n^{-3/2}S_{s,n}^{1/2}\) in \(\mathcal H_n^{-s}\), with its original coefficient preserved.

Every \(y\in\mathcal H_n^{-s}\) defines a distribution on \(O_n\). For \(\phi\in C_c^\infty(O_n)\), repeated integration by parts gives
\(\lambda_{k,n}^r\phi_k=\langle(-\Delta)^r\phi,e_{k,n}\rangle\), with no boundary term because the support is interior. Taking \(2r\ge s\) shows
\(\|\phi\|_{s,n}\le c_{n,s,r}\|(-\Delta)^r\phi\|_2\), where
\(c_{n,s,r}^2=\sup_{\lambda\ge3\pi^2/(4n^2)}(1+\lambda)^s/\lambda^{2r}<\infty\).
This proves continuity for the test-function topology and the exact distribution pairing. Denote this map by \(I_{n,s}:\mathcal H_n^{-s}\to\mathcal D'(O_n)\). Its kernel must be retained:
\[
 \mathcal N_{n,s}=\{y:\sum_k y_k\phi_k=0
                           \text{ for every }\phi\in C_c^\infty(O_n)\},
 \qquad \mathcal V_n^{-s}=\mathcal H_n^{-s}/\mathcal N_{n,s}.
 \tag{DH9a}
\]
The kernel is closed as an intersection of kernels of continuous linear functionals. The quotient map into distributions is injective by its exact definition. Boundary-supported Hilbert functionals can be invisible to interior tests; no injectivity of the unquotiented map is asserted. The Hilbert representatives used below are kept explicitly before this quotient.

\subsection*{4. Hilbert moment bounds and tightness}

For each orientation let \(Y_{j,n}^{de}(t)\) have coordinates
\(\langle\mathscr Y_j^{de}(t),e_{k,n}\rangle\). It is the restriction of the original finite atomic distribution, represented in (DH9), not a new random field. For \(s>3/2\), Minkowski in \(L^p\), followed by (DH6), gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E_j\|Y_{j,n}^{de}(t)-Y_{j,n}^{de}(u)\|_{-s,n}^{2p}
 &\le K_{p,n}\, n^{-3p}S_{s,n}^{p}|t-u|^p.
 \end{aligned}\tag{DH11}
\]
For finite sums, take the \(L^p\) norm of the sum of squared weighted coordinates and bound it by the sum of their \(L^p\) norms. Increase the number of coordinates and apply monotone convergence. This proves (DH11) and membership at each time directly.

The original paths are continuous in \(\mathcal H_n^{-s}\): there are finitely many point masses with fixed positions and continuous coefficients. Anchoring gives a useful maximal estimate for every integer \(p>1\):
\[
 \left(\mathbb E_j\sup_{0\le t\le T}
                         \|Y_{j,n}^{de}(t)\|_{-s,n}^{2p}\right)^{1/(2p)}
 \le\frac{K_{p,n}^{1/(2p)}n^{-3/2}S_{s,n}^{1/2}\sqrt T}
               {1-2^{-(p-1)/(2p)}}.
 \tag{DH12}
\]
At dyadic level \(r\), the \(L^{2p}\) norm of the largest adjacent increment is at most
\(K_{p,n}^{1/(2p)}n^{-3/2}S_{s,n}^{1/2}\sqrt T\,2^{-r(p-1)/(2p)}\).
This follows by bounding the maximum's \(2p\)-th power by the sum of the \(2^r\) powers. Every dyadic time can be connected to zero by at most one adjacent increment from each level; add the norms and then use continuity. Summing the geometric series proves (DH12). The same argument on negative times, or time reversal, covers \([-T,T]\), with the two halves retained if a single maximal bound is desired.

For \(\gamma<(p-1)/(2p)\), the probability that some adjacent level-\(r\) increment exceeds \(B2^{-r\gamma}\) is at most
\[
 K_{p,n}n^{-3p}S_{s,n}^{p}T^p B^{-2p}
                      2^{-r[p-1-2p\gamma]}.
 \tag{DH13}
\]
Its summable series and the same dyadic chains give a uniform probabilistic Hölder bound in \(\mathcal H_n^{-s}\), with all \(\gamma<1/2\) available by choosing \(p\) large.

If \(3/2<s_0<s\), the inclusion \(\mathcal H_n^{-s_0}\to\mathcal H_n^{-s}\) is compact. In fact on a ball of radius \(B\), its squared coordinate tail after \(\max k_d\le M\) is at most
\[
 B^2\left(1+\frac{\pi^2(M+1)^2}{4n^2}\right)^{-(s-s_0)}.
 \tag{DH14}
\]
Finite coordinate balls are compact and this tail is uniform, proving total boundedness and compact closure. Apply (DH12)–(DH13) at exponent \(s_0\). Outside a set of arbitrarily small probability the paths have bounded \(\mathcal H_n^{-s_0}\) norm and a common Hölder modulus there. Their values then lie in a compact subset of \(\mathcal H_n^{-s}\) and have a common modulus in that space. A finite time mesh and finite nets of values prove total boundedness in the uniform path norm; completeness gives compact closure. This proves tightness in
\[
 C([-T,T],\mathcal H_n^{-s}),\qquad s>3/2.
 \tag{DH15}
\]
It proves compactness, not merely boundedness of balls in the infinite-dimensional path space.

\subsection*{5. One compatible spatial distribution and all smooth tests}

Take a countable collection of exponents \(s\downarrow3/2\), all \(n,T\in\mathbb N\), and all three orientations. Enlarge the CP countable family by every \(e_{k,n}\) and by countable dense subsets of the smooth tests supported in each interior compact subcube. Retain rational linear combinations and rational phase parameters. CP's word, character and time arguments apply to this enlarged family with the same finite local constants.

The product of the tight spaces (DH15), together with CP's compact initial character space, is tight: assign each factor a compact set whose failure probability is less than \(\epsilon2^{-r}\), and take their compact product. Its factors are separable complete metric spaces. Diagonal subsequence selection on finite nets of these compact sets gives a weakly convergent subsequence of the probability laws. Include the original CP determining correlations in that selection; if a specific ultrafilter construction is used, select each successive index from the corresponding finite intersection of ultrafilter sets. This gives the same CP correlations rather than selecting a different state.

The limit restrictions agree as distributions on overlapping cubes. At finite \(j\), their pairings with each interior smooth test agree exactly by (DH4). These pairings are continuous on both Hilbert spaces, so agreement passes to the limit. First impose it on the countable dense test subsets and rational times. Distribution continuity and Hilbert path continuity extend it to every smooth compactly supported test and every real time simultaneously. The interior distributions therefore glue to one
\[
 \mathscr Y^{de}\in C(\mathbb R,\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^3)),\qquad
 \mathscr Y^{de}(0)=0,
 \quad \mathscr Y^{de}|_{O_n}=I_{n,s}Y_n^{de},\quad
 Y_n^{de}\in C(\mathbb R,\mathcal H_n^{-s})\quad(s>3/2).
 \tag{DH16}
\]
Here the distribution continuity holds even for uniform convergence on bounded test sets locally: such a set has uniformly bounded \(\mathcal H_n^s\) norm, and dual Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the uniform pairings by the \(\mathcal H_n^{-s}\) path difference. No boundary trace of a distribution is being identified; equality is on interior test functions.

The Hilbert representatives, and hence their exact quotient classes in (DH9a), are locally Hölder of every exponent \(\gamma<1/2\) in every displayed space. Use (DH13) with \(p\) sufficiently large, pass the bounds through the Hilbert weak limit using bounded truncations, and intersect the countable exponent, cube and horizon events. Inclusion from any smaller selected \(s'>3/2\) gives every \(s>s'\).

For a fixed \(\phi\in C_c^\infty(O_n)\), the Fourier series in (DH8) converges uniformly to \(\phi\). Its finite sums are compactly supported continuous tests after extension by zero. Applying (DH6) and the scalar version of (DH12) to their difference from \(\phi\) shows convergence in \(L^{2p}\) of the entire anchored path on each finite horizon, uniformly in sufficiently large \(j\). In the Hilbert limit the same sums converge to the distribution pairing. Consequently the exact receiving identity is
\[
 Y_{\phi}^{de}(t)=\langle\mathscr Y^{de}(t),\phi\rangle,
 \qquad
 \chi(t)(\phi)=\chi(0)(\phi)
       \exp\bigl(i\langle\mathscr Y^{de}(t),\phi\rangle\bigr)
 \tag{DH17}
\]
whenever the absolute character coordinate \(\phi\) is in the chosen enlarged family. The real distribution pairing itself exists for every smooth compactly supported \(\phi\). For a new test, its relative phases for all real parameters are the continuous map
\(\exp(i\theta\langle\mathscr Y^{de}(t),\phi\rangle)\), obtained by the same joint approximation. No absolute initial character for an unchosen test is invented.

\subsection*{6. What the distribution construction receives}

The original finite stationary identity passes to the distribution paths:
\[
 (\mathscr Y(r+t)-\mathscr Y(r))_{t\in\mathbb R}
       \stackrel{\rm law}{=}(\mathscr Y(t))_{t\in\mathbb R}.
 \tag{DH18}
\]
Indeed it holds on every finite collection of test values before taking the limit. Those values determine the glued distribution path law; continuity gives (DH18). The stronger determination of the actual Hilbert path laws follows from the explicit interior-cutoff recovery in \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/yang-mills-interacting-workbench/blob/main/yang-mills/continuations/20261011-central-signs-shrinking-window/DISTRIBUTION_HISTORY_REVIEW.md}{DR5–DR14}, with the ambient boundary kernel retained. Joint stationarity with the CP initial characters has the full form CP34. Independence, Gaussianity and a Markov property for \(\mathscr Y\) are not consequences of (DH18).

For any smooth test in the selected phase algebra, CP44–CP47 now become the explicit distribution correlations
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 K_{\theta,\phi}(t)=\mathbb E\exp
       (i\theta\langle\mathscr Y^{de}(t),\phi\rangle),\\
 \|(e^{-tA_{\mathcal K}}-e^{-2tA_{\mathcal K}})
                     B_{\theta,\phi}\Omega\|^2
 =K_{\theta,\phi}(2t)-2K_{\theta,\phi}(3t)+K_{\theta,\phi}(4t).
 \end{gathered}\tag{DH19}
\]
This is an exact morphism from the constructed spatial distribution histories to the physical cyclic spectral test. Its right side is positive exactly when that scalar anchored history is not almost surely identically zero, for \(\theta\ne0\), by CP45 and continuity. Its value is still to be calculated. The original shrinking windows retain CP49 and are not evaluated by tightness.

The initial phase-character regularity defect of CP38–CP42 remains unchanged. Even a regular real additive initial functional on a countable family need not be continuous in the smooth test topology; no such initial spatial distribution has been proved here. The anchored differences have acquired that continuity because their uniform local test bounds were proved. The global smooth interacting Yang–Mills state and the no-gap result therefore remain the programme goal. The next receiving calculation is the actual distribution correlation (DH19), together with control of the initial character law and the first-energy loss CP46.

\section*{Independent review and exact recovery of the spatial Hilbert representatives}

This note reviews DH1–DH19 and DH9a in DISTRIBUTION\_CURVATURE\_HISTORIES.md and proves a strengthening of its distribution map. The reviewed source retains the original Yang–Mills Hamiltonians, actual vacua, spatial positions, coefficient \(a_j\), and anchored curvature differences. None is changed here. The accepted CP1–CP50 proof remains sealed and unchanged.

\subsection*{1. Review of the existing calculation}

The following receiving calculations were read and independently checked in full.

* DH1–DH7: the original four-factor face traces, all three orientations, full drift, actual local moments and every coefficient agree with LC and CP. The uniform bound uses \(a_jq\le R_n+4a_2\), \(a_j(q+1)\le R_n+5a_2\) and \(a_j^2p\rho_j=2\kappa_*p a_j^3\). The two terms \(9\kappa_*R_n^3\) and \(24R_n^2\) are both retained. The quantities indexed by \(p\), including the recurrence defining \(U_{p,n,j}\), have integer \(p\ge1\); the maximal statements use integer \(p\ge2\).
* DH8–DH10 and DH9a: the three-dimensional sine coefficient is exactly \(n^{-3/2}\); its eigenvalue is \(\pi^2|k|^2/(4n^2)\). The shell contains \(3r^2-3r+1\) points, giving the displayed tail. The test-function map is continuous, but its ambient boundary kernel must indeed be retained.
* DH11–DH15: Minkowski is applied to the sum of squared weighted coordinates in \(L^p\), giving \(n^{-3p}S_{s,n}^p\), with no additional component factor. The maximal geometric denominator, dyadic probability exponent, compact embedding and compact path argument are correct. The finitely many initial volumes before a fixed patch fits do not affect tightness.
* DH16–DH17: agreement on countably many dense interior test sets passes through the Hilbert limits and extends to all test functions and real times. Bounded test sets have a common compact support and bounded derivatives, hence bounded \(\mathcal H_n^s\) norm. The resulting distribution paths are continuous for uniform convergence on bounded test sets locally. Smooth test Fourier sums converge in the exact Hilbert test norm and uniformly; the scalar maximal estimate identifies their original anchored limits. No unchosen absolute character is introduced.
* DH18–DH19: distribution stationarity and the full heat detector follow from the original finite identities. The heat expression is positive exactly for a nonconstant actual anchored coordinate at a selected nonzero parameter. Its value is not evaluated. The original first-energy loss, endpoint atoms and shrinking-window quantities remain unchanged.

There is no mathematical defect in these bounds or in the distribution construction. The sentence in DH18 saying that interior test values determine the Hilbert path laws requires the actual-law recovery argument below: for unrestricted elements of the ambient Hilbert space, DH9a's kernel prevents that inference. Alternatively that sentence can refer only to the glued distribution path law. The stronger statement is proved below for the actual limits.

\subsection*{2. The exact compact-embedding tail and a nonzero ambient kernel}

Use the precise spaces \(\mathcal H_n^s,\mathcal H_n^{-s}\) and map \(I_{n,s}\) defined in DH8–DH9a. If \(3/2<s_0<s\), the squared tail operator norm of the inclusion after removing all coordinates with \(\max_d k_d\le M\) is exactly
\[
\left(1+\frac{\pi^2[(M+1)^2+2]}{4n^2}\right)^{-(s-s_0)}.
\tag{DR1}
\]
Indeed a coordinate in that tail has one index at least \(M+1\) and its other two indices at least one. Therefore its eigenvalue is at least the displayed value. The ratio of its two squared norm weights is \((1+\lambda)^{-(s-s_0)}\). This gives the upper bound, and a vector supported only at \((M+1,1,1)\) attains it. DH14 is valid; (DR1) is its sharp refinement, retaining the two other minimal indices.

The kernel in DH9a is nonzero for every displayed exponent \(s>3/2\). Define
\[
z^{(\ell_2,\ell_3)}_k
=\frac{\pi k_1}{2n^{3/2}}\,
       \mathbf1_{\{k_2=\ell_2,\ k_3=\ell_3\}},
\qquad \ell_2,\ell_3\ge1.
\tag{DR2}
\]
Its squared Hilbert norm is
\[
\frac{\pi^2}{4n^3}\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}
 r^2\left(1+\frac{\pi^2[r^2+\ell_2^2+\ell_3^2]}{4n^2}\right)^{-s},
\tag{DR3}
\]
which is finite exactly when \(s>3/2\), by comparison with \(\sum r^{2-2s}\). For an interior smooth test \(\phi\), the sine series and all its differentiated series converge uniformly, because repeated integration by parts makes its coefficients decrease faster than any fixed power. Pairing (DR2) with that series gives
\[
\sum_k z^{(\ell_2,\ell_3)}_k\phi_k
=\int_{(-n,n)^2}
 \partial_{x_1}\phi(-n,x_2,x_3)\,
 n^{-1}\sin\frac{\pi\ell_2(x_2+n)}{2n}
          \sin\frac{\pi\ell_3(x_3+n)}{2n}\,dx_2dx_3
=0.
\tag{DR4}
\]
Thus \(z^{(\ell_2,\ell_3)}\in\mathcal N_{n,s}\). These nonzero vectors have disjoint coordinate supports as \((\ell_2,\ell_3)\) varies, and are mutually orthogonal in \(\mathcal H_n^{-s}\). In particular the abstract kernel is infinite-dimensional. This is a boundary normal-derivative functional, not a proposed physical-vacuum component.

\subsection*{3. Recovering every actual Hilbert coordinate from interior tests}

Fix a smooth function \(\eta:\mathbb R\to[0,1]\) equal to zero on \((-\infty,1/2]\) and one on \([1,\infty)\). Such a function can be defined explicitly: put \(h(u)=0\) for \(u\le0\), \(h(u)=e^{-1/u}\) for \(u>0\), and set
\(\eta(u)=h(u-1/2)/(h(u-1/2)+h(1-u))\).
For integers \(l\ge1\) let
\[
\begin{gathered}
\delta_{n,l}=n\,2^{-l-2},\\
\chi_{n,l}(x)=\prod_{d=1}^3
 \eta((x_d+n)/\delta_{n,l})\eta((n-x_d)/\delta_{n,l}),\\
\phi_{k,n,l}=\chi_{n,l}e_{k,n}\in C_c^\infty(O_n).
\end{gathered}\tag{DR5}
\]
The product is one whenever all six distances to faces are at least \(\delta_{n,l}\), and zero near every face. If \(1-\chi_{n,l}(x)\ne0\), at least one such distance is less than \(\delta_{n,l}\). The associated sine factor has absolute value at most \(\pi k_d\delta_{n,l}/(2n)\). Keeping the other two sine factors at their bound one gives the exact useful estimate
\[
\|e_{k,n}-\phi_{k,n,l}\|_\infty
\le \frac{\pi\,\max_d k_d}{2n^{5/2}}\,\delta_{n,l}
=\frac{\pi\,\max_d k_d}{8n^{3/2}}\,2^{-l}.
\tag{DR6}
\]
The extensions by zero are continuous, including their boundary values. They are therefore legitimate tests in DH6, regardless of the derivatives of the cutoff.

For integer \(p\ge2\), abbreviate only the displayed scalar maximal coefficient:
\[
\mathsf A_{p,n,T}
=\frac{K_{p,n}^{1/(2p)}\sqrt T}
       {1-2^{-(p-1)/(2p)}}.
\tag{DR7}
\]
Applying the scalar version of DH12 to \(e_{k,n}-\phi_{k,n,l}\), and retaining both halves of \([-T,T]\), gives
\[
\mathbb E_j\sup_{|t|\le T}
\left|Y^{de}_{e_{k,n},j}(t)-Y^{de}_{\phi_{k,n,l},j}(t)\right|^{2p}
\le 2\,\mathsf A_{p,n,T}^{\,2p}
       \left(\frac{\pi\,\max_d k_d}{8n^{3/2}}\,2^{-l}\right)^{2p}.
\tag{DR8}
\]
The factor two bounds the maximum of the two half-interval powers by their sum. The estimate holds at every sufficiently large original volume; their laws and test coefficients are unchanged.

Let \(Y_n^{de}\) be any actual Hilbert path limit constructed in DH15–DH16 along its common subsequence. The map
\[
y(\cdot)\longmapsto
\sup_{|t|\le T}|y_k(t)-\langle I_{n,s}y(t),\phi_{k,n,l}\rangle|
\]
is continuous in the uniform \(\mathcal H_n^{-s}\) path norm: both the coordinate functional and the interior test functional are continuous linear functionals on that Hilbert space. Truncate its \(2p\)-th power at a finite constant, pass expectations through the weak limit, and then increase the truncation. Equation (DR8) therefore holds for
\[
Y_{n,k}^{de}(t)
-\langle\mathscr Y^{de}(t),\phi_{k,n,l}\rangle
\tag{DR9}
\]
with exactly the same right side.

For \(p=2\), Markov's inequality at threshold \(2^{-l/2}\) bounds the probability that the supremum of (DR9) exceeds that threshold by
\[
2\,\mathsf A_{2,n,T}^{\,4}
 \left(\frac{\pi\,\max_d k_d}{8n^{3/2}}\right)^4 2^{-2l}.
\tag{DR10}
\]
The sum over \(l\) is finite. The probability of infinitely many failures is bounded by the tail sum and hence zero. Consequently, simultaneously for every \(k,n,T\), orientation and selected exponent \(s\),
\[
Y_{n,k}^{de}(t)
=\lim_{l\to\infty}
  \langle\mathscr Y^{de}(t),\phi_{k,n,l}\rangle,
\qquad\text{uniformly for }|t|\le T
\quad\text{almost surely}.
\tag{DR11}
\]
The countable intersection has probability one. Inclusion from a smaller selected exponent extends the statement to every \(s>3/2\), with the same coordinates. This proves recovery of the actual Hilbert representatives from the interior distribution path. It is stronger than identifying only their quotient classes.

\subsection*{4. The exact section space and its limits}

Define the following actual receiving subspace of the original Hilbert space:
\[
\mathcal S_{n,s}
=\left\{y\in\mathcal H_n^{-s}:
 y_k=\lim_{l\to\infty}
        \langle I_{n,s}y,\phi_{k,n,l}\rangle
 \text{ for every }k\right\}.
\tag{DR12}
\]
It is linear. It is Borel: convergence of each sequence to its coordinate is a countable combination of inequalities between continuous linear functionals. If \(y\in\mathcal S_{n,s}\cap\mathcal N_{n,s}\), every pairing in (DR12) is zero, hence every \(y_k=0\); thus the intersection is zero. In particular \(I_{n,s}\) and the quotient map \(q:\mathcal H_n^{-s}\to\mathcal V_n^{-s}\) are injective on \(\mathcal S_{n,s}\). Equation (DR11) says that every actual path value belongs to this subspace, simultaneously in time, with probability one.

There is an explicit measurable inverse section on \(q(\mathcal S_{n,s})\). Each interior test functional annihilates \(\mathcal N_{n,s}\) and so descends to a continuous linear functional on the quotient. For \(v\) in that image, take the coordinate limits of those functionals along \(\phi_{k,n,l}\). They give exactly the coordinates of its unique representative in \(\mathcal S_{n,s}\). To see that both the domain and section are Borel without suppressing their domain, first require existence of every coordinate limit; then require finiteness of the weighted squared coordinate sum; construct the Hilbert vector as the norm limit of finite-coordinate vectors; finally require that its quotient equal \(v\). Each condition is Borel, and these conditions define precisely \(q(\mathcal S_{n,s})\). The finite-coordinate construction proves measurability of the section.

No continuous inverse or vanishing of the ambient kernel follows. For example fix \(\ell_2,\ell_3\) and the smooth tangential factor in (DR4). For \(0<\epsilon<n\), let \(z^\epsilon\) be the interior plane measure at \(x_1=-n+\epsilon\), paired against that tangential factor, with coefficient \(\epsilon^{-1}\). Its coefficients are
\[
z^\epsilon_k
=\frac{n^{-1/2}}{\epsilon}
 \sin\frac{\pi k_1\epsilon}{2n}\,
 \mathbf1_{\{k_2=\ell_2,\ k_3=\ell_3\}}.
\tag{DR13}
\]
For fixed \(\epsilon\), the cutoff factors in the normal direction are one once \(l\) is sufficiently large. The tangential factors tend to one at every interior point and are bounded by one. Dominated convergence in the finite tangential integral therefore proves \(z^\epsilon\in\mathcal S_{n,s}\). Its coefficients tend to (DR2) and have absolute value bounded by those of (DR2), using \(|\sin u|\le|u|\). The summable series (DR3) and dominated convergence give
\[
z^\epsilon\longrightarrow z^{(\ell_2,\ell_3)}
\quad\text{in }\mathcal H_n^{-s},
\qquad
qz^\epsilon\longrightarrow0
\quad\text{in }\mathcal V_n^{-s}.
\tag{DR14}
\]
Thus \(\mathcal S_{n,s}\) is not closed, and the section on its quotient image is not continuous at zero. This example concerns the exact ambient Hilbert map, not an asserted actual curvature law. It preserves the distinction between the proved measurable recovery and a stronger, unavailable topological isomorphism.

The actual-law consequence for DH18 is now exact. Interior test values determine every coordinate at every rational time by (DR11); continuity determines the Hilbert paths. Thus their laws determine the Hilbert path law within the actual limiting class. In an unrestricted Hilbert class this would fail by (DR2)–(DR4). The common ultrafilter/subsequence correlations, initial character defects, first-energy defect and heat detector of DH19 are not changed by this recovery.

\subsection*{5. Sharper limiting Hilbert moments and logarithmic modulus}

The full all-order local input gives another strengthening of DH11–DH16. The limiting coordinate bound CP27 applied to \(e_{k,n}\), whose exact supremum is \(n^{-3/2}\), is
\(\mathbb E|\Delta Y_{n,k}|^{2p}\le(2p-1)!!(16\kappa_*\mathsf L_{2n}n^{-3}|t-u|)^p\).
Minkowski on the squared weighted coordinates, followed by monotone convergence, therefore gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
\mathbb E\|Y_n^{de}(t)-Y_n^{de}(u)\|_{-s,n}^{2p}
\le (2p-1)!!\,(\mathsf c_{s,n}|t-u|)^p,\\
\mathsf c_{s,n}
=16\kappa_*\mathsf L_{2n}\,n^{-3}S_{s,n},
\qquad \mathsf L_{2n}=9\kappa_*(2n)^3+24(2n)^2 .
\end{gathered}\tag{DR15}
\]
For each finite coordinate sum, its \(L^p\) root is at most the sum of the individual roots
\([(2p-1)!!]^{1/p}16\kappa_*\mathsf L_{2n}n^{-3}|t-u|(1+\lambda_{k,n})^{-s}\).
This proves every factor in (DR15). No independence or absence of spatial correlations is used. The estimate concerns the actual limiting law; the finite-volume constants remain those of DH6–DH12.

The nonnegative even series of cosh and
\((2p-1)!!/(2p)!=1/(2^pp!)\) give
\[
\begin{gathered}
\mathbb E\cosh\bigl(\lambda\|Y_n^{de}(t)-Y_n^{de}(u)\|_{-s,n}\bigr)
\le e^{\mathsf c_{s,n}\lambda^2|t-u|/2},\\
\mathbb P\bigl(\|Y_n^{de}(t)-Y_n^{de}(u)\|_{-s,n}>r\bigr)
\le2\exp\!\left(-\frac{r^2}{2\mathsf c_{s,n}|t-u|}\right).
\end{gathered}\tag{DR16}
\]
The second line follows from \(\cosh(\lambda x)\ge e^{\lambda|x|}/2\), Markov's inequality and \(\lambda=r/(\mathsf c_{s,n}|t-u|)\). It is a Gaussian tail upper bound, not a Gaussian-law assertion.

Let \(H_{n,s,T}\) be the supremum of all adjacent dyadic Hilbert-norm increments on \([0,T]\) divided, at level \(l\ge0\), by \(\sqrt{T(l+1)2^{-l}}\). Applying (DR16) to its \(2^l\) intervals, and summing the geometric series, proves
\[
\begin{gathered}
\mathbb P(H_{n,s,T}>r)
\le\frac{2e^{-r^2/(2\mathsf c_{s,n})}}
          {1-2e^{-r^2/(2\mathsf c_{s,n})}},
\qquad r^2>2\mathsf c_{s,n}\log2,\\
\|Y_n^{de}(t)-Y_n^{de}(u)\|_{-s,n}
\le\sqrt2\,B\,H_{n,s,T}
 \sqrt{|t-u|\,[1+\log_2(T/|t-u|)]},\\
B=1+2\sum_{l\ge1}\sqrt{l+1}\,2^{-l/2}
\le\frac{2}{(1-2^{-1/2})^2}-1,\qquad 0<|t-u|\le T.
\end{gathered}\tag{DR17}
\]
Choose a dyadic mesh length between \(|t-u|\) and \(2|t-u|\). One coarse adjacent increment and the two endpoint refinement tails, bounded by the Hilbert triangle inequality, give the second line exactly as in CP36. The first line tends to zero as \(r\to\infty\), so \(H_{n,s,T}\) is finite almost surely. Countable intersection gives this bound on every selected cube, exponent, orientation and integer horizon; negative horizons follow by reversal or a time translation. Every \(s>3/2\) is obtained by inclusion from a smaller selected exponent. This strengthens the Hölder assertions without changing their topology.

For the product Hilbert norm of all three original orientations, the same calculation retains their three contributions: replace \(\mathsf c_{s,n}\) by \(3\mathsf c_{s,n}\) in (DR15)–(DR17). This follows by a second application of Minkowski to the three squared norms and does not remove any cross-orientation dependence.
