\section*{The full raw S6 phase: second energy and a stronger physical conjugate covariance}

This proof concerns the actual finite-volume vacuum and the unchanged path
\(L_j=j^4,a_j=(100j)^{-1},g_j^2=\kappa_*/(200j)\). It proves exact
first- and second-energy matrices for the original raw phase, an explicit
second-energy upper bound, and a physical conjugate variance bound whose
available upper function grows as \(j^{13}\), improving the earlier
\(j^{25}\) function. Neither bound determines the sign of
\(G_{F,j}-E_{F,j}/s_j\), where \(s_j=\kappa_*/j\).
The precise remaining signed covariance contraction is calculated below,
including its finite matrix and all original root coefficients.

The goal of a smooth interacting gapless four-dimensional theory is not a
conclusion of this note. All asymptotic statements about upper functions
or lower functions are identified as such; none is asserted to be an
asymptotic equivalence for an unknown actual expectation.

\subsection*{1. Original objects, metric, action, and raw vector}

Let \(m=2L,n=m+1,L\ge2\). Vertices are
\(z=(i,k,l)\in\{0,\ldots,m\}^3\), at positions
\(o+a(i-L,k-L,l-L)\). Every positive nearest-neighbour edge and every
elementary face of this open cube is present. Thus
\[
 N=3mn^2,\qquad M=3m^2n.
 \tag{RH1}
\]
The configuration space is \(SU(2)^N\), with probability Haar on each
factor and the round radius-two metric. Put
\(T_\alpha=-i\sigma_\alpha/2\),
\(X_{e\alpha}f=\partial_t f(\ldots,e^{tT_\alpha}U_e,\ldots)|_0\).
These fields are orthonormal and satisfy
\([X_{e\alpha},X_{e\beta}]=-\epsilon_{\alpha\beta\gamma}X_{e\gamma}\).
The sign follows by applying the two derivatives to the matrix coordinate:
\(X_\alpha X_\beta U=T_\beta T_\alpha U\).
Write
\[
 U=c(U)I+q(U)\cdot T,\quad c^2+|q|^2/4=1,\quad
 q^\alpha(U)=-2\operatorname{tr}(T_\alpha U),\quad
 \Delta=\sum_{e,\alpha}X_{e\alpha}^2.
 \tag{RH2}
\]
For each face \(p=(z;d,e),d<e\), its word, defect, and the full
Hamiltonian are
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 U_p=U_d(z)U_e(z+e_d)U_d(z+e_e)^{-1}U_e(z)^{-1},\quad
 D_p=2-\operatorname{tr}U_p\in[0,4],\quad W=\sum_pD_p,\\
 H=-\kappa\Delta+bW,\qquad
 \kappa=2g^2/a,\quad b=1/(2g^2a),\quad
 \xi=b/\kappa=1/(4g^4),\quad \kappa b=a^{-2}.
 \end{gathered}\tag{RH3}
\]
In particular \(bW=2bM-b\sum_p\operatorname{tr}U_p\).
The physical action is
\(U_{(s,t)}\mapsto h_sU_{(s,t)}h_t^{-1}\), for every original vertex,
including the boundary. Physical vectors are invariant under this action.

The positive unit ground state is denoted by \(\psi\), with
\(H\psi=E_0\psi\), \(w=\log\psi\), and \(d\mu=\psi^2dU\).
Compact ellipticity gives a smooth minimizer; replacing it by its absolute
value does not increase its form, and the strong maximum principle makes
the nonnegative minimizer strictly positive. For smooth \(f\), expansion
and integration by parts give
\[
 \langle f\psi,(H-E_0)f\psi\rangle=\kappa\mu|\nabla f|^2.
 \tag{RH4}
\]
It follows that every other ground vector is a scalar multiple of
\(\psi\): its quotient by \(\psi\) has zero gradient on the connected
configuration product. Gauge transformations and the reflection below
therefore fix \(\psi\). The full and physical ground energies coincide.
All functions used below are smooth at each finite volume; compactness and
strict positivity justify all differentiations and integrations.

The original rooted tree contains every direction-one edge, the
direction-two edges at first coordinate zero, and the direction-three
edges at first two coordinates zero. Its complete transport is
\[
 t_{i,k,l}=
 \left(\prod_{r=0}^{l-1}U_3(0,0,r)\right)
 \left(\prod_{s=0}^{k-1}U_2(0,s,l)\right)
 \left(\prod_{t=0}^{i-1}U_1(t,k,l)\right),\qquad
 Z_c=t_{s(c)}U_ct_{t(c)}^{-1}.
 \tag{RH5}
\]
Products are ordered increasingly from left to right. Empty products are
identity. The full chord sets are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathcal C_2&=\{(i,k,l;2):1\le i\le m,\ 0\le k<m,\ 0\le l\le m\},\\
 \mathcal C_3&=\{(i,k,l;3):0\le i,k\le m,\ (i,k)\ne(0,0),\ 0\le l<m\}.
 \end{aligned}\tag{RH6}
\]
With \(h=\pi/(2n),s=\sin h,c=\cos h,C=\cot h\), retain
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 v_0(r)=n^{-1/2},\quad v(r)=\sqrt{2/n}\cos\frac{\pi(r+1/2)}n,\quad
 w_1(r)=-\sqrt{2/n}\sin\frac{\pi(r+1)}n,\\
 a_{(i,k,l;2)}=-v(i)w_1(k)v_0(l)/\sqrt2,\quad a_{\mathcal C_3}=0,\\
 b_{(i,k,l;2)}=v_0(i)w_1(k)v(l)/\sqrt2,\quad
 b_{(i,k,l;3)}=-v_0(i)v(k)w_1(l)/\sqrt2,\\
 u_1=\sum_ca_cq(Z_c),\quad u_3=\sum_cb_cq(Z_c),\quad S=u_1\cdot u_3,\\
 (RU)_1(i,k,l)=U_1(m-i-1,k,l)^{-1},\quad
 (RU)_d(i,k,l)=U_d(m-i,k,l)\quad(d=2,3),\\
 S_R=S\circ R,\quad D=S+S_R,\quad
 \sigma_*=\sqrt8\sin h,\quad\beta_0=\sigma_*/(2g^2),\quad F=\beta_0(S-S_R).
 \end{gathered}\tag{RH7}
\]
Every reflected root word means substitution of this map in (RH5).
For example its tree transport is
\[
 t^R_{i,k,l}=
 \left(\prod_{r<l}U_3(m,0,r)\right)
 \left(\prod_{s<k}U_2(m,s,l)\right)
 \left(\prod_{t<i}U_1(m-t-1,k,l)^{-1}\right).
 \tag{RH8}
\]
Under a gauge action all \(Z_c\) are conjugated by the root gauge element,
so \(u_1,u_3\) rotate together. This proves that \(S,S_R,D,F\) are
physical. Reflection is an isometry, preserves the complete potential,
and makes \(F\) odd. Hence \(\mu F=0\).

For reference, strict nonzero raw norm can be proved on an original chord.
Take \(e=(1,L-1,0;2)\), \(K=Z_e\), \(H_\partial=Z_{(m,L-1,0;2)}\).
The ordered boundary comb is
\(A_{k,l}=(\prod_{t<l}Z_{(m,0,t;3)})(\prod_{s<k}Z_{(m,s,l;2)})\).
Solving the tree coordinates in (RH5) makes tree links identity by a
gauge action and preserves product Haar successively by left and right
invariance. Substituting (RH8) then gives the exact reflected word
\(A_{k,l}KH_\partial^{-1}A_{k,l}^{-1}\). Its original coefficients are
\(-a_e,b_e\). Thus the quadratic harmonic part, as a function of \(K\)
with the full exterior fixed, is
\[
 \Pi_2^{(e)}F=-\beta_0a_eb_e[\chi_1(K)+\chi_1(KH_\partial^{-1})],\quad
 \chi_1(U)=4c(U)^2-1,\quad
 \|\Pi_2^{(e)}F\|_{dK}^2
 =\tfrac43\beta_0^2a_e^2b_e^2[1+2c(H_\partial)^2]>0.
 \tag{RH9}
\]
Here \(a_eb_e\ne0\) for every odd \(n\ge5\). The norm follows from
\(\int z_iz_jz_kz_l=(\delta_{ij}\delta_{kl}+\delta_{ik}\delta_{jl}
+\delta_{il}\delta_{jk})/24\) on the unit quaternion coordinates;
this tensor is fixed by rotation invariance and two traces. Constants and
affine terms in the entire polynomial remain present; projection only
proves its nonconstancy. Consequently
\[
 G_F=\mu F^2>0,\qquad E_F=\kappa\mu|\nabla F|^2>0.
 \tag{RH10}
\]

\subsection*{2. Every root transport in the gradient and covariant Hessian}

For a physical edge define the orthonormal frame
\[
 E_{e\alpha}=\sum_\gamma
 (\operatorname{Ad}_{t_{s(e)}^{-1}})_{\gamma\alpha}X_{e\gamma},\qquad
 T_{ce}=\mathbf1_{e\in t_{s(c)}}+\delta_{ce}-\mathbf1_{e\in t_{t(c)}},\qquad
 R_{ce}=\mathbf1_{e\in t_{s(c)}}+\delta_{ce}+\mathbf1_{e\in t_{t(c)}}.
 \tag{RH11}
\]
Both occurrences of a shared tree edge remain in \(R_{ce}\). A field's
own coefficient matrix does not depend on its edge, so each \(E_{e\alpha}\)
is Haar divergence free and \(\sum E_{e\alpha}^2=\Delta\).
Direct differentiation of every letter of (RH5) gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 E_{e\alpha}q_c&=c_cT_{ce}\mathbf e_\alpha+
              \tfrac12R_{ce}\mathbf e_\alpha\times q_c=:J_{c,e\alpha},\\
 E_{e\alpha}c_c&=-\tfrac14T_{ce}q_c^\alpha,
 \end{aligned}\tag{RH12}
\]
where \(q_c=q(Z_c),c_c=c(Z_c)\). The signs and factor \(1/2\)
follow from
\((z\cdot T)(y\cdot T)=-(z\cdot y)I/4+(z\times y)\cdot T/2\).

Write \(e\prec f\) when the tree edge \(e\) lies in the root path to
\(s(f)\); a chord is never such an ancestor. Differentiating the frame,
and using the radius-two bi-invariant connection, gives exactly
\[
 \nabla_{E_{e\alpha}}E_{f\beta}
 =-\left(\mathbf1_{e\prec f}+\tfrac12\delta_{ef}\right)
             E_{f,\mathbf e_\alpha\times\mathbf e_\beta}.
 \tag{RH13}
\]
For distinct links the only connection term is the derivative of the
root transport, equal to minus the displayed ancestor rotation. For a
single link the coefficient of that rotation is \(1/2\), because its
invariant-field bracket has the sign in (RH2). This proves (RH13) with
no singular quotient geometry.

Let \(I=(e,\alpha),J=(f,\beta)\), and set
\(\gamma_{ef}=\mathbf1_{e\prec f}+\delta_{ef}/2\). The full vector
Hessian of each original word is therefore
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 H_{c,IJ}:=\nabla^2q_c(E_{e\alpha},E_{f\beta})
 ={}&-\tfrac14T_{ce}T_{cf}q_c^\alpha\mathbf e_\beta
       +\tfrac12R_{cf}\mathbf e_\beta\times J_{c,e\alpha}\\
 &+\gamma_{ef}\left[c_cT_{cf}(\mathbf e_\alpha\times\mathbf e_\beta)
       +\tfrac12R_{cf}(\mathbf e_\alpha\times\mathbf e_\beta)\times q_c\right].
 \end{aligned}\tag{RH14}
\]
This is an exact finite formula, including every repeated root occurrence
and connection term. Its symmetry also follows directly by subtracting
the two differentiated expressions and inserting their frame bracket.

Put \(J_{1,I}=\sum_ca_cJ_{c,I}\),
\(J_{3,I}=\sum_cb_cJ_{c,I}\),
\(H_{1,IJ}=\sum_ca_cH_{c,IJ}\), and
\(H_{3,IJ}=\sum_cb_cH_{c,IJ}\). The raw scalar derivatives are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 g_I:=E_IS&=u_3\cdot J_{1,I}+u_1\cdot J_{3,I},\\
 H^S_{IJ}&=u_3\cdot H_{1,IJ}+u_1\cdot H_{3,IJ}
                   +J_{1,I}\cdot J_{3,J}+J_{3,I}\cdot J_{1,J}.
 \end{aligned}\tag{RH15}
\]
The two product terms are both retained.

If \(e'\) is the reflected positive edge, the differential of reflection
in these frames is the orthogonal matrix
\[
 \Omega_e(U)=
 \begin{cases}
 -\operatorname{Ad}_{t_{s(e')}(RU)U_e^{-1}t_{s(e)}(U)^{-1}},&d(e)=1,\\
 \operatorname{Ad}_{t_{s(e')}(RU)t_{s(e)}(U)^{-1}},&d(e)=2,3.
 \end{cases}\tag{RH16}
\]
For a reversed edge, differentiating the inverse sends a left coefficient
\(Y\) to \(-U_e^{-1}YU_e\); converting to the target root frame proves
this formula. Consequently the complete reflected tensors are
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 g^R_e(U)=\Omega_e(U)^Tg_{e'}(RU),\quad
 H^{S_R}_{ef}(U)=\Omega_e(U)^TH^S_{e'f'}(RU)\Omega_f(U),\\
 \nabla F=\beta_0(g-g^R),\qquad
 \nabla^2F=\beta_0(H^S-H^{S_R}).
 \end{gathered}\tag{RH17}
\]
The second equality is the naturality of the covariant Hessian under the
isometry \(R\): differentiating the first equality with the connection
(RH13) supplies precisely the derivatives of \(\Omega\). Hence none may
be dropped by differentiating its entries as constants.

\subsection*{3. The actual vacuum Hessian and complete energy matrices}

The ground equation and curvature convention are
\[
 \Delta w+|\nabla w|^2=(bW-E_0)/\kappa,\quad
 \mathscr L=\Delta+2\nabla w\cdot\nabla,\quad
 \operatorname{Ric}=\tfrac12g,\quad
 \mathscr R(v,z,v,z)=\tfrac14\sum_e(|v_e|^2|z_e|^2-\langle v_e,z_e\rangle^2).
 \tag{RH18}
\]
Here \(g\) in tensor expressions is the metric, whereas \(g^2\) in
(RH3) is the coupling. To keep the imported bound verifiable, the full
stationary argument is recorded. If \(h_w=\nabla^2w\), scalar derivative
commutation on this locally symmetric product gives
\[
 \kappa^{-1}(\nabla^2(bW))_{ij}
 = (\mathscr Lh_w)_{ij}+2(h_w^2)_{ij}
 +2\mathscr R_{ikjl}(h_w)_{kl}
 -\operatorname{Ric}_{ik}(h_w)_{kj}-\operatorname{Ric}_{jk}(h_w)_{ik}
 +2\mathscr R_{ikjl}w_kw_l.
 \tag{RH19}
\]
Indeed \(\nabla_i(h_w)_{jk}-\nabla_k(h_w)_{ij}=\mathscr R_{ikjl}w_l\).
Differentiating \(|\nabla w|^2\) twice gives \(2h_w^2\), the covariant
drift, and the last curvature term. Commuting the Hessian of \(\Delta w\)
gives the remaining two Ricci terms and \(2\mathscr R*h_w\);
derivatives of Ricci vanish. This derives every term in (RH19).

At a negative global minimum eigenvalue \(\lambda\) of \(h_w\), extend
its unit eigenvector radially in geodesic coordinates. Its first covariant
derivative vanishes at the point and the correction to the scalar
Laplacian is \(2\lambda\langle v,\Delta v\rangle=0\), since the
extension has unit length. Thus \((\mathscr Lh_w)(v,v)\ge0\).
The curvature and Ricci terms combine to
\(2\operatorname{tr}[\mathscr R(v,\cdot,v,\cdot)(h_w-\lambda g)]\ge0\),
and the last curvature term is nonnegative. It follows that
\(2\lambda^2\le\kappa^{-1}\nabla^2(bW)(v,v)\).
Twice differentiating each four-letter face along a product geodesic
retains four repeated-letter and twelve ordered distinct-letter terms.
Their operator norms give
\[
 |\nabla^2D_p(y,y)|\le\tfrac12\left(\sum_{e\in\partial p}|y_e|\right)^2
 \le2\sum_{e\in\partial p}|y_e|^2,\quad
 \nabla^2(bW)\le8b\,g,\quad
 \boxed{\nabla^2w\ge-2\sqrt\xi\,g.}
 \tag{RH20}
\]
Every original boundary incidence is counted and is at most four. The
constant \(2bM\) and \(E_0\) have zero Hessian but remain in (RH18).
This is the OS17–OS21/HVR3–HVR10 result with its proof and signs retained.

For arbitrary real smooth \(f,h\), weighted integration gives
\(\mu\mathscr Lf=0\) and
\(\mu\Gamma(f,h)=-\mu(f\mathscr Lh)\), where
\(\Gamma(f,h)=\langle\nabla f,\nabla h\rangle\).
The full polarization of weighted Bochner is
\[
 \mu[(\mathscr Lf)(\mathscr Lh)]
 =\mu[\langle\nabla^2f,\nabla^2h\rangle_{\rm HS}
            +\tfrac12\Gamma(f,h)-2h_w(\nabla f,\nabla h)].
 \tag{RH21}
\]
To prove the sign, expand
\(\mathscr L\Gamma(f)/2-\Gamma(f,\mathscr Lf)\).
The two Hessian-of-\(f\) drift terms cancel and leave
\(\|\nabla^2f\|^2+(\operatorname{Ric}-2h_w)(\nabla f,\nabla f)\).
Its integral is \(\mu(\mathscr Lf)^2\); polarization proves (RH21).

Let \(m_S=\mu S=\mu S_R\), and define the centered pair
\(f_1=S-m_S,f_2=S_R-m_S\). Write
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 Q=\mu S^2,\quad Q_R=\mu SS_R,\quad
 K=\mu|\nabla S|^2,\quad K_R=\mu\langle\nabla S,\nabla S_R\rangle,\\
 H_S=\mu\|\nabla^2S\|^2,\quad H_R=\mu\langle\nabla^2S,\nabla^2S_R\rangle,\\
 J_S=\mu h_w(\nabla S,\nabla S),\quad
 J_R=\mu h_w(\nabla S,\nabla S_R),\\
 \mathsf G=\begin{pmatrix}Q-m_S^2&Q_R-m_S^2\\Q_R-m_S^2&Q-m_S^2\end{pmatrix},\quad
 \mathsf K=\begin{pmatrix}K&K_R\\K_R&K\end{pmatrix},\quad
 \mathsf H=\begin{pmatrix}H_S&H_R\\H_R&H_S\end{pmatrix},\quad
 \mathsf J=\begin{pmatrix}J_S&J_R\\J_R&J_S\end{pmatrix}.
 \end{gathered}\tag{RH22}
\]
Reflection invariance proves every repeated diagonal entry, including
that of \(\mathsf J\), because \(w\circ R=w\).
For \(A=H-E_0\) on the original physical space,
\(A(f_i\psi)=-\kappa(\mathscr Lf_i)\psi\). Hence the exact raw
first- and second-energy matrices and their receiving bound are
\[
 \boxed{\mathsf E=\kappa\mathsf K,\qquad
 \mathsf E_2=\kappa^2(\mathsf H+\tfrac12\mathsf K-2\mathsf J),\qquad
 \mathsf E_2\preceq\kappa^2\mathsf H+(\kappa/2+4/a)\mathsf E.}
 \tag{RH23}
\]
The final inequality follows by applying (RH20) to each real linear
combination of the gradients; this is a matrix inequality, and covers
complex coefficients by their real and imaginary parts. It retains all
cross terms in (RH14)–(RH17). The Gram matrix of
\((f_1\psi,f_2\psi,A f_1\psi,A f_2\psi)\) is
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}\mathsf G&\mathsf E\\\mathsf E&\mathsf E_2\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.
 \tag{RH24}
\]
In particular each of the original even and odd blocks has its own exact
moment inequality. The odd block, with the original coefficient
\(\beta_0(1,-1)\), is
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 G_F&=2\beta_0^2(Q-Q_R),\qquad E_F=2\kappa\beta_0^2(K-K_R),\\
 E_{2,F}&=2\kappa^2\beta_0^2[H_S-H_R+\tfrac12(K-K_R)-2(J_S-J_R)],\\
 E_F^2&\le G_FE_{2,F},\qquad
 E_{2,F}\le2\kappa^2\beta_0^2(H_S-H_R)+(\kappa/2+4/a)E_F.
 \end{aligned}\tag{RH25}
\]
Thus \(H_S-H_R\), and not two unrelated pointwise Hessian suprema, is
the exact receiving tensor. It is nonnegative because it equals half
\(\mu\|\nabla^2(S-S_R)\|^2\).

\subsection*{4. Complete occurrence constants and original-path powers}

Let \(n_{ce}=R_{ce}\) count every occurrence in the original word,
including opposite occurrences in a shared root prefix. Define
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 S_1=\sum_c|a_c|=\sqrt{2/n}C(C-c),\quad
 S_3=\sum_c|b_c|=\sqrt{2/n}[(2-1/n)C^2-(c/n)C],\\
 D_{1e}=\sum_c|a_c|n_{ce},\quad D_{3e}=\sum_c|b_c|n_{ce},\quad
 A_{\mu,ef}=\sum_c|M_{\mu c}|n_{ce}n_{cf},\quad
 A_\mu=\sum_c|M_{\mu c}|\sum_en_{ce}^2,\\
 A_1=m\sqrt{2/n}C(5C-4c),\qquad
 A_3=(m/n)\sqrt{2/n}[(9m+5)C^2-2cC].
 \end{gathered}\tag{RH26}
\]
Here \(M_{1c}=a_c,M_{3c}=b_c\). For verification, a direction-two
word has \(\sum_en_{ce}^2=2i+4k+4l+2\), and a direction-three word
has \(2i+2k+4l+2\). Their shared root prefixes have respectively
\(k+l\) and \(l\) links occurring twice. The absolute sums
\(\sum_{i=0}^m|v(i)|=\sqrt{2/n}C\),
\(\sum_{i=1}^m|v(i)|=\sqrt{2/n}(C-c)\), and
\(\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}|w_1(k)|=\sqrt{2/n}C\)
follow by the finite geometric sums of the exponentials on each side of
the middle zero. Reflection gives their first coordinate moments.
The first row's weighted coordinate means are
\(mC/[2(C-c)],(m-1)/2,m/2\); substitution proves \(A_1\).
The third direction-two row has mass \(\sqrt{2/n}(m/n)C^2\) and
squared-occurrence average \(5m+1\). Its unexcluded direction-three
rectangle has mass \(\sqrt{2/n}C^2\) and average \(4m\).
The excluded corner has mass \(\sqrt{2/n}cC/n\) and average \(2m\).
Adding and subtracting exactly these contributions proves \(A_3\).

Each first derivative of a word has vector norm at most its occurrence
count: one differentiated unit-quaternion factor has norm \(1/2\),
and the vector extraction has norm at most twice the quaternion norm.
Each covariant Hessian component has vector norm at most
\(n_{ce}n_{cf}/2\). For distinct edges this follows by inserting two
generators in every ordered pair of letter positions; for the same edge
use the symmetrized second derivative, equal to its covariant Hessian
in the invariant frame. Its repeated-letter insertions and the two
orders of distinct-letter insertions have the same bound. Rotating each
edge's unit tangent basis to (RH11) preserves this argument. Therefore
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 |\nabla S|^2\le3\sum_e(2S_3D_{1e}+2S_1D_{3e})^2
 \le\mathcal C_{\rm occ}:=12[S_3\sqrt{S_1A_1}+S_1\sqrt{S_3A_3}]^2,\\
 |H^S_{e\alpha,f\beta}|\le
 S_3A_{1,ef}+S_1A_{3,ef}+D_{1e}D_{3f}+D_{3e}D_{1f},\\
 \|\nabla^2S\|^2\le
 \mathcal H_{\rm occ}:=9[S_3A_1+S_1A_3+2\sqrt{S_1A_1S_3A_3}]^2.
 \end{gathered}\tag{RH27}
\]
To verify the last inequality,
\(\|A_{\mu,\cdot\cdot}\|_{\rm Frob}\le
\sum_c|M_{\mu c}|\|n_c n_c^t\|_{\rm Frob}=A_\mu\),
and \(\|D_\mu\|^2\le S_\mu A_\mu\) by coefficient-weighted
Cauchy–Schwarz. The four matrix terms in the preceding line then give
the displayed expression by the triangle inequality. The factor nine
counts both original colour indices; no root word was shortened.

The odd projection contracts the norm, gradient norm, and Hessian norm
in \(L^2(\mu)\): reflection acts isometrically on each corresponding
tensor bundle and fixes \(\mu\). Since
\(S-S_R=2P_-S\), (RH25) yields
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 G_F\le\overline G_F:=64\beta_0^2S_1^2S_3^2,\qquad
 E_F\le\overline E_F:=4\kappa\beta_0^2\mathcal C_{\rm occ},\\
 P_F:=4\kappa^2\beta_0^2\mathcal H_{\rm occ},\quad Q_a:=\kappa/2+4/a,\\
 \boxed{E_{2,F}\le P_F+Q_aE_F\le P_F+Q_a\overline E_F,\qquad
 G_F\ge\frac{E_F^2}{P_F+Q_aE_F}.}
 \end{gathered}\tag{RH28}
\]
All finite constants are original trigonometric expressions.

On the prescribed path, retain precisely
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 m_j=2j^4,\quad n_j=2j^4+1,\quad h_j=\pi/(4j^4+2),\quad
 \beta_{0,j}=\frac{200\sqrt2j}{\kappa_*}\sin h_j,\\
 \kappa_j=\kappa_*,\quad b_j=10000j^2/\kappa_*,\quad
 \xi_j=10000j^2/\kappa_*^2,\quad Q_{a_j}=\kappa_*/2+400j,\quad
 s_j=\kappa_*/j.
 \end{gathered}\tag{RH29}
\]
Let \(\tau=19/2+3\sqrt{10}\). Using \(C/n\to2/\pi\),
\(c\to1\), \(A_1/(nS_1)\to5\), \(A_3/(nS_3)\to9/2\),
\(S_1S_3/n^3\to64/\pi^4\), and
\(j^6\beta_{0,j}^2\to5000\pi^2/\kappa_*^2\), one obtains
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \mathcal H_{\rm occ}/n^8\longrightarrow36864\tau^2/\pi^8,\qquad
 \mathcal C_{\rm occ}/n^7\longrightarrow49152\tau/\pi^8,\\
 \frac{\overline G_{F,j}}{j^{18}}\longrightarrow
 \frac{83886080000}{\kappa_*^2\pi^6},\quad
 \frac{\overline E_{F,j}}{j^{22}}\longrightarrow
 \frac{125829120000\tau}{\kappa_*\pi^6},\\
 \frac{P_{F,j}+Q_{a_j}\overline E_{F,j}}{j^{26}}
 \longrightarrow\frac{188743680000\tau^2}{\pi^6}.
 \end{gathered}\tag{RH30}
\]
The \(Q_a\overline E_F\) contribution has order \(j^{23}\), so its
ratio to \(j^{26}\) tends to zero. These are limits of proved bound
functions, not estimates from a simulated vacuum.

\subsection*{5. An exact acceleration cancellation for the original conjugate}

Retain the original full soft cochain \(V=V_3\):
\[
 V_1(i,k,l)=0,\quad V_2(i,k,l)=w_1(k)v(l)/\sqrt{2n},\quad
 V_3(i,k,l)=-v(k)w_1(l)/\sqrt{2n}.
 \tag{RH31}
\]
It is defined on every physical edge of its direction. The finite sums
\(\sum v^2=\sum w_1^2=1\) give \(\sum_eV_e^2=1\).
Set \(W_r=\sum_{t<r}w_1(t)\), \(v_*=v(0)\). Its root integral is
\[
 p_{i,k,l}(V)=\frac{v(l)W_k-v_*W_l}{\sqrt{2n}},\quad
 Y_\alpha=\sum_eV_eE_{e\alpha},\quad Y_z=\sum_\alpha z_\alpha Y_\alpha,
 \quad B=Y_{u_1}.
 \tag{RH32}
\]
The fields \(Y_\alpha\) are orthonormal and divergence free. Let
\(d_c=p_{s(c)}+V_c-p_{t(c)}\) and
\(r_c=p_{s(c)}+V_c+p_{t(c)}\). Word differentiation gives
\[
 Y_zq_c=c_cd_cz+\tfrac12r_c z\times q_c,
 \quad Y_zc_c=-\tfrac14d_cz\cdot q_c,\qquad
 d_c=0\quad(c\in\mathcal C_2),\quad r_c=2p_{t(c)}\quad(c\in\mathcal C_2).
 \tag{RH33}
\]
The last two assertions follow by inserting (RH31) in (RH32), or by
the finite identities \(v(r+1)-v(r)=2\sin h\,w_1(r)\) and
\(v(r)=v_*+2\sin h\,W_r\). They hold before expectation.

For \(k\ge0\), introduce the exact auxiliary rows
\[
 u^{[k]}=\sum_{c\in\mathcal C_2}a_cr_c^kq_c,\qquad u^{[0]}=u_1.
 \tag{RH34}
\]
They record the original root coefficients; the phase \(F\) is
unchanged. Equation (RH33) proves
\(Y_\alpha u^{[k]}=\mathbf e_\alpha\times u^{[k+1]}/2\).
In particular
\[
 \operatorname{div}B=0,\quad |B|^2=|u_1|^2=:h_1,\quad
 Bu_1=\tfrac12u_1\times u^{[1]},\quad Bh_1=0.
 \tag{RH35}
\]
The field is physical: its root colour rotates together with its frame,
and their contraction is invariant under every gauge action. It is
smooth and complete on the compact product. Its flow preserves Haar,
so \(-iB\) is the generator of the resulting unitary pullback group.

The full connection in (RH13) now gives the cancellation
\[
 \boxed{\nabla_BB=Y_{Bu_1}=
 Y_{(u_1\times u^{[1]})/2},\qquad
 \operatorname{div}(\nabla_BB)
       =\tfrac12[u_1\cdot u^{[2]}-|u^{[1]}|^2].}
 \tag{RH36}
\]
For detail, the physical edge coefficient of \(B\) is
\(V_e\operatorname{Ad}_{t_{s(e)}^{-1}}u_1\). Its derivative along
\(B\) is
\(V_e\operatorname{Ad}_{t_s^{-1}}[Bu_1-p_s(V)u_1\times u_1]\).
The second term is exactly zero. The same-edge connection is a vector
crossed with itself and is also zero. This proves the first identity
with every root transport retained until it cancels.
For the divergence, use the divergence-free \(Y_\alpha\) and
(RH34). The two colour sums are
\[
 \sum_\alpha\mathbf e_\alpha\cdot
 [ (\mathbf e_\alpha\times u^{[1]})\times u^{[1]}]
 =-2|u^{[1]}|^2,\quad
 \sum_\alpha\mathbf e_\alpha\cdot
 [u_1\times(\mathbf e_\alpha\times u^{[2]})]
 =2u_1\cdot u^{[2]}.
\]
Their common factor is \(1/4\), proving the second identity.
The Ricci contribution has not been discarded: it is already included
in the exact product connection used here.

For a fixed colour vector \(z\), the same calculation has
\(\nabla_{Y_z}Y_z=0\), because both \(Y_zz\) and the root rotation
\(p_s(V)z\times z\) vanish. Hence the actual three-colour soft score
matrix has the volume-independent bound
\[
 \mu[(Y_\alpha w)(Y_\beta w)]_{\alpha,\beta=1}^3
 =-\tfrac12[\mu h_w(Y_\alpha,Y_\beta)]_{\alpha,\beta=1}^3
 \preceq\sqrt\xi I_3.
 \tag{RH36a}
\]
The equality follows by integrating \(Y_z[(Y_zw)\psi^2]\) and
polarizing in fixed \(z\). It cannot be multiplied by a variable
\(|u_1|^2\) outside the expectation; the acceleration correction in
(RH36) is what handles that original variable colour.

Put \(x=\mu h_1>0\), \(V_B=\mu(Bw)^2\), and
\(\mathcal D=\mu[u_1\cdot u^{[2]}-|u^{[1]}|^2]\).
The strict inequality for \(x\) follows by varying any independent
chord whose \(a_c\ne0\), with the others fixed: the vector-valued
function \(u_1\) cannot vanish identically, and the actual smooth
density is strictly positive.
Integration of \(B[(Bw)\psi^2]\), followed by the weighted divergence
identity for \(\nabla_BB\), proves the exact formula
\[
 \boxed{V_B=-\tfrac12\mu h_w(B,B)+\tfrac18\mathcal D
 \ \le\ \sqrt\xi\,x+\tfrac18\mathcal D.}
 \tag{RH37}
\]
Indeed \(B^2w=h_w(B,B)+\langle\nabla w,\nabla_BB\rangle\),
\(\mu B^2w=-2V_B\), and
\(\mu\langle\nabla w,A\rangle=-\mu\operatorname{div}A/2\).
The inequality is (RH20). The signed \(\mathcal D\) is retained in
the strongest displayed bound.

\subsection*{6. The complete root coefficient sum and its evaluated improvement}

Define the three deterministic absolute-row moments
\[
 R_k=\sum_{c\in\mathcal C_2}|a_c|r_c^k\quad(k=0,1,2),\qquad
 R_0=S_1,\quad t_0=R_1/S_1,\quad R_{2,c}=R_2-R_1^2/S_1.
 \tag{RH38}
\]
The notation \(R_{2,c}\) means a centered coefficient moment; the
subscript is not a chord index. Its full finite evaluation is
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 T=\sqrt{2/n}C,\qquad v_*=\sqrt{2/n}c,\qquad
 Q_3=(2/n)^{3/2}[3C-\cot(3h)]/4,\\
 t_0=\frac{\sqrt2c^2}{n^{3/2}\sin h},\qquad R_1=S_1t_0,\\
 R_2=\frac{2(C-c)}{n^2}\left[
 \frac{T^3}{3}+\frac T2+\frac{Q_3}{6}
 +\frac{v_*}{2\sin h}(T^2+1)
 +\frac{v_*^2(1+n v_*^2)T}{4\sin^2h}\right].
 \end{gathered}\tag{RH39}
\]
Here \(3h<\pi\) and none of the displayed denominators vanishes for
odd \(n\ge5\).

We give the whole sum calculation. The retained root coefficient is
\(r_{(i,k,l;2)}=\sqrt{2/n}[v(l)W_{k+1}-v_*W_l]\), independent of
\(i\). From \(W_l=(v(l)-v_*)/(2\sin h)\),
\[
 \sum_lv(l)=0,\quad\sum_lv(l)^2=1,\quad
 \sum_lv(l)W_l=(2\sin h)^{-1},\quad
 \sum_lW_l^2=(1+n v_*^2)/(4\sin^2h).
\]
Thus
\[
 \sum_lr_{k,l}=\sqrt{2/n}\,c^2/\sin h,\quad
 \sum_lr_{k,l}^2=\frac2n\left[W_{k+1}^2-
 \frac{v_*W_{k+1}}{\sin h}+
 \frac{v_*^2(1+n v_*^2)}{4\sin^2h}\right].
\]
Set \(q_k=-w_1(k)>0\), \(z_{k+1}=\sum_{t\le k}q_t=-W_{k+1}\).
Then \(\sum q_k=T\), \(\sum q_k^2=1\),
\(\sum q_k^3=Q_3\), and telescoping squares gives
\(\sum q_kz_{k+1}=(T^2+1)/2\).
Reflection \(q_k=q_{m-1-k}\) implies
\(z_{k+1}+z_{m-k}=T+q_k\), hence
\(\sum q_k^2z_{k+1}=(T+Q_3)/2\).
Telescoping cubes then gives
\(\sum q_kz_{k+1}^2=T^3/3+T/2+Q_3/6\).
Finally \(\sin^3t=(3\sin t-\sin3t)/4\) and the full finite sine
sums give the displayed \(Q_3\). Multiplying the preceding expressions
by \(\sum_{i=1}^m|v(i)|/\sqrt{2n}=(C-c)/n\) proves (RH39),
including all endpoints and the original sign of each root integral.

For any deterministic real \(t\), the complete algebraic identity is
\[
 u_1\cdot u^{[2]}-|u^{[1]}|^2
 =u_1\cdot\sum_ca_c(r_c-t)^2q_c
             -\left|\sum_ca_c(r_c-t)q_c\right|^2.
 \tag{RH40}
\]
This neither changes \(F\) nor deletes the original \(r_c\) terms:
expansion shows the two linear and quadratic powers of \(t\) cancel.
Since \(|q_c|\le2\), Cauchy–Schwarz and \(t=t_0\) give
\[
 \mathcal D\le2R_{2,c}\sqrt x,\qquad
 \boxed{V_B\le U_H(x):=\sqrt\xi\,x+\tfrac14R_{2,c}\sqrt x
 \le\overline U_H:=4\sqrt\xi S_1^2+\tfrac12S_1R_{2,c}.}
 \tag{RH41}
\]
The last step uses \(x\le4S_1^2\). The choice \(t_0\) minimizes
\(\sum|a_c|(r_c-t)^2\), as follows by completing that exact scalar
quadratic. This minimizes only an upper-bound constant; no physical
observable or state has been rescaled.

The deterministic uniform bound on the correction is attained by an
actual configuration of the independent original chords. In fact
\[
 u_1\cdot u^{[2]}-|u^{[1]}|^2\le4S_1R_{2,c}.
 \tag{RH41a}
\]
To see this directly, expand it as in (RH47), absorb
\(\operatorname{sgn}(a_c)\) into each \(q_c\), and bound their dot
products by four. The remaining nonnegative sum is
\(2\sum|a_ca_d|(r_c-r_d)^2=4(S_1R_2-R_1^2)\).
Choose every chord with \(a_c\ne0\) to have
\(q_c=2\operatorname{sgn}(a_c)e_1\), and every tree link identity.
These are legitimate unit quaternions with scalar coordinate zero and
give equality. This proves sharpness of that deterministic correction
constant; it says nothing about equality under the actual vacuum.

The full finite expressions in (RH39) yield
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 R_2/\sqrt n\longrightarrow\frac{304\sqrt2}{3\pi^4},\qquad
 R_{2,c}/\sqrt n\longrightarrow\frac{208\sqrt2}{3\pi^4},\\
 \frac{\overline U_{H,j}}{j^{13}}\longrightarrow
 \frac{102400}{\kappa_*\pi^4},\qquad
 \frac{S_{1,j}R_{2,c,j}/2}{j^8}\longrightarrow\frac{3328}{3\pi^6}.
 \end{gathered}\tag{RH42}
\]
For the first limit, the three order-\(n^{3/2}\) terms inside the
bracket of (RH39) have coefficients
\(16\sqrt2/(3\pi^3),8\sqrt2/\pi^3,12\sqrt2/\pi^3\).
The outside coefficient is asymptotic to \(4/(\pi n)\).
Also \(S_1t_0^2/\sqrt n\to32\sqrt2/\pi^4\), which proves the
centered limit. With \(S_{1,j}^2/j^{12}\to256/\pi^4\) and
\(\sqrt{\xi_j}=100j/\kappa_*\), the other two follow.
The old CV43 bound was
\(4S_1^2\mathcal E_0/\kappa_*\), with
\(\mathcal E_0=\min(2bM,3\sqrt{NM}/a)\), whose ratio to
\(j^{25}\) tends to \(7372800/(\kappa_*\pi^4)\).
Consequently the ratio of the new upper function to that old function,
multiplied by \(j^{12}\), tends to \(1/72\). Both inequalities may
be kept by taking their minimum at each finite path point.

\subsection*{7. Raw covariance, the remaining signed block, and the endpoint test}

The complete original commutator numerator is
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 A_{33}=\sum_cb_cd_cc_c,\qquad
 \Xi=2(A_{33}-1)|u_1|^2+u_3\cdot(u_1\times u^{[1]})-BD,\\
 BF=\beta_0(2|u_1|^2+\Xi),\qquad
 J_F:=\mu BF=\beta_0(2x+\mu\Xi),\qquad
 J_F=-2\mu(FBw).
 \end{gathered}\tag{RH43}
\]
To verify it, (RH33) gives
\(Bu_3=A_{33}u_1+u_1\times(\sum_cb_cr_cq_c)/2\).
Its second summand is orthogonal to \(u_1\); combine this with
\(Bu_1\) from (RH35), and use \(F=\beta_0(2S-D)\).
The quantity \(BD\) differentiates the full reflected words (RH8):
for \(Y_e=V_e\operatorname{Ad}_{t_s^{-1}}u_1\cdot T\),
\(BU_e=Y_eU_e\), \(B(U_e^{-1})=-U_e^{-1}Y_e\), and the derivative
of a product is the sum over all its letter positions. These rules
evaluate it by finite original-word operations; it is not assumed zero
or assigned an unsupported parity.

Weighted integration and Cauchy–Schwarz give the unchanged raw inequality
and its stronger available denominator:
\[
 \boxed{4G_FV_B\ge J_F^2,\qquad
 G_F\ge\frac{\beta_0^2(2x+\mu\Xi)^2}{4U_H(x)}.}
 \tag{RH44}
\]
The denominator is strictly positive because \(x>0\) and \(\xi>0\).
No sign or nonzero value is assumed for \(2x+\mu\Xi\).
More generally, put \(j_i=\mu Bf_i\) for the two centered functions in
(RH22). For every coefficient vector the same integration proves
\[
 \mathsf G\succeq\frac{jj^t}{4U_H(x)}.
 \tag{RH45}
\]
This is a covariance inequality for the original pair, not a statement
only about a unit vector. The matrix records the even and odd numerator
combinations before applying reflection.

We now calculate, rather than only name, the signed contraction in
(RH37). Let
\(M_{cd}=\mu[q_c\cdot q_d]\), and for nonnegative integers \(r,s\)
let
\[
 C_{rs}=\mu[u^{[r]}\cdot u^{[s]}]
       =\sum_{c,d\in\mathcal C_2}a_ca_dr_c^rr_d^sM_{cd}.
 \tag{RH46}
\]
The actual root gauge invariance implies
\(\mu q_c=0\) and
\(\mu(q_c^\alpha q_d^\beta)=\delta_{\alpha\beta}M_{cd}/3\):
all rotation-invariant vectors vanish and all rotation-invariant
two-tensors are scalar multiples of the identity, with scalar fixed by
their trace. Both \(M\) and \((C_{rs})\) are positive semidefinite
Gram matrices. The exact remaining contraction is
\[
 \boxed{\mathcal D=C_{02}-C_{11}
 =\tfrac12\sum_{c,d}a_ca_d(r_c-r_d)^2M_{cd}.}
 \tag{RH47}
\]
Every diagonal chord term cancels. Its deterministic coefficient matrix is
\(\frac12[a(ar^2)^t+(ar^2)a^t]-(ar)(ar)^t\); it has rank at most
three, with at most one positive and two negative directions. To check
the inertia bound, factor it through the three columns
\((a,ar,ar^2)\) and the fixed symmetric form
\(\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1/2\\0&-1&0\\1/2&0&0\end{pmatrix}\), whose
eigenvalues are \(1/2,-1/2,-1\). This is a proved low-rank receiving
block for the actual covariance, retaining all original root coefficients.
It does not fix its sign against \(M\).

There is a further exact covariance hierarchy with the same root rows.
Let \(B_r=Y_{u^{[r]}}\),
\(\mathsf V_{rs}=\mu(B_rw)(B_sw)\), and
\(\mathsf J_r=\mu B_rF\). For any finite real coefficient list
\(z\), the field \(\sum z_rB_r\) has zero divergence and the same
acceleration calculation as (RH36), with each \(u^{[k]}\) replaced by
\(\sum z_ru^{[r+k]}\). Polarizing (RH37) therefore proves
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \mathsf V_{rs}=-\tfrac12\mu h_w(B_r,B_s)
   +\tfrac1{16}[C_{r,s+2}+C_{r+2,s}-2C_{r+1,s+1}],\\
 \mathsf V\preceq\mathsf U,\qquad
 \mathsf U_{rs}=\sqrt\xi C_{rs}
   +\tfrac1{16}[C_{r,s+2}+C_{r+2,s}-2C_{r+1,s+1}],\\
 \begin{pmatrix}G_F&-\mathsf J^t/2\\-\mathsf J/2&\mathsf V\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.
 \end{gathered}\tag{RH48}
\]
The last matrix is the Gram matrix of \(F\) and the actual scores
\(B_rw\); it requires no inverse or positivity assumption on a
commutator numerator. In particular
\(4G_F(z^t\mathsf U z)\ge(z^t\mathsf J)^2\) for every real \(z\).
The right side of the upper matrix inequality is itself nonnegative,
because it exceeds the nonnegative actual Fisher matrix. This extends
the scalar calculation without changing the receiving raw phase.

For completeness the spectral measure remains
\(\nu_F(B)=\|\mathbf1_B(A)F\psi\|^2\). It has moments
\(G_F,E_F,E_{2,F}\) and zero mass at zero, by ground-state uniqueness
and \(\mu F=0\). Thus
\[
 \nu_F((0,s])\ge\max\{0,G_F-E_F/s\},\qquad
 \nu_F((0,R])\ge\max\{0,4E_F/R-4E_{2,F}/R^2\}.
 \tag{RH49}
\]
The first bound uses \(\mathbf1_{(0,s]}(\lambda)\ge1-\lambda/s\)
on the support of \(\nu_F\). The second uses
\(\mathbf1_{(0,R]}(\lambda)\ge4\lambda(1-\lambda/R)/R\)
for every \(\lambda\ge0\); the quadratic is nonpositive above \(R\).
In particular \(R=2E_{2,F}/E_F\) gives mass at least
\(E_F^2/E_{2,F}\). This window uses the actual original energy units.

The new upper second moment does not certify the prescribed shrinking
window. Its direct substitution gives
\[
 G_F-E_F/s_j\ge\frac{E_F^2}{P_F+Q_{a_j}E_F}-E_F/s_j,
 \qquad Q_{a_j}=\kappa_*/2+400j>s_j\quad(j\ge2).
 \tag{RH50}
\]
For every \(E_F>0\) the right side is strictly negative, since
\(E_F/(P_F+Q_{a_j}E_F)<1/Q_{a_j}<1/s_j\).
This establishes the limitation of that particular certificate, not
the sign of the actual endpoint.

The improved explicit conjugate denominator also has a precise scale
test. Pointwise \(|BF|^2\le h_1|\nabla F|^2\) is not integrated by
replacing \(h_1\) by its mean. Instead apply Cauchy–Schwarz directly to
\(\mu\langle B,\nabla F\rangle\); it gives
\(J_F^2\le xE_F/\kappa\). Since \(U_H(x)\ge\sqrt\xi x\),
\[
 \frac{J_F^2}{4U_H(x)}\le\frac{E_F}{4\kappa\sqrt\xi}
                         =\frac a4E_F.
 \tag{RH51}
\]
Consequently the lower bound produced by (RH44), minus the actual
\(E_F/s_j\), is negative once \(400j^2>\kappa_*\). No upper bound
on \(E_F\) was used in this test. Keeping the signed contraction in
(RH37), or the full block in (RH48), can be stronger; replacing it by
the positive coefficient bound in (RH41) loses that possibility.

The next calculation has therefore isolated and evaluated an actual
remaining mechanism. The acceleration is exactly (RH36); its scalar
covariance is the off-diagonal, rank-at-most-three contraction (RH47),
with the complete finite coefficient sums (RH39). Its higher receiving
matrix is (RH48). The other unchanged raw contractions are
\(H_S-H_R,J_S-J_R,Q-Q_R,K-K_R\) in (RH22)–(RH25), and
\(2x+\mu\Xi\) with the full reflected derivative in (RH43).
Their required cancellation is not supplied by a variance or norm
assumption. These formulas give explicit next quantities to calculate
in the actual state.

If a unit-vector statement is desired, its exact map is
\(F\psi\mapsto F\psi/\sqrt{G_F}\), permitted by (RH10), with spectral
measure \(\nu_F/G_F\), first moment \(E_F/G_F\), and second moment
\(E_{2,F}/G_F\). Every raw mass above is multiplied by \(1/G_F\) under
that map. No uniform bound on \(G_F\), or positive endpoint, is created
by it.

\section*{A retained kinetic square gives a stronger upper covariance bound at the original source}

Every expectation in this note is in the actual original positive ground state. The new bound improves the leading coefficient of an actual source-zero second-moment upper bound. Its remainder has order \(a\) after insertion into the curvature variance. The remaining mean-root term can still have order \(a^{-2}\); an upper bound of order \(a\) for the full original covariance is not proved here.

\subsection*{1. Original configuration and exact ground transform}

Let \(m=2L\), let the vertices be \(z\in\{0,\ldots,m\}^3\), and retain every positive edge \(e=(z,d)\) with both endpoints in this set. The geometric faces are \(p=(z;d,e)\), \(d<e\), with all four vertices present. Their original ordered words and scalars are
\[
\begin{gathered}
 U_p=U_d(z)U_e(z+e_d)U_d(z+e_e)^{-1}U_e(z)^{-1},\\
 W_p=\operatorname{Tr}U_p,\quad D_p=2-W_p,\quad 0\le D_p\le4,\\
 N=3m(m+1)^2,\quad M=3m^2(m+1),\quad
 T_\alpha=-i\sigma_\alpha/2,\\
 \Delta=\sum_{e,\alpha}X_{e,\alpha}^2,\quad K=-\Delta,\quad
 \Gamma(F,G)=\sum_{e,\alpha}(X_{e,\alpha}F)(X_{e,\alpha}G),\\
 H=\kappa K+b\sum_pD_p
   =\kappa K+2bM-b\sum_pW_p,\qquad
 \kappa=2g^2/a,\quad b=1/(2g^2a),\quad\kappa b=a^{-2}.
\end{gathered}\tag{ZU1}
\]
The metric is the radius-two metric on every \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) factor. Each Haar measure has total mass one. The physical subspace imposes every original vertex gauge action, including boundary vertices. The full compact elliptic operator has a smooth positive unit lowest eigenfunction \(\psi\). Taking the absolute value of a minimizing vector does not increase its first Sobolev quadratic form; elliptic regularity and the strong maximum principle give strict positivity. Put
\[
 H\psi=E_0\psi,\quad d\mu=\psi^2dU,\quad w=\log\psi,
 \qquad \mathscr L=\Delta+2\nabla w\cdot\nabla.
\tag{ZU2}
\]
Product expansion and Haar integration by parts give
\[
 \langle F\psi,(H-E_0)F\psi\rangle=\kappa\mu\Gamma(F,\overline F),
 \qquad \mu\Gamma(w,F)=-\tfrac12\mu\Delta F.          \tag{ZU3}
\]
The first identity proves uniqueness: the quotient of another ground vector by \(\psi\) has zero gradient and is constant on the connected product. Gauge transformations preserve Haar, the metric and every closed face trace, so they fix the positive unit ground vector. Thus the full and physical ground energies coincide. All calculations initially use smooth functions; the bounded first-Sobolev limits below extend (ZU3) by closure.

Fix real \(f\in C_c(\mathbb R^3)\), with the original centers
\[
 x_p=o+a\bigl(z-L\mathbf1+(e_d+e_e)/2\bigr),\quad f_p=f(x_p),
 \quad C_f=a\sum_p f_pD_p=2a\sum_pf_p-a\sum_pf_pW_p.
\tag{ZU4}
\]
All three orientations occur. Retain the actual mean and covariance
\[
 m_f=\mu C_f=2a\sum_pf_p-a\sum_pf_p\mu W_p,
 \qquad G_f=\mu C_f^2-m_f^2.                          \tag{ZU5}
\]
The sampled coefficients are constants on configuration space, so \(C_f\) is smooth even for continuous \(f\).

\subsection*{2. Full local budget and its positive remainder}

Choose a vertex cube \(Q=v+\{0,\ldots,q\}^3\) containing every edge of every face with \(f_p\ne0\). Inside edges have both endpoints in \(Q\); inside faces use four inside edges. Define
\[
\begin{gathered}
 N_Q=3q(q+1)^2,\quad M_Q=3q^2(q+1),\\
 \eta_Q=\sum_{d=1}^3
 [\mathbf1_{\{v_d>0\}}+\mathbf1_{\{v_d+q<m\}}],
 \quad C_Q=2q(q+1)\eta_Q,\\
 W_Q=\sum_{p\ \mathrm{inside}}D_p,\quad
 K_Q=-\sum_{e\ \mathrm{inside},\alpha}X_{e,\alpha}^2,
 \quad Z_Q=|\nabla_Qw|^2,\\
 H=\kappa K_Q+bW_Q+H_{\rm out}+bW_\times,
 \quad H_{\rm out}\ge E_{\rm out}I.
\end{gathered}\tag{ZU6}
\]
A mixed face has exactly one inside edge. Indeed two adjacent inside edges put three face vertices in the interval product \(Q\), which puts the fourth in \(Q\); two opposite inside edges already include all vertices. Each available outward side has \(2q(q+1)\) tangent edges, giving the stated \(C_Q\). The scalar parts are \(2bM_Q\), \(2b(M-M_Q-C_Q)\), and \(2bC_Q\), whose sum is the full \(2bM\).

Here is the local comparison used in LC14–LC15a and OS5–OS7, recalled with its proof. The positive outside ground is invariant under all original vertex actions restricted to outside edges. Start a crossing trace at its unique inside traversal. The remaining actual three-edge ordered outside path has distinct endpoints. The central gauge element \(-I\) at one endpoint negates that matrix path and preserves the outside ground density. Its matrix expectation is therefore zero. Any tensor of a unit inside vector with the outside ground has crossing energy exactly \(2bC_Q\).

For an inside edge put \(x=\operatorname{Tr}U/2\),
\[
 Z_t=\int e^{2tx}dU,\quad h_t=Z_t^{-1/2}e^{tx},\quad
 q_t=Z_t^{-1}\int xe^{2tx}dU.
\]
The marginal Haar measure is \((2/\pi)\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx\). After \(z=1-x\), the squared comparison density is proportional to \(e^{-2tz}z^{1/2}\sqrt{2-z}\mathbf1_{[0,2]}\). The extra factor relative to \(e^{-2tz}z^{1/2}\) is decreasing; applying

\(2\operatorname{Cov}(z,r(z))=\mathbb E[(z-z')(r(z)-r(z'))]\le0\)

and integrating that gamma density gives \(1-q_t\le3/(4t)\). Symmetry gives \(0<q_t<1\). The radius-two identities \(\Gamma(x)=(1-x^2)/4\), \(\Delta x=-3x/4\), integrated against \(e^{2tx}\), give kinetic energy \(3\kappa tq_t/8\) per edge. Centrality gives both matrix means \(\mathbb E_tU=\mathbb E_tU^{-1}=q_tI\). Thus the product inside comparison has energy
\[
 \frac{3\kappa N_Qtq_t}{8}+2bM_Q(1-q_t^4)
 \le \frac{3\kappa N_Qt}{8}+\frac{6bM_Q}{t}.
\]
Taking \(t=4\sqrt{bM_Q/(\kappa N_Q)}\), or taking the constant inside vector, proves
\[
\begin{gathered}
 0\le E_0-E_{\rm out}\le b\Lambda_Q,\qquad
 \Lambda_Q=\min\{2M_Q,6g^2\sqrt{N_QM_Q}\}+2C_Q,\\
 \kappa\mu Z_Q+b\mu W_Q\le E_0-E_{\rm out},\qquad
 \delta_Q=b\Lambda_Q-(E_0-E_{\rm out})\ge0.
\end{gathered}\tag{ZU7}
\]
The full/physical ground equality makes the tensor comparison legitimate without assuming a tensor decomposition of the physical Hilbert space. The actual measure remains \(\mu\).

For a nonnegative inside multiplier \(Y\) used below, define the retained outside remainder
\[
 \mathcal O_Q(Y)=
 \langle\sqrt Y\psi,(H_{\rm out}-E_{\rm out})\sqrt Y\psi\rangle
       +b\mu(YW_\times)\ge0.                         \tag{ZU8}
\]
The first term is the outside quadratic form and includes its whole kinetic and scalar potential contributions. The square-root regularization below proves its domain assertion.

\subsection*{3. Absolute weights and exact one-face derivatives}

Let \(F=\|f\|_\infty>0\), \(A_1=\sum_p|f_p|\), and put
\[
\begin{gathered}
 Y=\sum_p|f_p|D_p,\quad d=\mu Y,\quad
 Y_+=\sum_{f_p>0}f_pD_p,\quad
 Y_-=\sum_{f_p<0}(-f_p)D_p,\\
 Y=Y_++Y_-,\quad C_f=a(Y_+-Y_-),\quad 0\le Y\le FW_Q,\\
 J(Y)=6A_1-3Y,\quad\Delta Y=J(Y),\quad
 \gamma=\Gamma(Y)\le16FY.
\end{gathered}\tag{ZU9}
\]
For the Laplacian, on each of the four incident edges \(\sum_\alpha T_\alpha^2=-3I/4\), giving \(\Delta D_p=6-3D_p\) with the scalar (6) retained. A quaternion representation of the full ordered face word gives, for each incident edge,
\[
 \sum_\alpha(X_{e,\alpha}D_p)^2=1-W_p^2/4=D_p-D_p^2/4.
\tag{ZU10}
\]
The surrounding links and inverse orientations act by signs and orthogonal adjoint transports on this derivative vector. Cauchy–Schwarz at each edge, with at most four incident faces, gives
\[
 \gamma\le\sum_e r_e^f\sum_{p\ni e}|f_p|^2(D_p-D_p^2/4)
 \le16\sum_p|f_p|^2D_p\le16FY.
\tag{ZU11}
\]
Every boundary incidence remains in the first expression. There is no claimed independence between its derivative summands.

If \(A_1=0\), \(C_f=Y=0\) and the target variance is zero. Suppose henceforth \(A_1>0\). Strict positivity of \(\psi\) gives \(d>0\), because a face with a positive coefficient can have nonidentity holonomy on an open configuration set.

Apply (ZU3) to \(\sqrt{Y+\epsilon}\), \(\epsilon>0\), and use the decomposition (ZU6). Inside derivative expansion cancels the identical \(\kappa\mu\gamma/[4(Y+\epsilon)]\) terms on both sides. Its cross term is
\[
 \mu\Gamma(w,Y)=-\tfrac12\mu J(Y)=-3A_1+\tfrac32d.
\]
Letting \(\epsilon\downarrow0\) yields the exact identity
\[
 b\Lambda_Qd
 =b\mu(W_QY)+\kappa\mu(YZ_Q)
       -\kappa(3A_1-3d/2)+\mathcal O_Q(Y)+\delta_Qd.
\tag{ZU12}
\]
All limits are finite: \(Y,w\) and their derivatives are bounded at fixed regulator, and \(\gamma/(Y+\epsilon)\le16F\). Outside derivatives act only on \(\psi\), so the outside quadratic forms converge directly. No crossing energy was dropped in (ZU12).

\subsection*{4. The evaluated weighted square}

Define \(B(Y)=J(Y)/(32F)\). Complete the following actual score square:
\[
 \mathcal Q_\epsilon=
 \mu\left[(Y+\epsilon)
  \left|\nabla_Qw+\frac{B(Y)}{Y+\epsilon}\nabla Y\right|^2\right]\ge0.
\tag{ZU13}
\]
Weighted Haar integration by parts gives exactly
\[
 2\mu[B(Y)\Gamma(w,Y)]
   =-\mu[B'(Y)\gamma+B(Y)\Delta Y],\qquad B'=-3/(32F).
\tag{ZU14}
\]
Consequently
\[
 \mu[(Y+\epsilon)Z_Q]
 =\mathcal Q_\epsilon+
   \mu\left[\frac{J(Y)^2}{32F}-\frac{3\gamma}{32F}
       -\frac{J(Y)^2\gamma}{1024F^2(Y+\epsilon)}\right].
\tag{ZU15}
\]
The last ratio is bounded by \(16F\max J^2\) before its displayed coefficient. All other terms are integrable and fixed. Thus \(\mathcal Q=\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\mathcal Q_\epsilon\) exists, is finite and nonnegative. Set \(\gamma/Y=0\) when \(Y=0\), which is precisely the regularized ratio's pointwise limit. Put
\[
 \mathcal R=
 \mu\left[\frac{3}{32F}(16FY-\gamma)
       +\frac{J(Y)^2}{1024F^2}
                       \left(16F-\frac\gamma Y\right)\right]\ge0.
\tag{ZU16}
\]
Each summand is nonnegative by (ZU11), including the stipulated zero set. Rearranging (ZU15) and taking the limit proves the evaluated source-zero square identity
\[
 \boxed{\quad
 \mu(YZ_Q)=\mathcal Q+\mathcal R
                  +\frac{\mu J(Y)^2}{64F}-\frac32d.
 \quad}                                               \tag{ZU17}
\]
This is stronger than retaining only \(\mu(YZ_Q)\ge0\). In particular it retains the square of the original full scalar \(6A_1\).

Define the original coupling ratio and polynomial
\[
\begin{gathered}
 \alpha=\kappa/b=4(g^2)^2=\kappa^2a^2,\quad c=9\alpha/64,
 \quad \Lambda_f=F\Lambda_Q,\\
 P_f(s)=(1+c)s^2-(\Lambda_f+4cA_1)s+4cA_1^2,\\
 \mathcal D_f=
 \alpha F(\mathcal Q+\mathcal R)
 +\mu[Y(FW_Q-Y)]
 +\frac F b[\mathcal O_Q(Y)+\delta_Qd]\ge0.
\end{gathered}\tag{ZU18}
\]
Multiply (ZU12) by \(F/b\), insert (ZU17), and use

\(F W_QY=Y^2+Y(FW_Q-Y)\).

Every term is now evaluated, and the exact result is
\[
 \boxed{\quad \mu P_f(Y)+\mathcal D_f=3\alpha F A_1.\quad}
\tag{ZU19}
\]
This is an identity for the original actual source, with its complete nonnegative remainder. It contains no source derivative, covariance-sign assumption, Gaussian comparison measure or spatial symmetry assumption.

\subsection*{5. The two mean roots and stronger upper bounds}

For clarity the root interval follows directly from the same actual state. By (ZU7), \(d\le F\mu W_Q\le\Lambda_f\), and
\[
 \mu Z_Q\le\alpha^{-1}(\Lambda_Q-\mu W_Q)
              \le(\alpha F)^{-1}(\Lambda_f-d).
\]
The full scalar identity \(\mu J(Y)=-2\mu\Gamma(w,Y)\), Cauchy–Schwarz and (ZU11) give
\[
 (6A_1-3d)^2\le4\mu Z_Q\,\mu\gamma
                 \le\frac{64}{\alpha}d(\Lambda_f-d).
\tag{ZU20}
\]
Equivalently \(P_f(d)\le0\). Therefore its discriminant is nonnegative and its roots are
\[
\begin{gathered}
 \mathfrak D_f=(\Lambda_f+4cA_1)^2-16c(1+c)A_1^2,\\
 r_\pm=\frac{\Lambda_f+4cA_1\pm\sqrt{\mathfrak D_f}}{2(1+c)},
 \qquad 0<r_-\le d\le r_+\le\Lambda_f.
\end{gathered}\tag{ZU21}
\]
The root product and sum are positive. To verify the last bound without an unstated branch choice, observe \(P_f(\Lambda_f)=c(\Lambda_f-2A_1)^2\ge0\) and \(d\le\Lambda_f\). The alternative \(\Lambda_f\le r_-\) forces \(d=\Lambda_f=r_-\), \(\Lambda_f=2A_1\). In that case the other root is \(2cA_1/(1+c)<2A_1\), so \(\Lambda_f\) is the upper root. This proves the claim in every case, including a repeated root.

Let \(\varepsilon_f=3\alpha F A_1/(1+c)\). Since

\(\mu P_f(Y)=(1+c)\operatorname{Var}_\mu Y+P_f(d)\),

the exact covariance remainder form of (ZU19) is
\[
 \boxed{\quad
 \operatorname{Var}_\mu Y
 =(d-r_-)(r_+-d)+\varepsilon_f-\frac{\mathcal D_f}{1+c}.
 \quad}                                                \tag{ZU22}
\]
In particular, with the full actual \(d\) first retained,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{Var}_\mu Y
 &\le(d-r_-)(r_+-d)+\varepsilon_f
 \le\frac{(r_+-r_-)^2}{4}+\varepsilon_f,\\
 \mu Y^2
 &\le(r_-+r_+)d-r_-r_++\varepsilon_f
 \le r_+^2+\varepsilon_f.
\end{aligned}\tag{ZU23}
\]
No observed mean was set equal to either root.

For the unchanged signed observable, the following scalar and sign contributions are exact:
\[
 C_f^2=a^2Y^2-4a^2Y_+Y_-,\qquad
 G_f=a^2\mu Y^2-m_f^2-4a^2\mu(Y_+Y_-).              \tag{ZU24}
\]
Combining with (ZU19) proves the complete source-zero upper identity
\[
\boxed{\begin{aligned}
 G_f={}&a^2[(r_-+r_+)d-r_-r_++\varepsilon_f]
      -m_f^2-4a^2\mu(Y_+Y_-)
      -\frac{a^2\mathcal D_f}{1+c}\\
 \le{}&a^2[(r_-+r_+)d-r_-r_++\varepsilon_f]
      -m_f^2-4a^2\mu(Y_+Y_-)\\
 \le{}&a^2[r_+^2+\varepsilon_f]-m_f^2.
\end{aligned}}\tag{ZU25}
\]
The product \(Y_+Y_-\) is nonnegative pointwise; no assertion about the sign of its connected covariance has been made. When \(f\ge0\), \(Y_-=0\) and \(m_f=ad\), so the sharper upper bound is
\[
 G_f\le a^2[(d-r_-)(r_+-d)+\varepsilon_f]
       \le a^2\left[\frac{(r_+-r_-)^2}{4}+\varepsilon_f\right].
\tag{ZU26}
\]
The same statement applies to \(f\le0\) after retaining \(m_f=-ad\).

\subsection*{6. Exact strength and limit on the original path}

Retain
\[
 L_j=j^4,\quad a_j=(100j)^{-1},\quad
 g_j^2=\kappa_*/(200j),\quad\kappa_j=\kappa_*,\quad
 b_j=1/(\kappa_*a_j^2),\quad\alpha_j=\kappa_*^2a_j^2.
\tag{ZU27}
\]
Choose a physical support cube \(\prod_d[c_d,c_d+R]\) and exactly
\[
 v_{d,j}=L_j+\lfloor(c_d-o_d)/a_j\rfloor-1,\quad
 q_j=\lceil R/a_j\rceil+3.
\tag{ZU28}
\]
This includes the original four edges of every supported face. Because \(a_jL_j=j^3/100\to\infty\), it is strictly inside the original box for all sufficiently large \(j\); the finite boundary indicators remain in (ZU6). The local counts and original comparison give
\[
 a_j^2\Lambda_{Q_j}\longrightarrow
 \mathsf L_R=9\kappa_*R^3+24R^2.                     \tag{ZU29}
\]
For each of the three face orientations the mesh is a translate of \(a_j\mathbb Z^3\). Partition a fixed support enlargement into its mesh cubes. The quadrature error for \(|f|\) is at most its volume times the modulus of continuity of \(|f|\) at \(\sqrt3a_j/2\), per orientation. Thus, with \(J_1=\int|f(x)|\,d^3x>0\),
\[
 a_j^3A_{1,j}\to3J_1,\qquad d_j\le F\Lambda_{Q_j}=O(a_j^{-2}).
\tag{ZU30}
\]
The full finite roots in (ZU21), with every coefficient retained, consequently satisfy
\[
\begin{gathered}
 a_j^2r_{\pm,j}\to
 \mathsf r_\pm=
 \frac{F\mathsf L_R\pm
 \sqrt{F^2\mathsf L_R^2-81\kappa_*^2J_1^2/4}}2,\\
 \frac{a_j^2\varepsilon_{f,j}}{a_j}
       \longrightarrow9\kappa_*^2FJ_1.
\end{gathered}\tag{ZU31}
\]
The discriminant is strictly positive: \(J_1\le FR^3\), while \(\mathsf L_R\ge9\kappa_*R^3\), so its subtracted term is at most one quarter of the square of the cubic part. Both limiting roots are positive. Thus (ZU25)–(ZU26) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \limsup_j a_j^2G_{f,j}&\le\mathsf r_+^2
                  &&(f\ \mathrm{real}),\\
 \limsup_j a_j^2G_{f,j}&\le
          \frac{F^2\mathsf L_R^2-81\kappa_*^2J_1^2/4}{4}
                  &&(f\ge0\ \mathrm{or}\ f\le0).
\end{aligned}\tag{ZU32}
\]
These inequalities do not discard the finite \(m_f^2\) or sign term: the stronger equations retaining them are (ZU25). The final asymptotic displays give an explicit bound when those actual expectations are not evaluated.

The comparison to the previous upper estimate can also be proved exactly. Dropping the local kinetic form before testing with \(\sqrt{Y+\epsilon}\) gives
\[
 \mu Y^2\le\Lambda_f d+4\alpha F^2=:B_{\rm old}.
\tag{ZU33}
\]
Indeed \(bW_Q\le H-E_{\rm out}\) as forms, \(Y\le FW_Q\), and \(\Gamma(Y)/(4Y)\le4F\). The new mean-retaining bound is
\[
 B_{\rm new}=
 \frac{(\Lambda_f+4cA_1)d-4cA_1^2+3\alpha F A_1}{1+c}.
\tag{ZU34}
\]
Their difference is exactly
\[
 B_{\rm old}-B_{\rm new}
 =\frac{c\Lambda_fd-4cA_1d+4cA_1^2
             +4\alpha F^2(1+c)-3\alpha F A_1}{1+c},
\quad
 a_j^4(B_{\rm old}-B_{\rm new})
       \longrightarrow\frac{81\kappa_*^2J_1^2}{16}>0.
\tag{ZU35}
\]
All other terms vanish after multiplication by \(a_j^4\), using (ZU27)–(ZU30). Thus the new bound is strictly stronger at every sufficiently fine original regulator for each fixed nonzero test. In the covariance, the upper envelope decreases by \(81\kappa_*^2J_1^2/(16a_j^2)+o(a_j^{-2})\), before the additional retained sign and mean subtractions. At a coarse regulator one can take the minimum of (ZU33), (ZU34), and the already proved finite bounds; no assertion of strict improvement at every coarse regulator is needed.

The exponent is unchanged. Formula (ZU22) gives an exact reason: the remaining term \((d-r_-)(r_+-d)\) is nonnegative and can have order \(a^{-4}\) under the proved root interval. It is not zero by the mean uncertainty inequality. For a nonnegative test, (ZU22) and (ZU26) identify precisely how this term and the nonnegative evaluated remainder enter the actual covariance. No value or sign beyond what is proved is assigned to their difference. The source-zero calculation has advanced the upper bound; it has not established a smooth interacting continuum theory or its spectral endpoint.

\subsection*{7. The next actual calculation: optimizing the score square}

The remaining term in (ZU22) calls for an evaluated subtraction, not a choice of mean within its allowed interval. The same calculation can be continued by optimizing the square rather than fixing its coefficient. All quantities here are again at source zero. Put
\[
 U=\mu J(Y)^2,\quad S=\mu\gamma,\quad
 T=\mu\left[\frac{J(Y)^2\gamma}{Y}\right]\le16FU.
\tag{ZU36}
\]
The ratio uses the convention and dominated limit of (ZU16). Both \(U,T\) are positive. To see this, \(Y\) is a nonconstant real analytic function: it is zero at the identity configuration and positive on an open set. Its gradient is nonzero on some open set; \(J(Y)\) cannot vanish throughout that open set, since then \(Y\) would be constant there. Strict positivity of the density proves \(T>0\) and \(U>0\).

For every real \(t\), replace \(B(Y)\) in (ZU13) by \(tJ(Y)\). The full limiting square is
\[
 0\le\mu(YZ_Q)-t(U-3S)+t^2T.
\]
Minimizing this scalar quadratic at \(t=(U-3S)/(2T)\) proves
\[
 \mu(YZ_Q)\ge\frac{(U-3S)^2}{4T}
              \ge\frac{(U-3S)^2}{64FU}.
\tag{ZU37}
\]
The first expression retains the exact original derivative ratio. There is no need to assume a sign for \(U-3S\), since the square is valid for every real \(t\). Combining the last bound with (ZU12), and retaining the nonnegative spatial and outside terms
\[
 \mathcal B_f=\mu[Y(FW_Q-Y)]
                  +\frac F b[\mathcal O_Q(Y)+\delta_Qd],
\]
gives the further proved upper estimate
\[
 \boxed{\quad
 \mu P_f(Y)\le3\alpha FA_1
 -\frac{3\alpha}{32}(16Fd-S)
 -\frac{9\alpha S^2}{64U}-\mathcal B_f.
 \quad}                                                \tag{ZU38}
\]
Every displayed subtraction is nonnegative. This follows by expanding \((U-3S)^2/U=U-6S+9S^2/U\) and the original \(J(Y)^2\); no omitted covariance sign is involved. It can be used together with (ZU19), taking the smaller of the two evaluated upper bounds.

There is also a coefficient-sensitive incidence improvement. If \(n_f\) is the number of nonzero sampled face coefficients, the same first inequality as (ZU11), before its last simplification, gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 16FY-\gamma
 &\ge16\sum_p |f_p|(F-|f_p|)D_p
                       +4\sum_pf_p^2D_p^2\\
 &\ge4Y^2/n_f.
\end{aligned}\tag{ZU39}
\]
Here scalar Cauchy–Schwarz is applied to the \(n_f\) numbers \(|f_p|D_p\). Thus (ZU16) implies
\[
 \alpha F\mathcal R\ge
 \frac{3\alpha}{8n_f}\mu Y^2
       +\frac{\alpha}{256Fn_f}\mu[J(Y)^2Y].
\tag{ZU40}
\]
These terms strengthen (ZU25) after division by \(1+c\). The exact first line of (ZU39) retains more information than its universal second line. Neither (ZU38) nor (ZU40), with the estimates proved here, closes the order-\(a^{-2}\) mean-root contribution. They are completed source-zero receiving calculations of the next remainders, not assumptions that these remainders cancel it.

For comparison, directly multiplying the original ground equation by a smooth real \(F_0\) and integrating twice gives
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}_\mu(F_0,V)
  +\kappa\operatorname{Cov}_\mu(F_0,|\nabla w|^2)
  =\frac\kappa2\mu\Delta F_0,
 \quad V=b\sum_pD_p.                                  \tag{ZU41}
\]
Indeed \(V-E_0=\kappa(\Delta w+|\nabla w|^2)\), while

\(\mu(F_0\Delta w)=-\mu\Gamma(F_0,w)-2\mu(F_0|\nabla w|^2)\)

and \(\mu\Gamma(w,F_0)=-\mu\Delta F_0/2\). Taking \(F_0=1\) first and subtracting its product with \(\mu F_0\) proves (ZU41). At \(F_0=V\), the variance equals \(\kappa\mu\Delta V/2\) minus the potential-score covariance. That covariance cannot be deleted by the stationary identity. The independent PVI proof contains explicit positive-ground-state counterexamples to a universal sign, including one on the compact gauge-invariant configuration space with an explicitly different potential. It does not assert that the original plaquette potential has that counterexample's sign. The actual original-potential progress in this note uses the nonnegative forms (ZU12)–(ZU19) instead.

The independent weighted derivation further retains every term in the optimized square. Define
\[
 Q_*=\mu(YZ_Q)-\frac{(U-3S)^2}{4T}\ge0.
\]
Inserting this equality in (ZU12), and using
\[
 \frac{\alpha F(U-3S)^2}{4T}
 =\frac{\alpha(U-3S)^2}{64U}
  +\frac{\alpha(U-3S)^2(16FU-T)}{64UT},
\]
proves the stronger exact decomposition
\[
\boxed{\begin{aligned}
 \mu P_f(Y)+\mathcal B_f+\alpha FQ_*
 &+\frac{3\alpha}{32}(16Fd-S)
    +\frac{9\alpha S^2}{64U}\\
 &+\frac{\alpha(U-3S)^2(16FU-T)}{64UT}
     =3\alpha FA_1.
\end{aligned}}\tag{ZU42}
\]
All retained defects are nonnegative by (ZU11), (ZU36) and (ZU37). Formula (ZU39), divided by \(Y\) on its positive set, multiplied by \(J(Y)^2\) and integrated, also gives
\[
 16FU-T\ge\frac4{n_f}\mu[J(Y)^2Y].                 \tag{ZU43}
\]
At the zero set its left integrand is nonnegative and the right integrand is zero, so the same inequality holds with the earlier ratio convention.

The mean-root calculation itself can retain the incidence correction. Replace \(S\le16Fd\) in (ZU20) by \(S\le16Fd-4\mu Y^2/n_f\). Since \(\Lambda_f-d\ge0\), no sign reverses. Multiplication by \(\alpha/64\) gives the complete strengthening
\[
 \boxed{\quad P_f(d)+
       \frac{\Lambda_f-d}{4Fn_f}\,\mu Y^2\le0.\quad}  \tag{ZU44}
\]
No division by \(\Lambda_f-d\) has occurred, so this includes its zero endpoint. An independent weighted verification established these last three formulas. The complete arguments above check them by substitution into the full original local identity. They further evaluate the same remaining upper-variance terms without changing the established power of \(a\).

\section*{Stationary potential identities and the local square estimate}

This independent calculation uses the actual finite-volume Hamiltonian
\(H=-\kappa\Delta+V\), \(V=b\sum_p(2-\operatorname{Tr}U_p)\), the radius-two
product metric on \(\mathrm{SU}(2)^E\), and its positive unit ground state
\(\psi\). All original vertex gauge actions, including boundary vertices,
are retained. Set \(H\psi=\mathcal E\psi\), \(w=\log\psi\),
\(d\mu=\psi^2dU\), and \(Z=|\nabla w|^2\).
The scalar \(2bM\) remains part of \(V\).

\subsection*{PVI1. Exact stationary covariance identity}

For every real smooth function \(F\),
\[
 \boxed{\operatorname{Cov}_\mu(F,V)
       +\kappa\operatorname{Cov}_\mu(F,Z)
       ={\kappa\over2}\mu\Delta F.}                 \tag{PVI1}
\]
Indeed, division by the strictly positive ground state gives
\(V-\mathcal E=\kappa(\Delta w+Z)\). Haar integration by parts gives
\[
 \mu(F\Delta w)=-\mu\Gamma(F,w)-2\mu(FZ),\qquad
 \mu\Gamma(F,w)=-\tfrac12\mu\Delta F.
\]
Consequently
\(\mu(FV)=\mathcal E\mu F+(\kappa/2)\mu\Delta F-\kappa\mu(FZ)\).
Taking \(F=1\) proves
\(\mu V=\mathcal E-\kappa\mu Z\); subtracting its product with \(\mu F\)
proves (PVI1), with the means retained.

In particular,
\[
 \boxed{\operatorname{Var}_\mu V
   ={\kappa\over2}\mu\Delta V
                  -\kappa\operatorname{Cov}_\mu(V,Z).} \tag{PVI2}
\]
The original full potential obeys
\[
 \Delta V=6bM-3V,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Var}_\mu V
 ={3\kappa b\over2}(2M-\mu\textstyle\sum_pD_p)
                  -\kappa\operatorname{Cov}_\mu(V,Z). \tag{PVI3}
\]
The last covariance has not been deleted or assigned a sign.

For the unchanged signed smearing
\(C_f=a\sum_p f(x_p)D_p=2aA_0-a\sum_p f(x_p)W_p\),
\(A_0=\sum_p f(x_p)\), \(m_f=\mu C_f\), the exact consequence is
\[
 b\sum_q\operatorname{Cov}_\mu(C_f,D_q)
    +\kappa\operatorname{Cov}_\mu(C_f,Z)
        ={\kappa\over2}(6aA_0-3m_f).                \tag{PVI4}
\]
All three original face orientations occur in both sums. The first
term is a row sum of the full face covariance matrix; it is not
\((b/a)\operatorname{Var}C_f\) for a nonconstant smearing.

\subsection*{PVI2. Kinetic variance and the exact Hessian remainder}

Write \(K=-\Delta\), \(T=\langle\psi,K\psi\rangle=\mu Z\).
The ground equation implies the exact vector equality
\[
 (V-\mu V)\psi=-\kappa(K-T)\psi,
 \quad
 \operatorname{Var}_\mu V
   =\kappa^2\bigl(\|K\psi\|^2-T^2\bigr).           \tag{PVI5}
\]
This is an equality of variances, not an upper bound on either variance.
All quantities are finite because the original configuration manifold
is compact and \(\psi\) is smooth.

Let \(h=\nabla^2w\) and \(\mathscr L=\Delta+2\nabla w\cdot\nabla\).
The integrated Bochner identity gives
\[
 \mu(\mathscr Lw)^2
 =\mu\|h\|^2+\mu\operatorname{Ric}(\nabla w,\nabla w)
      -2\mu h(\nabla w,\nabla w).
\]
Since \(V-\mu V=\kappa[\mathscr Lw-(Z-\mu Z)]\) and
\(\mu(Z\mathscr Lw)=-2\mu h(\nabla w,\nabla w)\), expansion gives
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_\mu V
 =\kappa^2\bigl[
  \mu\|h\|^2+\mu\operatorname{Ric}(\nabla w,\nabla w)
  +\operatorname{Var}_\mu Z+2\mu h(\nabla w,\nabla w)\bigr]. \tag{PVI6}
\]
Differentiating \(V-\mathcal E=\kappa(\Delta w+Z)\), applying the
scalar Bochner identity, and integrating yields
\[
 \mu\Delta V=2\kappa[\mu\|h\|^2+
                           \mu\operatorname{Ric}(\nabla w,\nabla w)].
                                                               \tag{PVI7}
\]
Thus the remainder omitted by a proposed
\(\operatorname{Var}V\le(\kappa/2)\mu\Delta V\) is exactly
\[
 -\kappa\operatorname{Cov}_\mu(V,Z)
  =\kappa^2[\operatorname{Var}_\mu Z
                         +2\mu h(\nabla w,\nabla w)].            \tag{PVI8}
\]
Here \(\operatorname{Ric}=\tfrac12g\). The available bound
\(h\ge-2\sqrt{b/\kappa}\,g\) supplies a lower bound on this remainder,
not the upper sign required to delete it.

\subsection*{PVI3. Exact localization and its exterior term}

Use the original cube patch \(Q\), its inside edges, inside face sum
\(W=\sum_{p\subset Q}D_p\), crossing sum \(W_\times\), and outside
Hamiltonian \(H_{\mathrm{out}}\). Set
\[
 Z_Q=|\nabla_Qw|^2,\quad
 e_Q={(-\kappa\Delta_Q+bW)\psi\over\psi},\quad
 r_{\mathrm{out}}={H_{\mathrm{out}}\psi\over\psi}.
\]
These are well-defined smooth functions. The exact decomposition is
\(e_Q=\mathcal E-r_{\mathrm{out}}-bW_\times\), and partial integration
in the original inside coordinates gives
\[
 \boxed{b\operatorname{Cov}_\mu(F,W)
 ={\kappa\over2}\mu\Delta_QF
   -\kappa\operatorname{Cov}_\mu(F,Z_Q)
   -\operatorname{Cov}_\mu(F,r_{\mathrm{out}}+bW_\times).} \tag{PVI9}
\]
The proof repeats the two integrations in (PVI1) with \(\Delta_Q\):
\(bW-e_Q=\kappa(\Delta_Qw+Z_Q)\), then center the resulting equality.
In particular, since \(\Delta_QW=6M_Q-3W\),
\[
 b\operatorname{Var}_\mu W
 ={\kappa\over2}(6M_Q-3d)
   -\kappa\operatorname{Cov}_\mu(W,Z_Q)
   -\operatorname{Cov}_\mu(W,r_{\mathrm{out}}+bW_\times),\quad d=\mu W.
                                                               \tag{PVI10}
\]
An operator lower bound on \(H_{\mathrm{out}}\) does not give a sign
to this last covariance. The pointwise function
\((H_{\mathrm{out}}\psi)/\psi\) is retained exactly.

\subsection*{PVI4. Verified local square improvement on the original potential}

This section verifies and slightly strengthens the parent calculation.
Write \(M=M_Q\), \(\Lambda=\Lambda_Q\), \(\alpha=\kappa/b\),
\(S=\Gamma(W)\), \(J(W)=6M-3W\). These symbols are local to this section;
the full potential and full score above are unchanged.
The original local budget OS34 is
\[
 \mu W^2+\alpha\mu(WZ_Q)
       \le\Lambda d+\alpha(3M-3d/2).                \tag{PVI11}
\]
It follows by applying the original local Hamiltonian lower bound to
\(\sqrt{W+\varepsilon}\psi\), retaining the inside kinetic energy, and
cancelling its \(\Gamma(W)/(4(W+\varepsilon))\) term against the full
ground-transform form. The surviving cross term is
\(\mu\Gamma(w,W)=-(1/2)\mu\Delta W=3d/2-3M\).
Monotone convergence of \((W+\varepsilon)Z_Q\) proves (PVI11).

Expand the nonnegative square
\[
 \mu\left[(W+\varepsilon)
 \left|\nabla_Qw+{J(W)\over32(W+\varepsilon)}\nabla W\right|^2\right]\ge0.
\]
Since \(J'(W)=-3\), integration by parts gives exactly
\[
 \mu[J(W)\Gamma(w,W)]
       =-\tfrac12\mu[J(W)^2-3S].                  \tag{PVI12}
\]
The square is therefore
\[
 \mu[(W+\varepsilon)Z_Q]-{\mu J^2\over32}
       +{3\mu S\over32}
       +\mu{J^2S\over1024(W+\varepsilon)}.
\]
Using \(S\le16W\), this square is at most
\(\mu[(W+\varepsilon)Z_Q]-\mu J^2/64+3\mu S/32\).
Letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) proves
\[
 \boxed{\mu(WZ_Q)\ge{\mu J^2\over64}-{3\mu S\over32}
                         \ge{\mu J^2\over64}-{3d\over2}.}       \tag{PVI13}
\]
In particular all signs in the parent's proposed estimate are correct.

Put
\[
 c=1+{9\alpha\over64},\quad
 B=\Lambda+{9\alpha M\over16},\quad D={9\alpha M^2\over16}.
\]
Combining (PVI11) with the stronger first inequality in (PVI13) gives
\[
 \boxed{c\mu W^2-Bd+D
       \le3\alpha M-{3\alpha\over32}(16d-\mu S).}               \tag{PVI14}
\]
The term \(16d-\mu S\) is nonnegative. If \(d^-\le d^+\) are the
original uncertainty roots of \(cx^2-Bx+D=0\), already supplied by
OS8a, then the same algebra, with no change of mean, gives
\[
 \boxed{\operatorname{Var}_\mu W\le
 (d-d^-)(d^+-d)+{3\alpha M\over c}
                  -{3\alpha\over32c}(16d-\mu S).}              \tag{PVI15}
\]
The parent bound follows by deleting its final nonpositive term.
This deletion is legitimate; deleting the covariance in (PVI2) is not.

There is a further evaluated, nonnegative local improvement. Retaining
the individual face squares in edge Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 S\le16W-4\sum_{p\subset Q}D_p^2
       \le16W-{4W^2\over M}.                                  \tag{PVI16}
\]
For the first inequality, each inside edge has at most four incident
inside faces, and each face has four distinct edges; for each incident
edge, its squared derivative is exactly \(D_p-D_p^2/4\).
The second inequality is the finite scalar Cauchy--Schwarz inequality.
Substitute (PVI16) in the final term of the square and use dominated
convergence (all functions are bounded at this fixed lattice) to obtain
\[
 \mu(WZ_Q)\ge{\mu J^2\over64}-{3\mu S\over32}
                       +{\mu(J^2W)\over256M}.                 \tag{PVI17}
\]
Thus both right sides of (PVI14) and, after division by \(c\), (PVI15)
can be decreased by respectively
\(\alpha\mu(J^2W)/(256M)\) and
\(\alpha\mu(J^2W)/(256Mc)\).
The stronger face sum version replaces \(W^2/M\) in the proof by
\(\sum_pD_p^2\); no independence is used.

For an arbitrary signed smearing, a variance bound on \(W\) alone
does not imply \(\operatorname{Var}C_f\le a^2\|f\|_\infty^2
\operatorname{Var}W\). The valid receiving bound is the second-moment
bound, retaining the actual mean:
\[
 G_f\le {a^2\|f\|_\infty^2\over c}
 \left[Bd-D+3\alpha M-{3\alpha\over32}(16d-\mu S)
                    -{\alpha\over256M}\mu(J^2W)\right]-m_f^2. \tag{PVI18}
\]
Indeed \(|C_f|\le a\|f\|_\infty W\), and (PVI14),(PVI17) bound
\(\mu W^2\). The cube contains every supported face and its edges.
Along the given path, \(\alpha=\kappa_*^2a^2\), \(M=O(a^{-3})\),
\(d,\Lambda=O(a^{-2})\). The subtraction \(D\) changes the leading
constant of this source-zero upper bound. These estimates still give
\(G_f=O(a^{-2})\); no estimate of order \(a\) follows from them.

\subsection*{PVI5. Actual positive ground counterexample in Euclidean space}

For \(x\in\mathbb R^8\), \(r=|x|\), put
\[
 \psi(x)=c_8(1+r^2)^{-5/2},\quad
 V(x)=40-{5(r^2+8)\over(1+r^2)^2},\quad H=-\Delta+V.
\]
The constant \(c_8>0\) is chosen so \(\|\psi\|_2=1\), which is
possible because the radial density at infinity is \(O(r^{-3})dr\).
Direct differentiation gives
\(\Delta\psi/\psi=-5(r^2+8)/(1+r^2)^2\), hence \(H\psi=40\psi\).
Also \((r^2+8)/(1+r^2)^2\le8\), so \(V\ge0\).
For every compactly supported smooth \(F\),
\(\langle F\psi,(H-40)F\psi\rangle=\int\psi^2|\nabla F|^2\ge0\).
Cutoff and form closure therefore prove that \(40\) is the actual
bottom eigenvalue. No gap assertion is required.

For \(y=r^2/(1+r^2)\), the normalized radial law is
\(4y^3\,dy\) on \([0,1]\). The full score and potential are
\[
 Z=25y(1-y),\qquad V=40+5(7y-8)(1-y).
\]
Integrating these polynomials against \(4y^3dy\) gives exactly
\[
 \mu(V-40)=-10/3,\quad \mu Z=10/3,\quad
 \operatorname{Cov}_\mu(V,Z)=-775/126,\quad
 \operatorname{Var}_\mu V=325/18,\quad
 \tfrac12\mu\Delta V=250/21.                                  \tag{PVI19}
\]
Thus \(\operatorname{Var}V>(1/2)\mu\Delta V\). Direct integration
of the displayed rational functions also gives the integration
identities, and the displayed decay makes their boundary terms vanish.

\subsection*{PVI6. Compact gauge-invariant counterexample with explicit parameter}

This construction tests what stationarity, compactness, positivity and
the original gauge constraints alone can prove. Its explicitly written
potential differs from the original linear plaquette potential; it
therefore does not disprove any assertion specific to that potential.

Choose three elementary plaquettes \(p_1,p_2,p_3\) with pairwise disjoint
edge sets inside an open cubic lattice, and keep every other original
edge and every original vertex gauge action. Write
\[
 d_i=2-\operatorname{Tr}U_{p_i},\quad q=d_1+d_2+d_3,
 \quad r_2=d_1^2+d_2^2+d_3^2,\quad\varepsilon=1/100.
\]
Each \(d_i\) is gauge invariant and \(0\le d_i\le4\). Disjointness
of their edge sets and the one-edge radius-two identities give exactly
\[
 \Gamma(q)=4q-r_2,\qquad \Delta q=18-3q.                        \tag{PVI20}
\]
Define the positive unit function
\(\psi_\varepsilon=c_\varepsilon(\varepsilon^2+q)^{-3}\), and
\[
 Z_\varepsilon={9(4q-r_2)\over(\varepsilon^2+q)^2},\quad
 T_\varepsilon={\Delta\psi_\varepsilon\over\psi_\varepsilon}
   =-{3(18-3q)\over\varepsilon^2+q}
                  +{12(4q-r_2)\over(\varepsilon^2+q)^2},
\]
\[
 \mathcal E_\varepsilon={54\kappa\over\varepsilon^2},\qquad
 V_\varepsilon=\mathcal E_\varepsilon+\kappa T_\varepsilon,
 \qquad H_\varepsilon=-\kappa\Delta+V_\varepsilon.              \tag{PVI21}
\]
Here \(4q-r_2\ge0\), and
\(-54/(\varepsilon^2+q)+9q/(\varepsilon^2+q)\ge-54/\varepsilon^2\).
Thus \(V_\varepsilon\ge0\), and equality holds when all three
plaquette holonomies are the identity. The ground transform proves
\(H_\varepsilon-\mathcal E_\varepsilon\ge0\) and uniqueness of its
positive ground state. This ground state and potential respect all
the original vertex constraints.

Under probability Haar measure the three plaquette holonomies are
independent Haar variables. This follows by conditioning on three of
the four edges of each face: the remaining Haar edge makes its ordered
face product Haar. The three sets of four edges are disjoint.
The exact marginal density of each \(d_i\) is
\(\sqrt{d_i(4-d_i)}\,dd_i/(2\pi)\).

Set \(d_i=\varepsilon^2t_i\), \(t=t_1+t_2+t_3\),
and use the reference probability law on \(\mathbb R_+^3\)
with density proportional to
\((t_1t_2t_3)^{1/2}(1+t)^{-6}\).
Under this law, \(y=t/(1+t)\) has beta parameters
\((9/2,3/2)\). Its expectation satisfies \(\mu_0t=9\).
The exact actual law is the reference law tilted by
\[
 R_\varepsilon(t_1,t_2,t_3)=
 \prod_{i=1}^3\sqrt{1-\varepsilon^2t_i/4}\,
                       \mathbf1_{\{t_i\le4/\varepsilon^2\}}.
\]
The product is interpreted as zero outside its indicated box. Since
\(1-\sqrt{1-u}\le u\) for \(0\le u\le1\),
\[
 0\le1-R_\varepsilon\le\min(1,\varepsilon^2t/4),\qquad
 \delta:=1-\mu_0R_\varepsilon\le9\varepsilon^2/4.               \tag{PVI22}
\]
For every bounded \(F\), normalization of this tilt gives
\(|\mu_\varepsilon F-\mu_0F|\le2\|F\|_\infty\delta/(1-\delta)\).

Write \(A_\varepsilon=\varepsilon^2T_\varepsilon\),
\(B_\varepsilon=\varepsilon^2Z_\varepsilon\), and
\[
 A_0=-{54+6t\over(1+t)^2}=6(8y-9)(1-y),\qquad
 B_0={36t\over(1+t)^2}=36y(1-y).
\]
The exact formulas (PVI21) show
\(|A_\varepsilon-A_0|\le12\varepsilon^2\),
\(|B_\varepsilon-B_0|\le9\varepsilon^2\),
\(|A_0|\le54\), and \(0\le B_\varepsilon\le B_0\le9\) on the
actual support. For \(\varepsilon\le1/10\), (PVI22) gives
\(\delta/(1-\delta)\le(900/391)\varepsilon^2\).
Consequently
\[
 |\mu_\varepsilon A_\varepsilon-\mu_0A_0|<261\varepsilon^2,
 \quad |\mu_\varepsilon B_\varepsilon-\mu_0B_0|<51\varepsilon^2,
\]
\[
 |\mu_\varepsilon A_\varepsilon B_\varepsilon-\mu_0A_0B_0|
 <2832\varepsilon^2,
\quad
 |\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu_\varepsilon}(A_\varepsilon,B_\varepsilon)
       -\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu_0}(A_0,B_0)|<7935\varepsilon^2. \tag{PVI23}
\]
For the third estimate the pointwise product error is at most
\((12\cdot9+54\cdot9)\varepsilon^2=594\varepsilon^2\);
the tilt error is at most \(972(900/391)\varepsilon^2\).
For the fourth use \(2832+9\cdot261+54\cdot51=7935\).
The beta moments \(\mu_0y^k=(9/2)_k/(6)_k\) give
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}_{\mu_0}(A_0,B_0)=-8721/784.
\]
At the explicit parameter \(\varepsilon=1/100\),
\[
 \boxed{\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu_\varepsilon}(V_\varepsilon,Z_\varepsilon)
 ={\kappa\over\varepsilon^4}
   \operatorname{Cov}_{\mu_\varepsilon}(A_\varepsilon,B_\varepsilon)
 <{\kappa\over\varepsilon^4}
          \left(-{8721\over784}+{7935\over10000}\right)<0.}     \tag{PVI24}
\]
By (PVI2), this actual compact physical ground state violates
\(\operatorname{Var}V_\varepsilon\le(\kappa/2)\mu\Delta V_\varepsilon\).
The additional argument needed for the original Hamiltonian must use
its original linear plaquette structure beyond the properties tested here.

Figure: the red curve is the rigorous covariance bound in PVI23–PVI24,
