\section*{Exact evaluation of the assigned gamma integral}

Status: complete independent derivation, 2026-10-11. This note evaluates the exact constant supplied in the task. The receiving cochain construction and its convergence to this constant are owned by the receiving calculation. No novelty claim is made. Every analytic identity used below is derived here; no unread external theorem is imported.

\subsection*{1. Original object and result}

For the original coordinates \((x,y)\in[0,\pi]^2\), retain

\[
a(x,y)=-\sin x\cos y,\qquad b(x,y)=\cos x\sin y,
\]

\[
\begin{gathered}
F(x,y)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{|a(x,y)b(x,y)(b(x,y)-a(x,y))|}
{\sqrt{a(x,y)^2+b(x,y)^2}},&(a(x,y),b(x,y))\ne(0,0),\\[2mm]
0,&(a(x,y),b(x,y))=(0,0),
\end{cases}\\
C_\gamma=\frac{2}{\pi^2}\int_0^\pi\int_0^\pi F(x,y)\,dx\,dy.
\end{gathered}\tag{G1}
\]

The assigned cochain expression motivating this constant is

\[
v_2=\frac{w(k)v(l)}{\sqrt{2n}},\qquad
v_3=-\frac{v(k)w(l)}{\sqrt{2n}},\qquad
\gamma=\frac{v_2v_3(v_3-v_2)}{\sqrt{v_2^2+v_3^2}},
\tag{G2}
\]

with zero at simultaneous zeros. This note preserves the prefactor in (G1); it does not replace or rederive the definitions of \(v,w\), their supports, or the receiving sum.

For \(|z|<1\), define

\[
\operatorname{Li}_2(z)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{z^k}{k^2},
\tag{G3}
\]

and also define \(\operatorname{Li}_2(1)=\sum_{k\ge1}k^{-2}\), a convergent sum. Put

\[
A=\sqrt2,\qquad q=A-1,\qquad \tau=q^2=3-2A.
\tag{G4}
\]

Theorem G. The original integral (G1) satisfies

\[
\boxed{
C_\gamma=
\frac{2+\frac{\sqrt2}{2}
+3\log\!\left(\frac{2}{1+\sqrt2}\right)
-\frac{\operatorname{Li}_2(3-2\sqrt2)}{2\sqrt2}}{\pi^2}
-\frac{1}{24\sqrt2}.
}
\tag{G5}
\]

It is strictly positive and obeys the exact elementary bounds

\[
\frac{\sqrt2}{\pi^2}<C_\gamma<\frac{2}{\pi^2}.
\tag{G6}
\]

The standard-library rational calculation in `verify\_gamma\_integral.py`, using the proved remainders of Section 8, establishes the strict finite enclosure

\[
\boxed{
0.181178439743214882282299233973
<C_\gamma<
0.181178439743214882282299233974.
}
\tag{G7}
\]

Both a dilogarithm evaluation and an independent geometrically convergent moment series give (G7). Their complete arithmetic certificates are reproduced by running `python verify\_gamma\_integral.py`; the result is `GAMMA\_INTEGRAL\_CERTIFICATE.json`.

First, (G1) defines a continuous function, including its specified zero value. Indeed, for \(r=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\),

\[
|ab|\le\frac{r^2}{2},\qquad |b-a|\le\sqrt2\,r,
\qquad 0\le\frac{|ab(b-a)|}{r}\le\frac{r^2}{\sqrt2}.
\tag{G8}
\]

Thus this expression tends to zero when \((a,b)\to(0,0)\). Elsewhere its denominator is nonzero and the expression is continuous. Since \(a,b\) are continuous on the compact original square, so is \(F\). In particular its integral is finite and ordinary Riemann sums converge to the original integral. This observation concerns (G1) itself; any additional cochain prefactor must still be retained in its receiving proof.

\subsection*{2. Exact quadrant and triangle maps}

Write \(Q=[0,\pi/2]^2\). On \(Q\), let

\[
p=\sin x\cos y\ge0,\qquad q_0=\cos x\sin y\ge0,
\qquad r=\sqrt{p^2+q_0^2}.
\tag{G9}
\]

The name \(q_0\) here is separate from the constant \(q=\sqrt2-1\) in (G4). The original coordinate reflections, with absolute Jacobian one, give the following four values at the corresponding points:

The four original point / original \((a,b)\) / original \(F\) rows are:

\((x,y)\); \((-p,q_0)\); \(p q_0(p+q_0)/r\).

\((\pi-x,y)\); \((-p,-q_0)\); \(p q_0|p-q_0|/r\).

\((x,\pi-y)\); \((p,q_0)\); \(p q_0|p-q_0|/r\).

\((\pi-x,\pi-y)\); \((p,-q_0)\); \(p q_0(p+q_0)/r\).

Zero denominators have the original zero interpretation. The shared boundaries have area zero, so this table proves, without discarding a quadrant,

\[
\int_{[0,\pi]^2}F
=2\int_Q\frac{p q_0(p+q_0+|p-q_0|)}r
=4\int_Q\frac{p q_0\max(p,q_0)}r.
\tag{G10}
\]

On the interior of \(Q\), \(p\ge q_0\) is equivalent to \(\tan x\ge\tan y\), and hence to \(x\ge y\). The map \((x,y)\mapsto(y,x)\) has absolute Jacobian one, exchanges \(p,q_0\), and exchanges the two triangular regions. Their integrands agree under this map. Consequently, with \(T=\{0\le y\le x\le\pi/2\}\),

\[
\int_{[0,\pi]^2}F=8\int_T\frac{p^2q_0}{r}\,dx\,dy,
\qquad
C_\gamma=\frac{16}{\pi^2}\int_T\frac{p^2q_0}{r}\,dx\,dy.
\tag{G11}
\]

\subsection*{3. Exact one-dimensional reduction}

On the open triangle, use the bijection

\[
u=\tan x>0,\qquad v=\tan y\in(0,u),
\quad
x=\arctan u,\quad y=\arctan v.
\tag{G12}
\]

Every factor is

\[
p=\frac{u}{\sqrt{(1+u^2)(1+v^2)}},\quad
q_0=\frac{v}{\sqrt{(1+u^2)(1+v^2)}},\quad
r=\frac{\sqrt{u^2+v^2}}{\sqrt{(1+u^2)(1+v^2)}},
\]

\[
dx\,dy=\frac{du\,dv}{(1+u^2)(1+v^2)},\qquad
\frac{p^2q_0}{r}\,dx\,dy
=\frac{u^2v\,du\,dv}
{(1+u^2)^2(1+v^2)^2\sqrt{u^2+v^2}}.
\tag{G13}
\]

Set \(v=tu\), so \(t\in(0,1)\) and \(du\,dv=u\,du\,dt\). Then set \(s=u^2\), so \(u^3du=s\,ds/2\). The nonnegative integral becomes

\[
C_\gamma
=\frac8{\pi^2}\int_0^1\frac{t}{\sqrt{1+t^2}}
\left(\int_0^\infty\frac{s\,ds}{(1+s)^2(1+t^2s)^2}\right)dt.
\tag{G14}
\]

Finally put \(z=t^2\), retaining \(t\,dt=dz/2\). Define, for \(0<z\le1\),

\[
K(z)=\int_0^\infty\frac{s\,ds}{(1+s)^2(1+zs)^2}>0.
\tag{G15}
\]

The exact reduction is

\[
\boxed{C_\gamma=\frac4{\pi^2}\int_0^1\frac{K(z)}{\sqrt{1+z}}\,dz.}
\tag{G16}
\]

All these changes are bijections on the stated interiors. One can first apply them on compact subregions and then increase those subregions to the full interiors. Their integrands are nonnegative, so the limiting integrals agree. No endpoint or boundary term is suppressed.

To evaluate the radial integral, put \(t_0=s/(1+s)\). Direct substitution yields

\[
K(z)=\int_0^1\frac{t_0(1-t_0)}{(1-(1-z)t_0)^2}\,dt_0.
\tag{G17}
\]

For \(0<z<1\), the further substitution \(w=1-(1-z)t_0\) gives

\[
K(z)=\frac1{(1-z)^3}
\int_z^1\left[-1+\frac{1+z}{w}-\frac z{w^2}\right]dw
=\frac{-(1+z)\log z-2(1-z)}{(1-z)^3}.
\tag{G18}
\]

At \(z=1\), (G17) gives \(K(1)=\int_0^1t_0(1-t_0)dt_0=1/6\). The apparent singularity in (G18) at that endpoint is therefore removable. At \(z=0\), \(K(z)\) has an integrable logarithmic divergence: (G18) directly shows \(K(z)=O(1+|\log z|)\) for \(0<z\le1/2\). No finite value is assigned to \(K(0)\); the integral in (G16) is an improper integral there.

For a useful exact mass identity, use the nonnegative integrand of (G15):

\[
\int_0^1 K(z)\,dz
=\int_0^\infty\frac{s}{(1+s)^2}
\left(\int_0^1\frac{dz}{(1+zs)^2}\right)ds
=\int_0^\infty\frac{s\,ds}{(1+s)^3}
=\frac12.
\tag{G19}
\]

For \(s>0\), the inner integral is \(1/(1+s)\), by its elementary antiderivative. The last integral follows on writing \(s=(1+s)-1\). Since \(K(z)>0\) and \(1/\sqrt2<1/\sqrt{1+z}<1\) for \(0<z<1\), (G16) and (G19) prove the strict inequalities (G6), and hence positivity.

\subsection*{4. Endpoint-controlled integration by parts}

In (G16), set \(y_0=\sqrt{1+z}\), so \(1<y_0<A=\sqrt2\), \(dz/\sqrt{1+z}=2dy_0\), and \(1-z=2-y_0^2\). For this section write \(y=y_0\) and \(D=2-y^2\). Then

\[
C_\gamma=\frac8{\pi^2}\int_1^A f(y)\,dy,\qquad
f(y)=-\frac{y^2\log(y^2-1)}{D^3}-\frac2{D^2}.
\tag{G20}
\]

Let

\[
\ell=\log(1+A),\quad
h(y)=\frac12\log\frac{A+y}{A-y},\quad
R(y)=-\frac y{4D^2}+\frac y{16D}.
\tag{G21}
\]

Since \((A-1)(A+1)=1\), \(h(1)=\ell\). Direct differentiation gives

\[
h'(y)=\frac A D,\qquad
\left(R(y)+\frac{h(y)}{16A}\right)'=-\frac{y^2}{D^3}.
\tag{G22}
\]

For verification of the remaining rational terms,

\[
-\frac{2yR(y)}{y^2-1}-\frac2{D^2}
=\frac1{4D}-\frac1{D^2}
+\frac3{16(y-1)}-\frac3{16(y+1)}
=\left(-\frac y{4D}+\frac3{16}\log\frac{y-1}{y+1}\right)'.
\tag{G23}
\]

Define the full boundary expression

\[
B(y)=\left(R(y)+\frac{h(y)-\ell}{16A}\right)\log(y^2-1)
-\frac y{4D}+\frac3{16}\log\frac{y-1}{y+1}.
\tag{G24}
\]

Equations (G22)-(G23) prove by differentiation on \(1<y<A\) that

\[
B'(y)=f(y)+\frac{(h(y)-\ell)y}{8A(y^2-1)}.
\tag{G25}
\]

At the lower endpoint, \(R(1)=-3/16\), and \(h(y)-\ell=O(y-1)\). Therefore the product of the latter difference with \(\log(y^2-1)\) tends to zero, and the two logarithmic divergences in (G24) give the finite limit

\[
B(1+)= -\frac14-\frac38\log2.
\tag{G26}
\]

In detail, \(\log(y^2-1)=\log(y-1)+\log(y+1)\), so the sum of its coefficient \(-3/16\) with the final log term is \(-3\log(y+1)/8\) in the limit.

At the upper endpoint, \(y^2-1=1-D\), and

\[
\log(1-D)=-D-\frac{D^2}{2}+O(D^3).
\]

It follows directly that

\[
R(y)\log(1-D)-\frac y{4D}=\frac y{16}+O(D).
\]

Also \(h(y)=O(1+|\log D|)\), so \((h(y)-\ell)\log(1-D)\to0\). The ratio \((A-1)/(A+1)=(A-1)^2=e^{-2\ell}\) supplies the final term. Thus

\[
B(A-)=\frac A{16}-\frac38\ell.
\tag{G27}
\]

The residual integral

\[
J=\int_1^A (h(y)-\ell)\frac y{y^2-1}\,dy
\tag{G28}
\]

is finite: at \(y=1\) its integrand tends to \(A/2\), from \(h'(1)=A\); at \(y=A\) it has at most a logarithmic divergence. Integrating (G25) first over \([1+\varepsilon,A-\delta]\) and taking these proved endpoint limits gives

\[
\int_1^A f(y)\,dy
=\frac14+\frac A{16}+\frac38(\log2-\ell)-\frac J{8A},
\]

\[
C_\gamma=\frac{2+A/2+3(\log2-\ell)-J/A}{\pi^2}.
\tag{G29}
\]

\subsection*{5. Exact residual dilogarithm}

Set

\[
t=\frac{A-y}{A+y},\quad
y=A\frac{1-t}{1+t},\quad
\tau=(A-1)^2.
\tag{G30}
\]

This is a decreasing bijection from \(1<y<A\) onto \(0<t<\tau\). Its endpoints are \(t(1)=\tau\), \(t(A)=0\). The exact factors are

\[
h(y)-\ell=-\frac12\log(t/\tau),\qquad
y^2-1=\frac{(1-t/\tau)(1-\tau t)}{(1+t)^2},
\]

\[
\frac y{y^2-1}\,dy
=\frac12\left[\frac1{t-\tau}+\frac1{t-\tau^{-1}}-\frac2{t+1}\right]dt.
\tag{G31}
\]

The quadratic factorization is exact because \(\tau+\tau^{-1}=6\). Substitution into (G28), including the reversed orientation, and then \(u=t/\tau\) yields

\[
J=\frac14\int_0^1\log u
\left[\frac1{u-1}-\frac{\tau^2}{1-\tau^2u}
-\frac{2\tau}{1+\tau u}\right]du.
\tag{G32}
\]

For each integer \(k\ge0\), integration by parts gives
\(\int_0^1u^k\log u\,du=-1/(k+1)^2\); the endpoint term at zero vanishes because \(u^{k+1}\log u\to0\). Expanding the three geometric series in (G32) now gives

\[
J=\frac14\left[\operatorname{Li}_2(1)+\operatorname{Li}_2(\tau^2)
-2\operatorname{Li}_2(-\tau)\right].
\tag{G33}
\]

The first expansion has nonnegative terms after multiplying \(-\log u\), so termwise integration follows from increasing partial sums. The other two converge absolutely with ratios at most \(\tau^2<1\) and \(\tau<1\), and their integrated absolute sums are finite. These facts justify the integrations.

Selecting the even terms in the absolutely convergent defining sums proves

\[
\operatorname{Li}_2(\tau)+\operatorname{Li}_2(-\tau)
=\frac12\operatorname{Li}_2(\tau^2).
\tag{G34}
\]

Hence the exact residual evaluation is

\[
\boxed{J=\frac14\operatorname{Li}_2(1)+\frac12\operatorname{Li}_2(\tau).}
\tag{G35}
\]

\subsection*{6. Self-contained evaluation at one}

Here is a short derivation of \(\operatorname{Li}_2(1)=\pi^2/6\), to identify every constant used in (G5). For \(0<\rho<1\), the power series obtained by integrating the geometric series is

\[
\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{\rho^n e^{int}}n=-\log(1-\rho e^{it}).
\]

On \(0\le t\le\pi\), the real part of \(1-\rho e^{it}\) is positive. Thus the imaginary part is the unambiguous real arctangent

\[
S_\rho(t)=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{\rho^n\sin(nt)}n
=\arctan\frac{\rho\sin t}{1-\rho\cos t},\qquad
0\le S_\rho(t)\le\frac\pi2.
\tag{G36}
\]

For fixed \(0<t<\pi\), as \(\rho\uparrow1\), the fraction tends to \(\cot(t/2)\), so \(S_\rho(t)\to(\pi-t)/2\). The displayed bound permits integration of this limit. For each fixed \(\rho<1\) the series converges uniformly and absolutely, so

\[
\lim_{\rho\uparrow1}\int_0^\pi S_\rho(t)dt
=\int_0^\pi\frac{\pi-t}2dt=\frac{\pi^2}4
=\lim_{\rho\uparrow1}\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{\rho^n(1-(-1)^n)}{n^2}.
\tag{G37}
\]

The nonzero terms on the right are positive and increase to their limits. Therefore
\(\pi^2/4=2\sum_{n\text{ odd}}1/n^2\). The full sum \(Z=\sum_{n\ge1}1/n^2\) converges, for instance by comparison with \(1+\int_1^\infty t^{-2}dt\). Its even terms sum to \(Z/4\), hence its odd terms sum to \(3Z/4\). Equation (G37) gives \(\pi^2/4=3Z/2\), so

\[
\operatorname{Li}_2(1)=Z=\frac{\pi^2}6.
\tag{G38}
\]

Substituting (G35) and (G38) into (G29), and retaining both resulting terms of \(J/A\), proves exactly (G5).

\subsection*{7. Independent exact series with geometric error}

Expand (G17) using \((1-u)^{-2}=\sum_{m\ge0}(m+1)u^m\), whose identity follows by differentiating the geometric series. For \(0<z\le1\), the resulting positive terms give

\[
K(z)=\sum_{m\ge0}\frac{m+1}{(m+2)(m+3)}(1-z)^m.
\tag{G39}
\]

Define positive moments

\[
M_j=\int_0^1(1-z)^j K(z)dz
=\sum_{m\ge0}\frac{m+1}{(m+2)(m+3)(m+j+1)}.
\tag{G40}
\]

Termwise integration is justified by nonnegative summands. In particular \(0<M_j\le M_0=1/2\). The first moments evaluate as

\[
M_0=\frac12,\qquad M_1=2-\frac{\pi^2}6,\qquad M_2=\frac{\pi^2}3-3.
\tag{G41}
\]

For \(M_0\) the summands telescope as \(1/((m+2)(m+3))\). For \(M_1\), put \(k=m+2\ge2\), and use

\[
\frac{k-1}{k^2(k+1)}=\frac2k-\frac1{k^2}-\frac2{k+1}.
\]

For \(M_2\), put \(k=m+3\ge3\), and use

\[
\frac{k-2}{(k-1)k^2}=-\frac1{k-1}+\frac1k+\frac2{k^2}.
\]

Summing these finite telescoping expressions, taking the limit, and applying (G38) proves (G41).

For \(j\ge3\), set \(H_k=\sum_{r=1}^k1/r\). One obtains the rational expression

\[
\boxed{M_j=\frac{jH_{j-1}-2(j-1)}{(j-2)(j-1)}\quad(j\ge3).}
\tag{G42}
\]

For completeness, if \(n\ge0\), writing \(-\log z=\int_z^1dt/t\) and integrating the nonnegative integrand in either order yields

\[
I_n:=\int_0^1(1-z)^n(-\log z)dz
=\frac1{n+1}\int_0^1\frac{1-(1-t)^{n+1}}t dt
=\frac{H_{n+1}}{n+1}.
\]

The last step uses \([1-(1-t)^{n+1}]/t=\sum_{r=0}^n(1-t)^r\). Also
\(\int_0^1z(1-z)^n(-\log z)dz=I_n-I_{n+1}\). Multiply (G18) by \((1-z)^j\), set \(n=j-3\), integrate, and use these identities and \(\int_0^1(1-z)^{j-2}dz=1/(j-1)\). The result is

\[
M_j=\frac{H_{j-2}}{j-2}
+\frac{H_{j-1}-1}{(j-2)(j-1)}-\frac2{j-1},
\]

which equals the full rational expression (G42).

The Taylor expansion, obtainable by successive differentiation, is

\[
\frac1{\sqrt{1+z}}
=\frac1{\sqrt2}\sum_{j\ge0}c_j(1-z)^j,
\qquad c_j=\frac{\binom{2j}{j}}{8^j},\qquad 0\le z\le1.
\tag{G43}
\]

Its convergence on this closed interval follows, for example, from \(c_j\le2^{-j}\), since \(\binom{2j}j\le\sum_{k=0}^{2j}\binom{2j}k=4^j\). Every summand is nonnegative. Thus (G16) gives a second exact evaluation,

\[
\boxed{
C_\gamma=\frac{2\sqrt2}{\pi^2}\sum_{j\ge0}c_jM_j
=\frac{2\sqrt2}{\pi^2}
\left[\frac{23}{32}-\frac{\pi^2}{96}
+\sum_{j\ge3}\frac{\binom{2j}{j}}{8^j}
\frac{jH_{j-1}-2(j-1)}{(j-2)(j-1)}\right].
}
\tag{G44}
\]

The finite prefix \(23/32-\pi^2/96\) equals \(c_0M_0+c_1M_1+c_2M_2\) with \(c_0=1,c_1=1/4,c_2=3/32\). For every integer \(N\ge1\), the omitted sum satisfies the explicit positive bound

\[
0<\sum_{j=N}^{\infty}c_jM_j
\le\frac12\sum_{j=N}^{\infty}2^{-j}=2^{-N}.
\tag{G45}
\]

This establishes geometric convergence with a fully explicit error. The implementation uses \(N=110\), and recursively computes \(c_j/c_{j-1}=(2j-1)/(4j)\) with exact rational arithmetic. This supplies an independent enclosure of the original integral, without using the integrations of Sections 4-5.

\subsection*{8. Reproducible rational enclosure}

The script `verify\_gamma\_integral.py` uses only integers and rational numbers. Each quantity is stored as a containing interval. For intervals \([a,b]\) and \([c,d]\), addition uses \([a+c,b+d]\), negation uses \([-b,-a]\), and multiplication takes the minimum and maximum of the four endpoint products. Reciprocal of a strictly positive interval is \([1/b,1/a]\). These formulas follow directly from monotonicity or extrema of the bilinear product on a rectangle, so every operation preserves enclosure.

1. Square root. Set \(Q=10^{50}\) and \(m=\lfloor\sqrt{2Q^2}\rfloor\), computed by integer square root. The script checks
   \((m/Q)^2<2<((m+1)/Q)^2\). Thus \(A\in[m/Q,(m+1)/Q]\).

2. Pi. The exact identity used is
   \[
   \pi=16\arctan(1/5)-4\arctan(1/239).
   \tag{G46}
   \]
   To prove it, put \(\theta=\arctan(1/5)\), \(\phi=\arctan(1/239)\). The double-angle formula gives \(\tan(2\theta)=5/12\) and \(\tan(4\theta)=120/119\). Therefore
   \[
   \tan(4\theta-\phi)
   =\frac{120/119-1/239}{1+(120/119)(1/239)}=1.
   \]
   From \(x/(1+x^2)<\arctan x<x\) for \(x>0\), obtained by integrating \((1+t^2)^{-1}\), one has \(0<4\theta-\phi<4/5\). Also \(\pi/2=2\arctan1>1\). Thus \(4\theta-\phi\in(0,\pi/2)\), where tangent is injective, and this angle is \(\pi/4\), proving (G46). Integrating the finite geometric expansion for \((1+t^2)^{-1}\) gives
   \[
   \arctan x=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\frac{(-1)^kx^{2k+1}}{2k+1}+R_N,
   \quad |R_N|\le\frac{x^{2N+1}}{2N+1},
   \quad \operatorname{sign}(R_N)=(-1)^N
   \tag{G47}
   \]
   for \(0<x<1\). The calculation uses 40 terms at \(1/5\) and 12 terms at \(1/239\).

3. Logarithm. Let \(r=(A-1)/(A+3)\in(0,1)\). Exact algebra gives \((1+r)/(1-r)=(A+1)/2\), hence
   \[
   \log\frac2{1+A}
   =-2\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\frac{r^{2k+1}}{2k+1}-E_N,
   \quad 0<E_N\le\frac{2r^{2N+1}}{(2N+1)(1-r^2)}.
   \tag{G48}
   \]
   This follows by integrating the geometric expansion of \(2/(1-r^2)\) from zero. For the remainder, replace every omitted denominator by \(2N+1\) and sum a geometric series. Every term increases with positive \(r\); evaluating the lower and upper partial sums at the rational interval endpoints and adding the upper remainder therefore encloses the logarithm. The script uses \(N=20\).

4. Dilogarithm. For \(0<z<1\), the definition gives
   \[
   0<\operatorname{Li}_2(z)-\sum_{k=1}^N\frac{z^k}{k^2}
   \le\frac{z^{N+1}}{(N+1)^2(1-z)}.
   \tag{G49}
   \]
   Again this follows by replacing omitted denominators by \((N+1)^2\). Every partial-sum term and this bound increase with \(z\). Apply the formula to the interval for \(\tau=3-2A\) using \(N=50\).

5. Assembly and verification. Substitute these containing intervals into every term of (G5), retaining the separate term \(-1/(24A)\). Exact rational comparisons check that both resulting interval endpoints lie strictly inside the two rational decimal endpoints in (G7). The script separately evaluates (G44)-(G45) with 110 terms and the same certified \(A,\pi\). It checks that this second interval also lies strictly inside (G7), and that the two containing intervals intersect. None of these comparisons uses a floating-point approximation.

For further inspection, the closed-form containing interval rounded outward to 36 fractional places is

\[
[0.181178439743214882282299233973232149,
\ 0.181178439743214882282299233973232150].
\tag{G50}
\]

The independent moment-series interval rounded outward to 33 fractional places is

\[
[0.181178439743214882282299233973232,
\ 0.181178439743214882282299233973233].
\tag{G51}
\]

These are additional certified containing intervals; (G7) is the simpler strict enclosure announced in the theorem.

G(t)=\frac{2tK(t^2)}{\sqrt{1+t^2}},\quad 0<t\le1,
\qquad G(0)=0,
\quad C_\gamma=\frac4{\pi^2}\int_0^1G(t)dt.

The endpoint at zero follows from \(t|\log(t^2)|\to0\); at one, \(G(1)=1/(3\sqrt2)\). These plotted samples illustrate the exact proofs and are not used for the certificate. The figure retains the original prefactors in its labels and its caption points to (G10)-(G18), (G45), and (G52).

\section*{Smooth connection holonomy, actual curvature growth, and a non-Abelian amplitude family}

The original lattice observable has a direct receiving map from smooth connections. Its exact curvature bound, combined with the actual lower-energy tail, forces a quantitative curvature scale for smooth preimages of typical vacuum configurations. We then construct smooth non-Abelian connection families at that scale, compute their complete original plaquette receiver, and give an exact globally smooth homogeneous Yang–Mills evolution. The latter has infinite spatial total energy; it is a dynamical comparison with a specified domain, not an identification of the quantum vacuum or the compact-support Cauchy construction. Every original scalar, coupling, face orientation and error term remains below.

The connection and gauge conventions are related to those of the \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/yang-mills-interacting-workbench/blob/50801f6c74543f26e6a227b831691290a0f7a3fc/yang-mills/continuations/20260930-s6-ns-moment-map-bridge/HIGHER_DOMAIN_PROGRAM.md}{retained higher-domain programme, Sections 2.1 and 7} by the exact inversion dictionary below. The actual-vacuum inputs are the complete \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/yang-mills-interacting-workbench/blob/50801f6c74543f26e6a227b831691290a0f7a3fc/yang-mills/continuations/20261011-central-signs-shrinking-window/BOUNDED_ENERGY_MULTIPLIER.md}{BM1–BM69}, especially BM4–BM9 and BM53–BM56. The exact source ledger records reading coverage and disk routing. The arguments below use no external theorem about the Yang–Mills vacuum and make no novelty claim.

\subsection*{1. The original connection-to-link map}

Let \(T_\alpha=-i\sigma_\alpha/2\), so \([T_\alpha,T_\beta]=\varepsilon_{\alpha\beta\gamma}T_\gamma\) and \(-2\operatorname{Tr}(T_\alpha T_\beta)=\delta_{\alpha\beta}\). For \(X\in\mathfrak{su}(2)\) write
\[
 |X|^2=-2\operatorname{Tr}(X^2),\qquad
 \|X\|_{\mathrm F}^2=|X|^2/2,\qquad
 \|X\|_{\rm op}=|X|/2.
 \tag{HC1}
\]
The middle norm is the matrix Frobenius norm. The last equality follows because the eigenvalues of \(X=x\cdot T\) are \(\pm i|x|/2\). These are the original radius-two metric factors.

Use the original open box, spacing and physical coordinates
\[
 L_j=j^4,\quad a_j=(100j)^{-1},\quad
 x_z=o+a_j(z-L_j\mathbf1),\quad z\in\{0,\ldots,2L_j\}^3,
 \quad g_j^2=\kappa_*a_j/2,
 \quad b_j=(\kappa_*a_j^2)^{-1}.
 \tag{HC2}
\]
Let \(A=\sum_{d=1}^3A_d(x)dx^d\) be any smooth \(\mathfrak{su}(2)\)-valued one-form on \(\mathbb R^3\). Its exact positive-edge map is the terminal value of
\[
 \frac{d}{ds}U_d(x;s)=U_d(x;s)A_d(x+s e_d),\qquad
 U_d(x;0)=I,\qquad U_d(x)=U_d(x;a_j).
 \tag{HC3}
\]
The solution is unitary of determinant one: differentiation of \(UU^*\) and of the determinant uses \(A_d^*=-A_d\), \(\operatorname{Tr}A_d=0\). Existence on each finite edge follows from the linear integral equation, whose iterated integral series is bounded by the exponential of the integral of the coefficient norm. The inverse edge is \(U_d(x)^{-1}\). The complete face is precisely
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 U_p=U_d(x)U_k(x+a_j e_d)U_d(x+a_j e_k)^{-1}U_k(x)^{-1},\\
 d<k,\quad D_p=2-\operatorname{Tr}U_p,\qquad
 F_{dk}=\partial_dA_k-\partial_kA_d+[A_d,A_k].
 \end{gathered}\tag{HC4}
\]
Thus the map \(\operatorname{Hol}_j:C^\infty(\mathbb R^3,T^*\mathbb R^3\otimes\mathfrak{su}(2))\to SU(2)^{E_j}\) has exactly the original domain coordinates and codomain. It is continuous for uniform convergence of the coefficients on the finite union of edges: variation of the integral equation, with the two unitary propagators retained, bounds the terminal difference by the integral of the coefficient difference.

For smooth \(h:\mathbb R^3\to SU(2)\), put \(A^h=hAh^{-1}-(dh)h^{-1}\). Differentiating \(h(x)U_d(x;s)h(x+s e_d)^{-1}\) proves
\[
 \operatorname{Hol}_j(A^h)_e=h(s(e))\operatorname{Hol}_j(A)_e h(t(e))^{-1},
 \quad F^h_{dk}=hF_{dk}h^{-1},\quad D_p(A^h)=D_p(A).
 \tag{HC5}
\]
The curvature identity follows by expanding the two derivative terms and the commutator, using \(d(h^{-1})=-h^{-1}(dh)h^{-1}\); the terms containing one derivative of \(h\) cancel, and the two second derivatives cancel. The programme writes its gauge parameter as \(g\), with \(A^g=g^{-1}Ag+g^{-1}dg\) and endpoint action \(g(s)^{-1}Ug(t)\). The exact smooth bijection is \(h=g^{-1}\): differentiating \(gg^{-1}=I\) gives \(d(g^{-1})=-g^{-1}(dg)g^{-1}\), so substitution in HC5 gives both of those original expressions term by term. Inversion also reverses the order of the two gauge parameters, exactly as their two action conventions require; the complete composition calculation is HCR1. Hence the exact map intertwines the original vertex gauge action. Every finite vertex gauge assignment is the restriction of a smooth \(h\): choose disjoint small balls about the vertices, a logarithm \(X_v\in\mathfrak{su}(2)\) of each assigned value, and a bump \(\chi_v\) equal to one at its vertex; the product of \(\exp(\chi_vX_v)\) has the required values because these supports are disjoint.

Every finite link configuration has a smooth compactly supported preimage. Choose disjoint tubes around the middle half of each positive edge, with radius less than \(a_j/8\), avoiding every other edge. Choose a smooth longitudinal function with integral one and support in that middle half, and a transverse bump equal to one on the edge and supported in its tube. Their product times \(ds\) is a smooth compactly supported one-form \(\eta_e\), with integral one along \(e\) and zero along every other edge. If \(\exp X_e=U_e\), then
\[
 A[U]=\sum_{e\in E_j}X_e\eta_e,\qquad
 \operatorname{Hol}_j(A[U])=U.
 \tag{HC6}
\]
Along the edge there is only its own coefficient and it commutes with itself at all positions; HC3 therefore gives \(\exp(X_e\int_e\eta_e)=U_e\). The finite sum is smooth and compactly supported. A Borel choice of \(X_e\) exists explicitly: for \(U=\cos\theta I-i\sin\theta\,n\cdot\sigma\), \(0<\theta<\pi\), use \(X=2\theta n\cdot T\); choose \(X=0\) at \(I\) and \(X=2\pi T_1\) at \(-I\). This section is Borel in its finite coefficients, and no continuity or gauge equivariance of the section itself is asserted. Equivariance belongs to the exact forward map HC5.

\subsection*{2. A curvature bound with its original metric factor}

For an individual square \(p\), define \(K_p(A)=\sup_{x\in p}|F_{dk}(x)|\). A gauge transformation on the square makes \(A_d=0\) on it and \(A_k=0\) on its left side. To construct it, first solve \(\partial_kh_0=h_0A_k\) on that left side, then solve \(\partial_dh=hA_d\) along each horizontal segment with initial value \(h_0\). These smooth ODE solutions have the prescribed properties by HC5. In this gauge,
\[
 A_k(a_j,y)=\int_0^{a_j}F_{dk}(s,y)\,ds,\qquad
 U_p-I=\int_0^{a_j}U_k(a_j;y)A_k(a_j,y)\,dy.
\]
All three other edge transports are the identity. Unitarity, the triangle inequality and HC1 give
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 D_p=\tfrac12\|I-U_p\|_{\mathrm F}^2,
 \qquad
 D_p\le\frac14\left(\int_p|F_{dk}(x)|\,d^2x\right)^2
       \le\frac{a_j^4}{4}K_p(A)^2 .
 \end{gathered}\tag{HC7}
\]
The equality uses \(\operatorname{Tr}U_p\in\mathbb R\) for \(SU(2)\): \(\|I-U_p\|_{\mathrm F}^2=4-2\operatorname{Tr}U_p\). Gauge conjugation preserves every norm and trace in HC7, so the estimate holds in the original gauge. No small-curvature assumption occurs.

Retain a nonzero original real \(f\in C_c(\mathbb R^3)\), its face centers \(x_{p,j}=o+a_j(z-L_j\mathbf1+(e_d+e_k)/2)\), coefficients \(f_p=f(x_{p,j})\), \(F_f=\|f\|_\infty\), \(A_{1,j}=\sum_p|f_p|\), and \(J_1=\int|f|>0\). For sufficiently large \(j\), \(A_{1,j}>0\). Define \(K_{f,j}(A)=\max_{p:f_p\ne0}K_p(A)\). The unchanged absolute and signed observables obey
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 Y_j=\sum_p|f_p|D_p,\qquad C_{f,j}=a_j\sum_pf_pD_p,\qquad
 |C_{f,j}|\le a_jY_j,\\
 Y_j(\operatorname{Hol}_jA)
 \le\frac{a_j^4A_{1,j}}4K_{f,j}(A)^2,\qquad
 |a_jC_{f,j}(\operatorname{Hol}_jA)|
 \le\frac{a_j^6A_{1,j}}4K_{f,j}(A)^2 .
 \end{gathered}\tag{HC8}
\]
Every summand and orientation remains in this inequality. In particular locally uniformly curvature-bounded connection families have \(a_jC_{f,j}\to0\), because \(a_j^3A_{1,j}\to3J_1\). This conclusion concerns the stated exact holonomy preimages; it does not identify a quantum field with a smooth connection.

\subsection*{3. The actual vacuum forces a curvature scale}

Use the original support cube of side \(R>0\), its fitting patch \(Q=v+\{0,\ldots,q\}^3\), \(q=\lceil R/a\rceil+3\), and all counts \(N_Q=3q(q+1)^2\), \(M_Q=3q^2(q+1)\), \(C_Q=2q(q+1)\sum_d(\mathbf1_{v_d>0}+\mathbf1_{v_d+q<2L})\). The actual positive vacuum measure is \(\mu_j=\psi_j^2dU\). Its original outside operator has bottom \(E_{\rm out}\), and BM gives
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \alpha=\kappa_*/b=\kappa_*^2a^2,\qquad
 e=F_f(E_0-E_{\rm out})/b,\qquad
 0<e\le\bar e:=F_f\Lambda_Q,\\
 \Lambda_Q=\min\{2M_Q,6g^2\sqrt{N_QM_Q}\}+2C_Q,\\
 c=9\alpha/64,\quad C_e=4cA_1^2,\quad B_e=e+4cA_1,\\
 r_-(e)=\frac{2C_e}{B_e+\sqrt{B_e^2-4(1+c)C_e}},\qquad
 p_0=\frac{3A_1}{8F_f},\\
 \mu_j\{Y_j\le u r_-(e)\}
 \le \exp[p_0(1-u+\log u)]\quad(0<u<1).
 \end{gathered}\tag{HC9}
\]
These are the actual BM53–BM56 square and lower-tail identities, not a comparison density. Its discriminant is strictly positive. Increasing \(e\) increases the denominator in \(r_-(e)\) and keeps the discriminant positive. Thus \(\bar r_j=r_-(\bar e_j)\le r_-(e_j)\) is an explicit positive lower threshold using the original finite counts.

For \(0<u<1\), put
\[
 K^{\rm cut}_{j,u}
 =\left(\frac{4u\bar r_j}{a_j^4 A_{1,j}}\right)^{1/2}.
 \tag{HC10}
\]
By HC8, every link configuration admitting a smooth preimage with \(K_{f,j}(A)\le K^{\rm cut}_{j,u}\) belongs to the measurable event \(\{Y_j\le u\bar r_j\}\). Its outer vacuum measure is therefore at most the right side of HC9. The outer-measure formulation requires no measurability assumption about the image of a family of connections. For the explicit Borel section HC6, \(K_{f,j}(A[U])\) is measurable: curvature is a polynomial in its finite matrix coefficients with fixed smooth functions, and its maximum over a compact finite union of faces is continuous in those coefficients. Hence
\[
 \mu_j\{K_{f,j}(A[U])\le K^{\rm cut}_{j,u}\}
 \le \exp[p_{0,j}(1-u+\log u)].
 \tag{HC11}
\]
The same statement holds for any measurable smooth-preimage choice, with its original curvature. It is a quantitative statement about the actual vacuum, valid without selecting a favorable section.

The full finite boundary expression yields
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 a_j^2\bar e_j\longrightarrow E_{\max}=F_f(9\kappa_*R^3+24R^2),\qquad
 a_j^4C_{e,j}\longrightarrow C_0=81\kappa_*^2J_1^2/16,\\
 a_j^2\bar r_j\longrightarrow
 \bar R_-:=\frac{2C_0}{E_{\max}+\sqrt{E_{\max}^2-4C_0}}>0,\\

 \left(\frac{4u\bar R_-}{3J_1}\right)^{1/2},\qquad

 \end{gathered}\tag{HC12}
\]
Indeed the patch is eventually strictly interior, so \(C_Q=12q(q+1)\); \(a^2 6g^2\sqrt{N_QM_Q}\to9\kappa_*R^3\), whereas \(a^2 2M_Q\to\infty\), and \(a^22C_Q\to24R^2\). Also \(J_1\le F_fR^3\), so \(E_{\max}>2\sqrt{C_0}=(9/2)\kappa_*J_1\). Substitution in the full rational root proves its limit. Because \(1-u+\log u<0\), HC11 tends to zero exponentially on the scale \(a^{-3}\). Thus local curvature bounds growing as \(o(a^{-3/2})\) cannot cover a nonvanishing actual-vacuum mass through the exact holonomy map. This establishes a precise constraint on the S6/NS-inspired smooth carrier; it does not end the construction problem.

\subsection*{4. An exact smooth family at the required non-Abelian scale}

Fix a reference length \(\ell>0\) in the original spatial coordinates, and any smooth compactly supported one-form \(A=\sum A_d dx^d\). Keep
\[
 t_j=(\ell/a_j)^{3/4},\quad \delta_j=a_jt_j=\ell^{3/4}a_j^{1/4},\qquad
 A^{(j)}=t_jA,\qquad
 F^{(j)}_{dk}=t_j(\partial_dA_k-\partial_kA_d)+t_j^2[A_d,A_k].
 \tag{HC13}
\]
Both terms in this exact curvature formula remain; the reference length makes \(t_j\) dimensionless. This family changes the connection input, not the original lattice spacing, Hamiltonian, coupling or observable.

Choose a fixed compact neighborhood containing all faces meeting the support of \(f\) for sufficiently large \(j\). Let \(M=\max_d\sup\|A_d\|_{\rm op}\) and \(L_A=\max_{d,k}\sup\|\partial_k A_d\|_{\rm op}\) on this neighborhood. For a face centered at \(x_p\), each point on its four edges differs from \(x_p\) by coordinate distances whose sum is at most \(a_j\). The unitary Duhamel estimate for HC3 bounds each exact edge transport's difference from \(\exp(\delta_j A_d(x_p))\), or its corresponding inverse, by \(t_ja_j^2L_A\). Telescoping all four unitary factors gives error at most \(4t_ja_j^2L_A\) relative to the full constant-coefficient group commutator.

For \(X,Y\in\mathfrak{su}(2)\), set \(P(s)=e^{sX}e^{sY}e^{-sX}e^{-sY}\). Direct differentiation gives \(P(0)=I\), \(P'(0)=0\), \(P''(0)=2[X,Y]\). Its third derivative is the sum of the four-factor Leibniz terms; unitarity and the multinomial formula give \(\|P'''(s)\|_{\rm op}\le(2\|X\|_{\rm op}+2\|Y\|_{\rm op})^3\le64M^3\). The integral Taylor remainder is \(\int_0^{\delta}(\delta-s)^2P'''(s)ds/2\), whose norm is at most \(32M^3\delta^3/3\). Consequently the exact original face satisfies
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 C_p=[A_d(x_p),A_k(x_p)],\qquad
 U_p(A^{(j)})=I+\delta_j^2C_p+R_{p,j},\\
 \|R_{p,j}\|_{\rm op}\le r_j
 :=\frac{32}{3}M^3\delta_j^3+4t_ja_j^2L_A .
 \end{gathered}\tag{HC14}
\]
Here \(R_{p,j}\) is defined by the exact equality. The proof retains the full derivative error, four ordered transports and integral Taylor remainder. In particular it has not replaced the Wilson face by an exponential of curvature.

The exact deficit and a bound on its complete signed remainder are
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 D_p(A^{(j)})
 =\frac{\delta_j^4}{4}|C_p|^2
 +\delta_j^2\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}(C_p^*R_{p,j})
 +\tfrac12\|R_{p,j}\|_{\mathrm F}^2,\\
 \left|D_p(A^{(j)})-\frac{\ell^3a_j}{4}|C_p|^2\right|
 \le4M^2\delta_j^2r_j+r_j^2 .
 \end{gathered}\tag{HC15}
\]
Indeed \(\|C_p\|_{\rm op}\le2M^2\), and a two-by-two matrix has \(\|R\|_{\mathrm F}\le\sqrt2\|R\|_{\rm op}\). Insert these inequalities in the displayed full square; its mixed term is kept before taking the absolute bound. Because \(\delta_j^4=\ell^3a_j\), the remainder divided by \(a_j\) tends to zero, with leading bound of order \(a_j^{1/4}\) and every coefficient explicit in HC14–HC15.

For every original signed \(f\), therefore,
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \left|a_jC_{f,j}(\operatorname{Hol}_j A^{(j)})
 -\frac{\ell^3}{4}a_j^3\sum_{p}f(x_{p,j})
                 |[A_{d_p}(x_{p,j}),A_{k_p}(x_{p,j})]|^2\right|
 \le a_j^2A_{1,j}(4M^2\delta_j^2r_j+r_j^2),\\
 \lim_j a_jC_{f,j}(\operatorname{Hol}_j A^{(j)})
 =\mathcal R_A(f):=\frac{\ell^3}{4}\int_{\mathbb R^3}
 f(x)\sum_{d<k}|[A_d(x),A_k(x)]|^2\,d^3x .
 \end{gathered}\tag{HC16}
\]
The error tends to zero because \(a_j^3A_{1,j}\to3J_1\) and the remaining deficit error divided by \(a_j\) tends to zero. For the Riemann sum, each orientation's face centers form a translated cubic mesh with cell volume \(a_j^3\). On a fixed compact neighborhood the integrand is uniformly continuous, so the difference from its cell integral is bounded by that neighborhood's volume times its modulus of continuity at \(\sqrt3a_j\). The box contains it eventually since \(a_jL_j=j^3/100\to\infty\). This proves the stated limit, with each of the three orientations retained individually. Replacing \(f\) by \(\lvert f\rvert\) gives the absolute receiver, and polarization of the exact deterministic values gives every product of these scalar receivers. No random law or vacuum covariance is assigned by this construction. The proof uses only the fixed compact neighborhood of the support of the test function. Thus HC14–HC16 also apply to any smooth connection on that neighborhood with the stated finite bounds, including the homogeneous connection below, irrespective of its behavior outside the neighborhood.

In a region where \(A_i=\lambda_iT_i\), all original derivative terms in HC13 vanish there and
\[
 \sum_{d<k}|[A_d,A_k]|^2=\sum_{d<k}\lambda_d^2\lambda_k^2,\qquad
 \mathcal R_A(f)=\frac{\ell^3}{4}
       \left(\sum_{d<k}\lambda_d^2\lambda_k^2\right)\int f
 \quad(\operatorname{supp}f\text{ inside that region}).
 \tag{HC17}
\]
Any three constants are realized on such a region by a smooth compactly supported one-form. If the retained divergence-free three-colour profile is wanted, take a smooth cutoff equal to one on a larger region, set vector potential \(V^{(i)}=\tfrac12\chi(x)(e_i\times x)\), and put \(u^{(i)}=\nabla\times V^{(i)}\). Then \(\nabla\cdot u^{(i)}=0\) by cancellation of mixed second derivatives and \(u^{(i)}=e_i\) where \(\chi=1\), by direct differentiation of the cross product. The connection \(A_d=\sum_i\lambda_i u_d^{(i)}T_i\) has precisely that core, with all cutoff contributions kept by HC13–HC16 outside it. This is a direct receiving construction from the existing three-colour profile space. It has a nonzero non-Abelian density whenever two of its core coefficients are nonzero.

\subsection*{5. The exact source and a globally smooth dynamical comparison}

Use the original Minkowski coordinate \(x^0=ct\), metric \(\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)\), temporal gauge \(A_0=0\), and \(D_\mu=\partial_\mu+[A_\mu,\cdot]\). For the static compact family HC13, the full source is
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 (D^\mu F_{\mu0})^{(j)}&=0,\\
 (D^\mu F_{\mu i})^{(j)}
 &=t_j\sum_k\partial_k(\partial_kA_i-\partial_iA_k)\\
 &\quad+t_j^2\sum_k\{\partial_k[A_k,A_i]
                    +[A_k,\partial_kA_i-\partial_iA_k]\}\\
 &\quad+t_j^3\sum_k[A_k,[A_k,A_i]].
 \end{aligned}\tag{HC18}
\]
This follows by inserting HC13 into \(\sum_k(\partial_kF_{ki}^{(j)}+[t_jA_k,F_{ki}^{(j)}])\). On the constant core it equals \(-t_j^3\lambda_i\sum_{k\ne i}\lambda_k^2T_i\), because \([T_k,[T_k,T_i]]=-T_i\) for \(k\ne i\). Thus this static profile is generally sourced. Its zero electric initial datum does satisfy the exact Gauss constraint \(\sum_iD_iF_{0i}=0\); the temporal Yang–Mills equation prescribes the initial acceleration \(\partial_0^2A_i=\sum_kD_kF_{ki}\), including all three terms of HC18. This is the next dynamical equation, not a deletion of the static defect.

There is an explicit global source-free comparison on all of \(\mathbb R^{1+3}\). Let real \(q_i(\tau)\) solve
\[
 q_i''=-q_i\sum_{k\ne i}q_k^2,\qquad
 q_i(0)=\lambda_i,\quad q_i'(0)=0,
 \qquad
 \mathcal E_q=\tfrac12\sum_i(q_i')^2
                 +\tfrac12\sum_{i<k}q_i^2q_k^2 .
 \tag{HC19}
\]
Differentiation gives \(\mathcal E_q'=\sum_iq_i'(q_i''+q_i\sum_{k\ne i}q_k^2)=0\). Local existence and uniqueness follow by iteration of the integral equation for the six-component polynomial vector field on a bounded ball: its derivative is bounded there, so successive differences form a convergent geometric series for a sufficiently short interval. Conservation bounds each \(|q_i'|\le\sqrt{2\mathcal E_q(0)}\), hence on every finite interval \(|q_i(\tau)|\le|\lambda_i|+|\tau|\sqrt{2\mathcal E_q(0)}\). The vector field and its derivative stay bounded on that interval's resulting ball. The same local iteration then extends any putative finite endpoint, proving existence for all real \(\tau\). Differentiation of the equation proves smoothness of every order.

Define the exact homogeneous connection
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \mathscr A_0^{(j)}=0,\qquad
 \mathscr A_i^{(j)}(x^0,x)=t_jq_i(t_jx^0)T_i,\\
 \mathscr F_{0i}^{(j)}=t_j^2q_i'(t_jx^0)T_i,\qquad
 \mathscr F_{ki}^{(j)}=t_j^2q_k(t_jx^0)q_i(t_jx^0)[T_k,T_i],\\
 D^\mu\mathscr F_{\mu i}^{(j)}
 =t_j^3\left[-q_i''-q_i\sum_{k\ne i}q_k^2\right](t_jx^0)T_i=0,
 \qquad D^\mu\mathscr F_{\mu0}^{(j)}=0.
 \end{gathered}\tag{HC20}
\]
For the last equality, spatial derivatives vanish and each individual \([\mathscr A_i,\mathscr F_{0i}]\) is zero. All original signs of the Minkowski contraction are displayed. The connection is globally smooth at each regulator. When \(\mathcal E_q(0)>0\), its geometric energy density is the positive spatial constant \(t_j^4\mathcal E_q(0)\), so its total energy on \(\mathbb R^3\) is infinite. No finite-energy or physical-vacuum claim follows from this homogeneous solution.

At the precisely specified time \(x^0_j=\tau/t_j\), HC14–HC16 apply with \(A_i=q_i(\tau)T_i\), zero spatial derivative error, and yield
\[
 \lim_j a_j C_{f,j}(\operatorname{Hol}_j\mathscr A^{(j)}(\tau/t_j))
 =\frac{\ell^3}{4}\left(\sum_{d<k}q_d(\tau)^2q_k(\tau)^2\right)
          \int f(x)\,d^3x .
 \tag{HC21}
\]
The bound is uniform on compact \(\tau\)-intervals because the preceding ODE bounds make \(M\) uniform there. The original physical time \(x^0=ct\) is still retained in HC20: HC21 explicitly samples \(t=\tau/(ct_j)\), and is not a fixed-physical-time limit. At fixed nonzero physical time the argument \(t_jx^0\) diverges, so no unproved time limit is assigned.

HC6–HC12 construct the exact smooth-preimage map and its actual-vacuum curvature constraint. HC13–HC17 then produce non-Abelian smooth families with a finite nonzero receiver of the original signed observable, retaining their full finite errors. HC18–HC21 calculate their source and an exact global dynamical comparison. Matching these classical receiving data to the actual interacting ground-state law, constructing the compact-support global state with the required limiting time behavior, and proving the reconstruction axioms remain active calculations. Neither a curvature obstruction nor this explicit classical construction is substituted for the no-gap quantum endpoint.

\subsection*{6. Exact finite identities behind the illustration}

The illustration uses the dimensionless test
\(f(x)=\prod_{d=1}^3(1-2|x_d|)_+\), original origin \(o=0\),
\(\kappa_*=\ell=R=1\), \(u=1/2\), and a connection whose constant core
contains \([-1,1]^3\), with \((\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3)=(1,0.8,0.6)\).
Its support lies in the original cube \([-1/2,1/2]^3\);
\(F_f=1\) and \(\int f=1/8\), by integrating each of its three factors.
For \(j\ge4\), every face with nonzero coefficient lies in the constant
core. Thus each of its four original edge transports is exactly a
constant matrix exponential.

For \(d\ne k\), set \(\alpha=\delta_j\lambda_d/2\) and
\(\beta=\delta_j\lambda_k/2\). Since \(T_d^2=-I/4\),
\(\exp(\delta_j\lambda_dT_d)=\cos\alpha I+2\sin\alpha T_d\).
Multiplying its conjugation of \(T_k\), using
\(T_dT_k=-T_kT_d\), gives
\(\cos(2\alpha)T_k+\sin(2\alpha)[T_d,T_k]\).
The trace pairing with \(T_k\) is \(-\cos(2\alpha)/2\);
the commutator is orthogonal to \(T_k\). Both single \(T_k\)
terms have trace zero. Hence the complete ordered product gives
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \operatorname{Tr}
 \big(e^{\delta_j\lambda_dT_d}e^{\delta_j\lambda_kT_k}
      e^{-\delta_j\lambda_dT_d}e^{-\delta_j\lambda_kT_k}\big)
 =2\cos^2\beta+2\sin^2\beta\cos(2\alpha),\\
 D_{dk,j}=4\sin^2(\delta_j\lambda_d/2)
                  \sin^2(\delta_j\lambda_k/2).
 \end{gathered}\tag{HC22}
\]
This is the exact four-link deficit, with no remainder removed.

Put \(N=50j\), so \(a_j=1/(2N)\). The integer and half-integer
one-dimensional face meshes have the exact sums
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \sum_{r\in\mathbb Z}(1-|r|/N)_+
 =1+2\sum_{r=1}^N(1-r/N)=N,\\
 \sum_{r\in\mathbb Z}(1-|r+1/2|/N)_+
 =2\sum_{r=0}^{N-1}(1-(r+1/2)/N)=N.
 \end{gathered}\tag{HC23}
\]
The displayed finite sums evaluate by
\(\sum_{r=1}^Nr=N(N+1)/2\) and
\(\sum_{r=0}^{N-1}(r+1/2)=N^2/2\).
Each face orientation has two half-shifted coordinates and one integer
coordinate. Its weighted sum is therefore \(N^3\), and
\(A_{1,j}=3N^3=3/(8a_j^3)\). The original box contains every nonzero
term for \(j\ge4\). A fitting patch has lower corner
\(v_d=j^4-50j-1\) and \(q=100j+3\), so both original boundary indicators
are one in every direction; all counts in HC9 remain exact.
Consequently the plotted observable and its limit are
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 a_jC_{f,j}(\operatorname{Hol}_j(t_jA))
 =\frac1{8a_j}\sum_{d<k}D_{dk,j},\\
 \lim_j a_jC_{f,j}(\operatorname{Hol}_j(t_jA))
 =\frac1{32}\sum_{d<k}\lambda_d^2\lambda_k^2
 =0.03845 .
 \end{gathered}\tag{HC24}
\]
The first equality uses \(a_j^2N^3=1/(8a_j)\).
The limit follows from \(\sin x/x\to1\) with
\(\delta_j^4=a_j\). The absolute curvature cutoff in the other panel
uses the complete finite formula HC9–HC10. Its scaled limit follows
from HC12, with \(E_{\max}=33\), \(C_0=81/(16\cdot64)\).

\subsection*{HCR1. Exact gauge-convention dictionary}

The programme Section 2.1 retains the endpoint rule below. Its
corresponding connection action is displayed alongside it and is proved
by the dictionary in this section:

\[
 \operatorname{Hol}(A^g)_e=g(s(e))^{-1}\operatorname{Hol}(A)_e g(t(e)),
 \qquad A^g=g^{-1}Ag+g^{-1}dg.
\tag{HCR1.1}
\]

HC5 retains

\[
 A^h=hAh^{-1}-(dh)h^{-1},\qquad
 \operatorname{Hol}(A^h)_e=h(s(e))\operatorname{Hol}(A)_e h(t(e))^{-1}.
\tag{HCR1.2}
\]

The exact map is h=g⁻¹, a smooth bijection on the space of smooth
SU(2)-valued gauge functions, with the same inverse. Differentiating
gg⁻¹=I gives d(g⁻¹)=−g⁻¹(dg)g⁻¹. Substitution in every term of
(HCR1.2) therefore gives

\[
 hAh^{-1}-(dh)h^{-1}
 =g^{-1}Ag+g^{-1}dg,
 \qquad h(s)Uh(t)^{-1}=g(s)^{-1}Ug(t).
\tag{HCR1.3}
\]

The two original expressions remain individually identifiable. This
map also respects their action conventions: if Hh denotes (HCR1.2),
then Hh₂∘Hh₁=Hh₂h₁ by direct substitution, while Gg₂∘Gg₁=Gg₁g₂ for
(HCR1.1). Inversion sends (g₁g₂)⁻¹ to g₂⁻¹g₁⁻¹, exactly the required
composition. Restriction to the original finite vertex set commutes
with inversion. Thus the two endpoint actions and their curvature
conjugations agree through a proved map, without identifying g and h
as the same gauge parameter.

The right multiplication ODE U′=UA is consistent with these formulas:
for V(s)=h(x)U(s)h(x+se\_d)⁻¹, differentiating gives
V′=V[hAh⁻¹−(∂dh)h⁻¹] at the moving point, and V(0)=I. This proves
the HC5 endpoint rule by uniqueness of the linear ODE. The curvature
sign is the original plus commutator in Fdk=∂dAk−∂kAd+[Ad,Ak].

The companion HC proof includes this exact dictionary; both original conventions and every sign are retained.

\subsection*{HCR2. Exact holonomy, section, curvature and coefficient checks}

HC1–HC6. For X=x·T with Tα=−iσα/2, the two eigenvalues are
±i|x|/2, and −2Tr X²=|x|². Consequently ||X||F²=|X|²/2 and ||X||op=|X|/2; these are the factors used subsequently. The linear
edge ODE preserves UU*=I, and then det U=1 follows by differentiating
the determinant with trace A=0. Its ordered integral series converges
absolutely on any finite edge. Variation between two skew-Hermitian
coefficients gives the norm bound ∫||A−B|| because the propagators on
both sides of the integrand are unitary. This proves the stated
holonomy continuity in the original coefficients.

The tubes in HC6 can be chosen pairwise disjoint. Their axes are middle
halves of distinct original cubic edges; they stay at distance at
least a/4 from other edges, and a radius smaller than a/8 suffices.
Longitudinal bumps vanish near the tube endpoints, so the forms extend
smoothly by zero. On its own edge the form is a scalar function times
the single constant Xe, and it is zero on every other edge. Its exact
ordered exponential is therefore exp Xe. The formula for the
logarithm away from ±I, and the two specified endpoint values, give a
Borel logarithm on SU(2), hence a Borel section into the finite linear
span of these smooth forms. Curvature is a quadratic polynomial in
those coefficients, with fixed smooth coefficient functions. Its sup
norm on each compact face depends continuously on the coefficients;
the maximum over finitely many relevant faces does as well. These
facts justify the section and measurability used in HC10–HC11.

HC7. The two-stage axial gauge solves ∂kh₀=h₀Ak on the left edge,
then ∂dh=hAd on each horizontal segment. It gives Ad\textasciicircum{}h=0 on the square
and Ak\textasciicircum{}h=0 on the left edge, so Fdk\textasciicircum{}h=∂dAk\textasciicircum{}h. The other three face
transport factors are exactly I. Hence

\[
 \|U_p-I\|_F\le\int_p\|F_{dk}^h\|_F
 =\frac1{\sqrt2}\int_p|F_{dk}|,
 \qquad
 D_p=\frac12\|I-U_p\|_F^2
 \le\frac14\left(\int_p|F_{dk}|\right)^2.
\tag{HCR2.1}
\]

The original 1/4 is correct and requires no small-field assumption.
Only a smooth gauge on the square is needed for this proof; no global
gauge choice or global axial gauge existence is being asserted.

HC8–HC12. Original BM4–BM9 and BM53–BM56 were checked in their
LaTeX source. The definitions e=Ff(E₀−Eout)/b, c=9α/64, Ce=4cA₁²,
Be=e+4cA₁, p₀=3A₁/(8Ff) agree exactly. The rational smaller-root
formula decreases with e: its denominator is Be+√(Be²−4(1+c)Ce),
both terms increasing for its strictly positive discriminant. Thus
the explicit larger energy bound gives the smaller valid lower

replace its actual law by a comparison density.

For completeness, in the eventual interior patch C\_Q=12q(q+1) and
√(N\_QM\_Q)=3q\textasciicircum{}(3/2)(q+1)\textasciicircum{}(3/2). With g²=κ*a/2 and aq→R,

\[

\subsection*{HCR3. Stronger actual-vacuum curvature conclusion}

The HC lower tail yields an almost-sure conclusion under any joint
coupling of its original marginal vacuum laws; no independence is
needed. This is an additional consequence of the actual-state result,
not a claim that a particular continuum coupling has been constructed.

Let (Uj) have any probability law with marginal μj at each j. For fixed
0<u<1, define Ej,u=\{Yj(Uj)≤u r̄j\}. Since a\_j=(100j)⁻¹ and
a\_j³p₀,j→9J₁/(8Ff)>0, the upper bound in HC9 implies

\[
 \sum_j\mathbb P(E_{j,u})<\infty.
\tag{HCR3.1}
\]

Indeed the summands for all sufficiently large j are at most exp(−cuj³)
for a fixed cu>0, and their series converges by comparison with a
geometric series. The union bound gives
P(∪j≥NEj,u)≤∑j≥NP(Ej,u)→0; hence with probability one only finitely
many Ej,u occur. On the complementary event, HC8 gives, simultaneously
for every smooth A with Holj(A)=Uj,
Kf,j(A)>Kcut\_j,u. Intersect these probability-one events for a countable
sequence of rational u increasing to 1 and use HC12. The result is

\[
 \boxed{\begin{gathered}
 \text{For almost every }(U_j),\\
 \text{ every smooth-preimage sequence }A_j\text{ satisfies }\\
 \liminf_j a_j^{3/2}K_{f,j}(A_j)
 \ge\sqrt{\frac{4\bar R_-}{3J_1}}>0.
 \end{gathered}}
\tag{HCR3.2}
\]

The quantifier over all preimages is allowed because the deterministic
event inclusion already holds for all preimages. No measurable choice
of that sequence is needed for this pathwise assertion. The random
event used in the proof is the countable intersection built from the
measurable Yj events.

For any measurable preimage choice and every p>0, the finite bound
E[K\textasciicircum{}p]≥(Kcut\_j,u)\textasciicircum{}p[1−P(Ej,u)] gives further

\[
 \liminf_j a_j^{3p/2}\mathbb E[K_{f,j}(A_j)^p]
 \ge\left(\frac{4\bar R_-}{3J_1}\right)^{p/2}.
\tag{HCR3.3}
\]

This follows by taking the lower limit for fixed u and then increasing
u to 1; the expectation may be infinite. Both statements retain the
same original marginal vacuum laws and the same holonomy map.

\subsection*{HCR4. Compact three-colour construction and nonzero signed receiver}

For a constant vector e\_i, direct differentiation gives
curl(e\_i×x)=2e\_i. Thus Vi=(1/2)χ(e\_i×x) yields ui=curl Vi=ei in the
region where χ=1, while it is smooth, compactly supported, and has
divergence zero everywhere by commutation of second derivatives.
For Ad=∑iλiui\_dTi this gives the stated core Ad=λdTd, with all cutoff
terms retained outside. The commutator norm is λd²λk² because
[Td,Tk] is the remaining unit generator up to sign. HC17 is exact.

There is also a constructive nonvanishing statement for every nonzero
original real continuous compactly supported f, including ∫f=0.
Choose a point where f is nonzero and a ball B on which f has its
fixed sign ε and |f|≥c>0. Choose a smaller ball B₀ compactly contained
in B and a smooth cutoff χ supported in B, equal to one on B₀. Use
the preceding curl construction with all three original calibrations
λ₁, λ₂, λ₃ nonzero. All Ad and their
commutators vanish outside B, their full squared commutator sum is
nonnegative everywhere, and on B₀ its value is
λ₁²λ₂²+λ₁²λ₃²+λ₂²λ₃². Hence

\[
 \varepsilon\mathcal R_A(f)
 \ge\frac{\ell^3}{4}c(\lambda_1^2\lambda_2^2+
 \lambda_1^2\lambda_3^2+\lambda_2^2\lambda_3^2)\operatorname{Vol}(B_0)>0.
\tag{HCR4.1}
\]

This preserves the original signed f and all cutoff
contributions. It does not require replacing f by its positive part
in the observable. At the core the curvature magnitude is exactly
t²|λ₁λ₂|=ell\textasciicircum{}(3/2)a\textasciicircum{}(−3/2)|λ₁λ₂|, establishing the stated scale for
this concrete family.

\subsection*{HCR5. Static source and global ODE with all signs}

For Fki\textasciicircum{}(j)=t(∂kAi−∂iAk)+t²[Ak,Ai], application of
∂k+[tAk,·] produces exactly the t, t² and t³ terms in HC18. On the

[Tk,[Tk,Ti]]=−Ti for k≠i, so its source is
−t³λi∑k≠iλk²Ti. In temporal gauge with metric (−,+,+,+),

∂₀²Ai=∑kDkFki, with the sign in HC18. The initial electric field is

For completeness, an elementary quantified existence argument for

\[
 y=(q,p),\qquad
 F(y)=\left(p,\left(-q_i\sum_{k\ne i}q_k^2\right)_{i=1}^3\right).
 \tag{HCR5.1}

In the supremum norm on
a ball |y|∞≤R, one has |F(y)|∞≤max(R,2R³) and ||DF(y)||∞≤max(1,6R²). Around an initial point y₀ choose
R>|y₀|∞+1 and an interval length h for which h max(R,2R³)≤1 and

y(τ)=y₀+∫₀\textasciicircum{}τF(y(s))ds maps the closed radius-one continuous-function
ball into itself and reduces successive differences by at least 1/2.
The resulting uniformly convergent iterates solve the integral
equation. The same difference estimate proves uniqueness. The equation
then implies differentiability and, by repeated differentiation,

The exact conserved quantity is
Eq=(1/2)∑p\_i²+(1/2)∑i<kqi²qk²: its derivative is
∑ipi[pi′+qi∑k≠iqk²]=0. Thus |p\_i|≤√(2Eq(0)) and |q\_i(τ)|≤|λi|+|τ|√(2Eq(0)). On any finite interval these give a fixed
ball and hence a uniform local existence interval h. Approaching any
putative finite endpoint, bounded F also makes y uniformly Lipschitz,

of q for all time is assumed for general initial data.

For A\_i=tqi(tx⁰)Ti the two curvature formulas in HC20 follow by direct

\subsection*{HCR6. Exact homogeneous face formula}

For the same homogeneous connection at any given time, let qd,qk be
its two real scalar values and let δ=at. Its exact face is
e\textasciicircum{}(δqdTd)e\textasciicircum{}(δqkTk)e\textasciicircum{}(−δqdTd)e\textasciicircum{}(−δqkTk), d≠k. The identity

holds at every finite a, without a remainder. To prove it, write
exp(αTd)=cos(α/2)I+2sin(α/2)Td. Its adjoint action rotates Tk by
angle α about e\_d, so the inner product of Ad\_exp(αTd)Tk with Tk is

exp(αTd)exp(βTk)exp(−αTd)exp(−βTk) is therefore
cos²(β/2)+sin²(β/2)cosα
=1−2sin²(α/2)sin²(β/2). Taking its two-dimensional trace and
subtracting from 2 proves (HCR6.1), including all angle and trace factors.
The adjoint rotation identity can equivalently be checked by multiplying
TiTk=−δikI/4+(1/2)εikℓTℓ twice.

This directly checks HC15's leading term
δ⁴qd²qk²/4 and gives a stronger finite receiver in the homogeneous

\subsection*{HCR7. Periodic isotropic solution and the full fixed-time accumulation set}

Take λ₁=λ₂=λ₃=λ>0 with the same zero velocities as HC19. Permuting
coordinates preserves the ODE and its initial data, so uniqueness gives
q₁=q₂=q₃=q. The exact scalar equation and conserved identity are

\[
 q''=-2q^3,\qquad q(0)=\lambda,\quad q'(0)=0,
 \qquad (q')^2+q^4=\lambda^4.
\tag{HCR7.1}
\]

While 0<q<λ after time zero, q′ is negative because q″<0 until the
first crossing. Its first zero occurs at

\[
 Q=\int_0^\lambda\frac{ds}{\sqrt{\lambda^4-s^4}}
   =\frac1\lambda\int_0^1\frac{du}{\sqrt{1-u^4}}<\infty.
\tag{HCR7.2}
\]

Indeed q′=−√(λ⁴−q⁴) there, giving the integral by separation. Its
integrability at λ follows from λ⁴−s⁴=(λ−s)(λ³+λ²s+λs²+s³), and
the other endpoint has nonzero denominator. The global solution
cannot stay positive forever: if its positive decreasing limit were
positive, q″ would stay strictly negative; if its limit were zero,
the energy identity would make q′ tend to −λ². Either contradicts
remaining positive for all time. Thus the crossing and its integral
are established, with q′(Q)=−λ².

The equation is odd in q and invariant under time reflection. Uniqueness
at the zero state implies q(Q+s)=−q(Q−s); hence q(2Q)=−λ and
q′(2Q)=0. Applying uniqueness again gives q(2Q+s)=−q(s), and therefore
q(4Q+s)=q(s). Thus P=4Q is a period. The trajectory decreases strictly
from λ to −λ on (0,2Q) and increases strictly on (2Q,4Q), so no smaller
positive period exists for q. In particular q takes every value in
[−λ,λ], and q⁴ takes every value in [0,λ⁴].

At any fixed nonzero original x⁰=ctphysical, the sampled argument is

\[
 \tau_j=t_jx^0=x^0(100\ell)^{3/4}j^{3/4}.
\tag{HCR7.3}
\]

The absolute values θj=|τj| increase to infinity, and
θj+1−θj→0, by the mean-value theorem applied to x\textasciicircum{}(3/4). For any target
phase r∈[0,P), choose the least j\_m with θj\_m≥mP+r. Then j\_m→∞ and
0≤θj\_m−(mP+r)≤θj\_m−θj\_m−1→0. Periodicity and continuity imply
q(θj\_m)\textasciicircum{}4→q(r)\textasciicircum{}4. The initial zero derivative and uniqueness give
q(−τ)=q(τ), so negative x⁰ has exactly the same conclusion. Thus the
set of subsequential limits of q(τj)\textasciicircum{}4 is the whole [0,λ⁴].

This time statement passes through the original finite receiver with a
uniform error. Since |q(τ)|≤λ at every real time, HC14–HC16 apply
uniformly with M=λ/2 and LA=0. More directly, every face has the exact
deficit 4sin⁴(δjq(τj)/2) by HCR6, so

\[
 a_jC_{f,j}
 =4a_j^2\sin^4\!\left(\frac{\delta_jq(\tau_j)}2\right)\sum_pf_p
 =\frac{3\ell^3}{4}\,q(\tau_j)^4\int f+o(1),
\tag{HCR7.4}
\]

where the error is uniform in the full range |q|≤λ. The last equality
uses δj⁴=ell³aj, the original three-orientation Riemann sum
aj³∑pfp→3∫f, and the uniform Taylor limit sin z/z→1 at zero, defining
it as 1 at zero. Thus at every fixed nonzero physical time the complete
accumulation set of the original signed receiver is

\[
 \boxed{\left[
 \min\!\left(0,\frac{3\ell^3\lambda^4}{4}\int f\right),
 \max\!\left(0,\frac{3\ell^3\lambda^4}{4}\int f\right)
 \right].}
\tag{HCR7.5}
\]

When ∫f≠0 the receiver therefore has no fixed-nonzero-physical-time
limit. When ∫f=0 it tends to zero uniformly in this homogeneous
isotropic subfamily. At physical time zero its limit instead is
(3ell³λ⁴/4)∫f. All statements concern the exact classical source-free
homogeneous comparison with its infinite spatial energy. They do not
provide an actual vacuum law or the compact-support evolution sought
by the programme.
